0.title: Hosea: How Can I Give You Up?
0.overview:
The message. Hosea is the story of a love that will not let go. God had bound himself to Israel as a husband to his bride, and Israel had run after other gods as an unfaithful wife runs after lovers. So God told his prophet to marry a woman who would betray him, then to love her again and buy her back, so that Israel could see in one broken home what its sin had done to God, and what God would do about it. Judgment is real: a people who “sow the wind” will “reap the whirlwind” (8:7). But beneath the judgment beats a heart that cries, “How can I give you up, O Ephraim?” (11:8), and the last word is a promise: “I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely” (14:4).

Background: the writer. We know Hosea only from his book. His name means “salvation”, close kin to the names Joshua and Jesus, “the LORD saves”. He seems to have been a northerner, speaking to his own nation: he calls Israel’s ruler “our king” (7:5). Jews and Christians have always received the book as his. Many modern scholars think editors in Judah added the lines about Judah and some promises, such as “David their king” (3:5). But warning and promise are woven together all through the book, as in the prophet’s own marriage, and this commentary takes it as Hosea’s own message, probably carried south to Judah when the north fell, which may be why its heading names Judah’s kings first (1:1).

When and where. Hosea preached to the northern kingdom of Israel, often called Ephraim after its leading tribe, from about 755 BC to about 715 BC. He began under Jeroboam II, when Israel was rich and strong; God had even let Jeroboam restore its old borders (2 Kings 14:25). In the thirty years after Jeroboam died, about 753 BC, six kings reigned in Samaria and four of them were murdered by the men who took their thrones: “All their kings have fallen, and none of them calls upon me” (7:7). As Assyria rose, Israel’s kings paid it tribute (2 Kings 15:19) or begged Egypt for help, and Hosea mocked them as “a dove, silly and without sense, calling to Egypt, going to Assyria” (7:11). The last king, Hoshea (not the prophet), rebelled against Assyria, and after a three-year siege Samaria fell in 722 BC and its people were carried away to Assyria (2 Kings 17:5–6). Amos had preached in the north just before him; Isaiah and Micah preached in Judah.

The first hearers. Israel was busily religious. As its fruit increased, “the more altars he built” (10:1). But ever since Jeroboam son of Nebat set up golden calves at Bethel and Dan nearly two centuries earlier (1 Kings 12:28–29), its worship had been mixed, and by Hosea’s day many served Baal, the Canaanite god of storm and rain. They thanked Baal for their harvests, not knowing “that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil” (2:8), and its hilltop shrines had cult prostitutes (4:14). Hosea calls Bethel, “house of God”, Beth-aven, “house of wickedness” (4:15). The root of its sickness: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” (4:6).

The kind of writing. Hosea is prophecy, almost all of it poetry, and its Hebrew is among the hardest in the Old Testament, so translations differ in places. Much of it is a covenant lawsuit: “the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land” (4:1). It speaks in vivid pictures: God as husband, father, lion and dew; Israel as an unfaithful wife, “a cake not turned” (7:8), a stubborn heifer. The marriage language is blunt; the threat to strip an unfaithful wife (2:3) describes God’s judgment on a nation, never a pattern for any husband; anyone harmed by a spouse should seek safety at once.

How the book makes its case. The marriage comes first (1–3). Hosea marries Gomer, and their children’s names announce judgment: Jezreel, No Mercy and Not My People (1). God charges his unfaithful wife, then promises to “allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her” (2:14) and betroth her to himself for ever (2). Hosea buys his wife back, a picture of Israel’s discipline and return (3). Then come the sermons (4–14), in three rounds, each moving from charge to hope. The first (4–7) exposes a people without knowledge of God, whose love is “like a morning cloud” (6:4), while God says, “I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings” (6:6). The second (8–11) traces kings, calves and alliances to exile, and ends with the father who taught his son to walk and cannot give him up (11). The third (11:12–14:9) holds up Jacob as a mirror and faces death itself, before the final call, “Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God” (14:1), with words of confession God himself supplies.

Did God tell a prophet to marry a prostitute? God’s command, “take to yourself a wife of whoredom” (1:2), has troubled readers in every age. Some think Gomer was already immoral, perhaps a shrine prostitute, and that the shock was the point. Some, John Calvin among them, thought it happened only in a vision or parable. Others read “a wife of whoredom” as naming Gomer by what she would become, just as Israel began with “the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride” (Jeremiah 2:2) and fell later. This commentary’s view is that the marriage was real, with a named wife, named children and a price paid in silver and barley (3:2), and that Gomer was faithful when Hosea married her and fell afterwards. God did not command his prophet to sin; he commanded him to love a woman who would betray him, as God loves us.

Where it leads: to Christ. Hosea leads to Christ by covenant, by pattern and by promise. The covenant is a marriage, and the husband pays to win back his bride. Christ “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25), and his people were ransomed not with silver or gold “but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:19). The pattern is the son: “out of Egypt I called my son” (11:1). Matthew saw it fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 2:15), the true Son who lived out Israel’s story without failing. The promises reach him too: Paul hears in the reversed names the gospel going out to the Gentiles (Romans 9:25–26), and Peter tells the church, “once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Peter 2:10). Hosea’s “O Sheol, where is your sting?” (13:14) becomes Paul’s song over the empty tomb (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). And Jesus took Hosea’s words on his lips when he ate with sinners: “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice’” (Matthew 9:13). At the cross the love that cried, “My heart recoils within me” (11:8), found its way: the Son bore the anger his people deserved, so that God could be just and still not give them up.

For us. Hosea shows that sin is not only breaking rules but breaking the heart of one who loves us. We do what Israel did, looking to other lovers, such as money, comfort and approval, for what only God gives. Timothy Keller often pointed out that the gospel tells us we are more sinful than we ever dared believe and more loved than we ever dared hope; Hosea tells that story in a marriage. God knows what we have done, and in Christ he has paid the price to bring us home. Come back to him with the words he gives, and find that “the ways of the LORD are right” (14:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hosea’s marriage is God’s own sermon: what Israel has done to the LORD is adultery. The heading sets the scene in the last prosperous decades of the northern kingdom, under Jeroboam II, and the list of Judah’s kings shows how long the prophet laboured, probably until Samaria fell (v. 1). Then the first word God speaks through Hosea is a command that takes over his home: marry a woman who will be unfaithful and raise a family that will carry the shame, “for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD” (v. 2). The prophet will preach with his life before he preaches with his lips, and will feel in his own heart something of what Israel’s sin has done to God.
verseByVerse.theology: God's people forsaking him is spiritual adultery, and God makes his prophet's own home the sermon.

verseByVerse.quote: The word of the LORD that came to Hosea, the son of Beeri, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What follows is the LORD’s word, spoken through Hosea to the northern kingdom in its last prosperous years before its fall.

The word of the LORD that came to Hosea. The book names its source at once: the word came to Hosea; he did not invent it. He is the first of the twelve Minor Prophets, “minor” for their length, not their importance, and he preached to the northern kingdom, Israel, with its capital Samaria.

In the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash. Hosea began under Jeroboam II, when Israel was prosperous and powerful; God had even let him restore Israel’s old borders (2 Kings 14:25). Yet Jeroboam “did what was evil in the sight of the LORD” (2 Kings 14:24), and the nation’s worship was mixed with golden calves and Baal (see the introduction).

Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. The kings of Judah show a ministry of several decades; Hosea probably lived to see Samaria fall to Assyria in 722 BC, “because the people of Israel had sinned against the LORD their God” (2 Kings 17:7). He was one of God’s last great warnings, and the warning was itself a mercy, pointing to the fuller Word still to come (Hebrews 1:1–2).
verseByVerse.note: Hosea prophesied to the northern kingdom (Israel, often called Ephraim) in its last decades, about 755–715 BC, through the fall of Samaria to Assyria in 722.

verseByVerse.quote: When the LORD first spoke through Hosea, the LORD said to Hosea, "Go, take to yourself a wife of whoredom and have children of whoredom, for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God told Hosea to marry a woman who would be unfaithful, so that his home would show Israel that its worship of other gods was adultery against the LORD.

When the LORD first spoke through Hosea. The very first word of his ministry is a command about his own home. The prophet will preach with his life before he preaches with his lips.

Take to yourself a wife of whoredom. One of the most shocking commands God ever gave a prophet. The reason follows at once: “for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD”. God had bound himself to Israel in a covenant, like a husband to a wife, so worshipping other gods was adultery. Hosea’s marriage would show what Israel had done to God and what God felt about it, and the prophet would feel that pain in his own home.

What this shows about God. God is not a distant, unfeeling ruler. He loves his people as a faithful husband loves his wife, and is grieved like a husband betrayed. Anyone betrayed by a husband or wife will feel this chapter sharply; Hosea does not make that wound small, but shows that God knows it from the inside, and, as the chapter’s end shows, does not let our unfaithfulness have the last word.

Who am I hurting? For many today that question is the whole of ethics. John Stuart Mill argued in On Liberty (1859) that the only good reason for restraining anyone against his will is to prevent harm to others, and most of us have absorbed it: if no one gets hurt, it is my business. It is a humane instinct, but it quietly assumes that there is no one else in the room. Hosea’s marriage says there is. Israel’s worship of Baal did not trample a neighbour’s field; it broke a husband’s heart. So sin is less like breaking a regulation than betraying a person, which is why it can be done in private and still wound. That changes what forgiveness must be too. A broken rule can be settled with a fine, but a betrayed love can only be healed if the one betrayed chooses to bear the hurt himself. That is exactly what God did. The one we wounded came to be wounded for us (Isaiah 53:5).

Where Christians differ: what kind of woman did Hosea marry, and did it really happen? Some think Gomer was already immoral, perhaps a shrine prostitute. Some, John Calvin among them, thought it a vision or parable, since a holy God could hardly command such a thing. Others read “a wife of whoredom” as naming her by what she would become. This commentary’s view: the book gives real names, real children and a real price paid (3:2), so the marriage was real. The likeliest reading is that Gomer was faithful when Hosea married her and fell later, just as Israel was devoted to the LORD at first, like a young bride, and fell away afterwards (Jeremiah 2:2–3). God did not command his prophet to sin; he commanded him to love a woman who would betray him, as God loves us.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea’s marriage to an unfaithful wife becomes a living picture of Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–9 — Jezreel, No Mercy, Not My People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three children are born, and each name takes Israel a step further down. Jezreel announces that the dynasty founded in bloodshed at Jezreel will end, and that Israel’s military strength will be broken in the same valley (vv. 3–5). No Mercy announces that God’s long patience with the north is over, though Judah will be spared, saved by the LORD and not by its weapons (vv. 6–7). Not My People reverses the heart of the covenant itself: “you are not my people, and I am not your God” (vv. 8–9). Judgment coming, patience ending, the bond broken: the names show where unfaithfulness leads when it is not turned from.
verseByVerse.theology: Persistent unfaithfulness brings God's judgment, and the covenant relationship itself is put under threat.

verseByVerse.quote: So he went and took Gomer, the daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son. And the LORD said to him, "Call his name Jezreel, for in just a little while I will punish the house of Jehu for the blood of Jezreel, and I will put an end to the kingdom of the house of Israel. And on that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hosea’s first son is named Jezreel, a name that announces the end of Jehu’s bloodstained dynasty and the breaking of Israel’s strength.

She conceived and bore him a son. Hosea obeyed. Gomer “bore him a son”; with the next two children the text does not say “him” (vv. 6, 8), and some wonder whether they were Hosea’s, though we cannot be sure. The names tell the story of a marriage, and a nation, coming apart.

Call his name Jezreel. Jezreel was a city and valley in northern Israel, and the name carried a dark memory. Nearly a century earlier, the commander Jehu had seized the throne and wiped out the family of wicked King Ahab at Jezreel in a bloodbath (2 Kings 9–10). Jeroboam II, the king in Hosea’s day, was Jehu’s great-grandson, so the boy’s name recalled the massacre on which the royal house was built.

For the blood of Jezreel. God had commanded Jehu to judge Ahab’s house (2 Kings 9:7) and even commended him for doing it (2 Kings 10:30). So why punish his family for that blood? Most likely because Jehu did the right thing in the wrong spirit, going far beyond what God commanded for his own political advantage: “Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of the LORD, the God of Israel, with all his heart” (2 Kings 10:31). God used Jehu’s sword, but he did not approve Jehu’s heart. It is possible to do God’s work and still be under God’s judgment for the way we do it.

In just a little while. Jeroboam’s son Zechariah reigned only six months before he was assassinated (2 Kings 15:8–10), ending Jehu’s dynasty; about thirty years later the kingdom itself was gone.

I will break the bow of Israel. The Valley of Jezreel was the great battlefield of northern Israel, and the bow stands for Israel’s military strength. All the power Jeroboam had built up would be broken in the valley where his dynasty began.

A purer zeal. Jehu’s zeal for the LORD (2 Kings 10:16) served his own ambition. Israel needed a king whose zeal was pure all the way down. Of Jesus it was written, “Zeal for your house will consume me” (John 2:17), and it consumed him, not his enemies.
verseByVerse.note: Jezreel recalls Jehu’s bloodbath there.

verseByVerse.quote: She conceived again and bore a daughter. And the LORD said to him, "Call her name No Mercy, for I will no more have mercy on the house of Israel, to forgive them at all. But I will have mercy on the house of Judah, and I will save them by the LORD their God. I will not save them by bow or by sword or by war or by horses or by horsemen."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second child’s name, No Mercy, announces that God’s long patience with the northern kingdom is at an end, while Judah will be spared and saved by God alone.

Call her name No Mercy. Imagine a father calling his little girl by that name every day. Each time, Israel heard that God’s patience, which had lasted for generations, was running out.

What mercy means here. The girl’s name is Lo-ruhamah, and its root, racham, is related to the Hebrew word for womb. It is the tender, gut-deep feeling of a mother for her baby: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb?” (Isaiah 49:15). So the name does not mean “no more favours” but something nearer to “I will no longer feel for you as a mother does.” See Mercy in the Theological Dictionary.

I will no more have mercy on the house of Israel. The LORD is “merciful and gracious, slow to anger”, yet he “will by no means clear the guilty” (Exodus 34:6–7). There comes a point when persistent, unrepentant sin meets the judgment it has been warned about.

But I will have mercy on the house of Judah. Judah would be spared for a time, saved by God, not by its armies: “I will not save them by bow or by sword”. That is what happened in 701 BC, when the Assyrian army surrounded Jerusalem and “the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians” (2 Kings 19:35). Jerusalem did not fire an arrow. That is always how God saves, “by the LORD their God”, not by our resources.

The unpitied one. Yet this is the very name God promises to reverse: “I will have mercy on No Mercy” (2:23). He did it by taking the place of the unpitied himself. On the cross his Son cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34), so that God, “being rich in mercy” (Ephesians 2:4), could take the forsaken in. If you fear you have worn out God’s patience, look at the cross.
verseByVerse.note: Lo-ruhamah means “she has not received mercy” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When she had weaned No Mercy, she conceived and bore a son. And the LORD said, "Call his name Not My People, for you are not my people, and I am not your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third name, Not My People, turns the covenant promise inside out: the relationship itself is broken.

When she had weaned No Mercy. Weaning took two or three years: years of room to repent, and still nothing changed in Israel.

You are not my people. At the heart of the covenant was a promise, “I will be your God, and you shall be my people” (Jeremiah 7:23). Now God speaks the reverse: “you are not my people, and I am not your God”. The ESV notes that the last phrase is literally “I am not yours”. It is the language of divorce.

A downward staircase. The three names form a downward staircase. Jezreel: judgment is coming. No Mercy: God’s patience is ending. Not My People: the relationship itself is broken. This is where unfaithfulness finally leads. The greatest punishment is not suffering but separation from God.

Only God can unsay it. If “Not my people” is ever to be reversed, God must do it, and the next verse says he will. In Christ he did, at the cost of his Son, forsaken so that those far off could be brought near (Ephesians 2:13).
verseByVerse.note: Lo-ammi means “not my people” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–11 — Children of the Living God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Grace has the last word, and it is greater than the judgment. Straight after “Not My People” comes “Yet”: the promise made to Abraham still stands, and Israel will be as countless as the sand of the sea (v. 10). In the very place where God said, “You are not my people,” he will call them “Children of the living God”. The divided kingdoms will be gathered under one head, and the name that meant slaughter will mean a harvest, for “great shall be the day of Jezreel” (v. 11). The New Testament hears this promise kept in Christ, the one head, who gathers Jews and Gentiles into God’s family.
verseByVerse.theology: God's last word is not rejection but adoption, fulfilled in the gospel that makes outsiders God's children.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet the number of the children of Israel shall be like the sand of the sea, which cannot be measured or numbered. And in the place where it was said to them, "You are not my people," it shall be said to them, "Children of the living God." And the children of Judah and the children of Israel shall be gathered together, and they shall appoint for themselves one head. And they shall go up from the land, for great shall be the day of Jezreel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after the worst name comes the promise of grace: God will make the disowned his children, countless as the sand, and gather them under one head. God’s last word to his people is not “Not mine” but “My children.”

Yet the number of the children of Israel. With no warning comes “Yet”: Israel will be as numerous as the sand of the sea, the very promise God made to Abraham (Genesis 22:17). Israel’s unfaithfulness has not cancelled it.

Children of the living God. In the very place where it was said, “You are not my people,” they will be called “Children of the living God”. (The ESV notes it may be “Sons”.) This is the rhythm of the whole book, and of the whole Bible: judgment, and then grace that is greater than the judgment.

They shall appoint for themselves one head. The divided kingdoms will be reunited under one leader, and chapter 3 names him: “David their king” (3:5), the promised descendant of David. The prophets spoke of him as “one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23). He is Jesus Christ, the Son of David, who gathers one people from every tribe and nation.

Great shall be the day of Jezreel. The name that meant judgment now means hope. The ESV notes at 2:22 that Jezreel means “God will sow”. The valley where Israel’s bow was broken becomes the field where God sows his people again: he turns the very place of shame into the place of blessing.

The names changed in Christ. The New Testament shows how far this promise reaches. Paul applies this verse to Gentiles brought into God’s family: “in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called ‘sons of the living God’” (Romans 9:26). Peter says the same to scattered believers: “Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Peter 2:10). Every Christian was once “Not My People” and “No Mercy”. In Christ, the names have been changed.

Words for Gentiles? Hosea was speaking about Israel, so how can Paul apply his words to Gentiles? Northern Israel, declared Not My People, had become no different from the nations. If God could make children again of those he had disowned, his mercy is not bound by birth or any claim people bring, and Paul follows that principle where it leads: God now calls Jews and Gentiles alike in Christ (Romans 9:24). He is not twisting Hosea, but showing how wide Hosea’s mercy is.

Where Christians differ: does this promise also look to a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ? Some read it with Romans 11:25–26 as foretelling a great ingathering of Jewish people; others take “all Israel” as the whole people of God; dispensationalists expect a restored national Israel under Christ’s earthly reign. This commentary’s view: all agree that the one head is Christ, and the promise is being fulfilled now as Jews and Gentiles are gathered to him. Romans 11 most naturally looks also for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ, within the one people of God, though this commentary does not press it.

Uncertain wording. “They shall go up from the land” is compressed. It may mean coming up out of exile, as Israel once came up out of Egypt, or springing up like a crop, which fits Jezreel, “God will sow”. Either way, the picture is of a people restored by God.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea 1:10–2:1 is 2:1–3 in the Hebrew numbering (ESV notes).

1.title: Not My People
1.overview:
Where we are. The book opens with its heading (v. 1) and goes straight into the prophet’s home. Chapters 1 to 3 tell the story of Hosea’s marriage, the key to all that follows; this chapter runs from his wedding to the birth of his third child.

The message. Israel’s worship of other gods is not a small religious slip but adultery against the God who bound himself to her, and it will end in judgment: the royal house will fall, God’s mercy will be withdrawn, and the covenant bond itself will be broken. Yet God’s last word is not “Not mine”. In the very place of rejection he promises to make the disowned his children, as countless as the sand, and to gather them under one head.

Why it was said. Israel under Jeroboam II was prosperous, secure and busily religious, and saw no danger (see the introduction). Its worship was mixed with Baal’s, and its throne stood on Jehu’s bloodshed. God’s word had to break through a confidence that took his blessings as proof of his approval.

How the chapter makes its case. The heading places Hosea in the last decades of the northern kingdom (v. 1). God commands the marriage as a living sign, “for the land commits great whoredom by forsaking the LORD” (v. 2). Then come three children and three names, each a step further down: Jezreel, the end of Jehu’s dynasty and Israel’s strength (vv. 3–5); No Mercy, the end of God’s long patience, with Judah spared by God’s hand alone (vv. 6–7); Not My People, the covenant promise turned inside out (vv. 8–9). Then, without warning, “Yet”: the promise to Abraham stands, the disowned become “Children of the living God”, the divided nation is gathered under one head, and the name of slaughter becomes the name of a harvest (vv. 10–11).

Where it leads. By promise, and by the need the chapter exposes. A people who have made themselves “Not My People” cannot make themselves God’s children again; only God can, and the New Testament shows how. Paul hears in verse 10 God calling Gentiles as well as Jews to be “sons of the living God” (Romans 9:26), and Peter tells scattered believers, “once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Peter 2:10). The one head is the Son of David, Jesus Christ, who bore the rejection his people deserved so that the disowned could be called children.

For us. Sin is unfaithfulness to a Person who loves us, and it can sit comfortably alongside prosperity and busy religion. Hear the warning. Then remember that every Christian was once “Not My People”, and that in Christ God has changed the name for good.
1.theology:
Idolatry is spiritual adultery against a God who loves his people as a husband loves his wife (v. 2; Isa 54:5; Jer 2:2).

God may use a person's actions while judging the spirit in which they were done (v. 4; 2 Kgs 10:30-31).

God is slow to anger but will not clear the guilty; persistent unfaithfulness ends in judgment and separation from God (vv. 4-9; Exod 34:6-7; 2 Kgs 17:6-7).

God saves by his own power, not by human strength (v. 7; 2 Kgs 19:35).

God's final word is grace greater than judgment: those who were not his people become children of the living God, a promise fulfilled as Jews and Gentiles are brought into God's family through Christ (v. 10; Rom 9:25-26; 1 Pet 2:10; Gen 22:17).

God's scattered people will be gathered under one head, the Son of David (v. 11; 3:5; Ezek 34:23-24).
1.examples: A prophet is told to marry a woman who will betray him, in a prosperous nation with a rotten heart. A little girl is named No Mercy, and a little boy carries a name that sounds like divorce: Not My People. Jehu did God's work with the wrong heart, while Jerusalem would be saved without firing an arrow. And at the end, a valley of judgment is renamed "God will sow".

keyVerse.quote: And in the place where it was said to them, “You are not my people,” it shall be said to them, “Children of the living God.”
keyVerse.note: The chapter descends through three names of judgment, and this verse turns the last of them inside out. God does not cancel his verdict on Israel’s sin; he promises to overcome it, in the very place it was spoken. Paul and Peter both hear in it the gospel that makes outsiders, Jews and Gentiles alike, God’s children in Christ (Romans 9:26; 1 Peter 2:10).

1.reflection:
God tells Hosea that Israel’s worship of other gods is “great whoredom” (v. 2), a betrayed marriage rather than a broken rule. How does it change your view of sin to see it as unfaithfulness to a Person who loves you? What does it show you about God’s heart?

Israel was prosperous and religious under Jeroboam II, yet God was about to judge it. Why is it easy to take blessing as a sign of God’s approval? Where might we be doing the same?

Jehu did what God commanded, yet his house was judged “for the blood of Jezreel” (v. 4). What does that teach about doing God’s work in the wrong spirit? Where might that be a danger for you or your church?

Every Christian was once “Not My People” and is now called a child of the living God (v. 10; 1 Peter 2:10). What difference does it make to know that this new name is God’s gift and not your achievement? How might it change how you treat those still outside?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel thanks Baal for gifts that came from the LORD, so God takes the gifts back and blocks her road, not to be rid of her but to bring her home. The section begins with the end of the story, the reversed names (v. 1), so that the painful middle can be read with hope. Then comes the case: the children are to plead with their mother, whose lovers, she says, give her bread, water, wool and oil (vv. 2–5). God hedges her way with thorns until she longs for her first husband (vv. 6–7). Because she did not know who gave her the grain, the wine and the oil, he takes them back, ends her feasts and lays waste her vines, for she “forgot me” (vv. 8–13).
verseByVerse.theology: Idolatry credits other lovers with God's gifts, and God lovingly takes those gifts away to bring his people back.

verseByVerse.quote: Say to your brothers, "You are my people," and to your sisters, "You have received mercy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chapter begins with the end of the story: God’s people will be his people again, and the unpitied will receive mercy.

You have received mercy. This verse finishes the thought of 1:10–11; the ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible it is 2:3. The Hebrew words are ammi, “my people”, and ruhama, “she has received mercy” (ESV note). Not My People becomes My People, and No Mercy becomes Mercy: God simply drops the “not”.

What the gospel does. It does not polish our old identity; it reverses it. And because the chapter gives the ending first, we can read the painful middle with hope, as a Christian may read the hard chapters of his own life.
verseByVerse.note: This verse completes the promise of 1:10-11: the children's names are reversed.

verseByVerse.quote: "Plead with your mother, plead— for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband— that she put away her whoring from her face, and her adultery from between her breasts; lest I strip her naked and make her as in the day she was born, and make her like a wilderness, and make her like a parched land, and kill her with thirst. Upon her children also I will have no mercy, because they are children of whoredom. For their mother has played the whore; she who conceived them has acted shamefully. For she said, 'I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water, my wool and my flax, my oil and my drink.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
God pleads with his unfaithful wife to give up her lovers before he strips her of everything, because she has credited the Baals with the gifts he gave her.

Plead with your mother. The scene is like a family court. On one level it is Hosea’s family; on a deeper level it is God speaking to Israel. The mother is the nation as a whole, the children are its people, and the faithful few are called to plead with the nation to repent.

For she is not my wife, and I am not her husband. The relationship is broken. Yet the goal of the whole speech is “that she put away her whoring”. The husband is not seeking a way out; he is seeking her return.

Lest I strip her naked. In ancient Israel a husband provided his wife’s clothing. To strip her was to take back all he had given and leave her as poor and exposed as “the day she was born”. Ezekiel used the same picture: God found Israel as an abandoned baby, clothed her and made her his bride, and she used his gifts to play the whore (Ezekiel 16:8, 15). The land itself would become “a parched land”, a terrible threat to people who worshipped Baal precisely because they thought he gave rain.

Upon her children also. The children are not innocent bystanders punished for their mother: they are the people of Israel, who share the nation’s idolatry.

I will go after my lovers. Verse 5 shows the heart of Israel’s sin. The lovers are the Baals, the Canaanite gods of storm and fertility, believed to send the rain and make the crops grow. It was practical religion: worship whichever god seems to deliver the goods. Her list is food, clothing and comfort. She did not love her lovers. She loved what they gave her.

The god who delivers the goods. That is the root of idolatry in every age: looking to anything for what only God can give, security, meaning, pleasure or approval, and going after money, career, relationships or success because they will “give me my bread”, forgetting the Father who has already given us everything in his Son (Romans 8:32). It may be the most modern thing in the chapter. Much spirituality today is offered on the same terms, as a route to calm, focus, better sleep or a stronger marriage, and even Christianity can be sold as the best lover on the market. But a god you come to for his gifts is a supplier, and you will leave him the moment another supplier seems to deliver more. C. S. Lewis saw what was wrong with the whole arrangement. In Mere Christianity he wrote, “God cannot give us a happiness and peace apart from Himself, because it is not there. There is no such thing.” The gifts were never meant to be the point; they were the husband’s way of saying that he loved her. The gospel does not offer a better deal. It offers God himself, who in Christ gave not grain and oil but his own Son, so that we might at last want the Giver more than the gifts.

Does a picture like this give a husband any right to shame, strip or control his wife? None at all. Here the husband is God, the wife is a nation, and the stripping is the covenant curse of a land laid bare by invasion and drought. God alone may judge, because he alone is perfectly just and loving. No human husband stands in his place, and Scripture commands husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church, gently and at cost to themselves (Ephesians 5:25; Colossians 3:19). Anyone being harmed by a spouse should seek safety at once and tell those who can help, including the elders of their church.
verseByVerse.note: Baal was worshipped as the giver of rain and harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will hedge up her way with thorns, and I will build a wall against her, so that she cannot find her paths. She shall pursue her lovers but not overtake them, and she shall seek them but shall not find them. Then she shall say, 'I will go and return to my first husband, for it was better for me then than now.' And she did not know that it was I who gave her the grain, the wine, and the oil, and who lavished on her silver and gold, which they used for Baal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God blocks his wayward wife’s road so that her lovers fail her and she longs to come home, though she still does not know that every good gift came from him.

I will hedge up her way with thorns. A surprising kind of judgment. God does not simply let her go; he blocks her road with thorns and a wall. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew says “your way”, as God turns to speak to her directly.) To her it feels like frustration, but it is mercy. Sometimes God lets the things we chase fail and the plans we lean on fall through, because he loves us too much to let us find happiness apart from him: “Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word” (Psalm 119:67); “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

It was better for me then than now. Her lovers keep slipping out of reach, and at last she comes to her senses, as the prodigal son did among the pigs: “How many of my father’s hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger!” (Luke 15:17). Her motive is not yet pure; she wants to go back because life was better. But God often begins there. Many people first turn to him because their idols have failed them, and he receives them, and then teaches them to love him for himself.

It was I who gave her the grain. The saddest verse in the chapter. Every good thing she thought came from Baal had come from God all along. He even lavished silver and gold on her, and she spent it on Baal. Moses had warned of this: “Beware lest you say in your heart, ‘My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth.’ You shall remember the LORD your God, for it is he who gives you power to get wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:17–18).

Our ingratitude too. Paul says of all humanity, “although they knew God, they did not honor him as God or give thanks to him” (Romans 1:21). Every meal, every pay packet and every breath is a gift from the God many people never thank: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above” (James 1:17). And the best gift came down in person: the Father who gave Israel its grain gave us his Son, “the bread of life” (John 6:35).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I will take back my grain in its time, and my wine in its season, and I will take away my wool and my flax, which were to cover her nakedness. Now I will uncover her lewdness in the sight of her lovers, and no one shall rescue her out of my hand. And I will put an end to all her mirth, her feasts, her new moons, her Sabbaths, and all her appointed feasts. And I will lay waste her vines and her fig trees, of which she said, 'These are my wages, which my lovers have given me.' I will make them a forest, and the beasts of the field shall devour them. And I will punish her for the feast days of the Baals when she burned offerings to them and adorned herself with her ring and jewelry, and went after her lovers and forgot me, declares the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Israel would not see that the gifts were his, God will take them back, end her festivals and show her lovers to be powerless, for she has forgotten him.

I will take back my grain in its time. The key word is “my”: my grain, my wine, my wool and my flax. God reclaims what was always his. If she will not see that the gifts come from him, he will show her by taking them away “in its time” and “in its season”, just when she expects the harvest.

No one shall rescue her out of my hand. Her lovers will be shown to be powerless to protect her. Idols always abandon us at the moment we need them most.

Her feasts, her new moons, her Sabbaths. Israel still kept the calendar God had given, the new moons, Sabbaths and appointed feasts, but had mixed it with Baal worship, and God calls them “her” feasts, not his. Religious activity without faithfulness means nothing to God, and he would put an end to it.

These are my wages. She called her vines and fig trees “my wages”, the payment a prostitute receives: that is how she saw her relationship with the gods, as a transaction. God would let them grow wild, a forest for wild animals.

And forgot me. The charge ends with words that break the heart. She put on her ring and jewellery for her lovers, and forgot the husband who loved her. That was Israel’s deepest sin: not only disobedience, but forgetfulness of God. It is still one of the commonest sins among those who have known him, and the cure is that God himself makes his people remember him again (vv. 14–20). Jesus gave his forgetful people a meal for that very purpose: “do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Instead of destroying his unfaithful wife, God woos her again and binds her to himself for ever, supplying everything the marriage needs. He brings her into the wilderness to speak tenderly to her, and turns the Valley of Achor, “trouble”, into a door of hope (vv. 14–15). He takes the Baals’ names from her lips, makes a covenant with the creatures for her sake and ends war (vv. 16–18). He betroths her to himself in righteousness, justice, steadfast love, mercy and faithfulness, and she will know the LORD (vv. 19–20). Then heaven, earth and harvest answer one another, and the names of judgment are reversed: “You are my people”; “You are my God” (vv. 21–23).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to unfaithfulness is a new betrothal in which he himself provides everything the marriage needs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her. And there I will give her her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope. And there she shall answer as in the days of her youth, as at the time when she came out of the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Instead of destroying his unfaithful wife, God will woo her again, lead her into the wilderness to speak to her heart, and turn her valley of trouble into a door of hope.

Therefore, behold, I will allure her. A turn no reader expects. After verse 13 we expect, “Therefore I will destroy her.” Instead God will woo her, like a young man courting. The same “therefore” that introduced judgment in verses 6 and 9 now introduces love: the very sin that deserved judgment moves him to go after her and win her back.

And bring her into the wilderness. The wilderness was where God first took Israel after the exodus, where he made his covenant with her and she was his bride: “I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed me in the wilderness” (Jeremiah 2:2). There, stripped of Baal’s vineyards, with nothing else to distract her, God will “speak tenderly to her”. He often does the same with his wandering people, bringing them into a season of loss or loneliness, not to destroy them but to speak to their hearts where they can finally hear him.

The Valley of Achor. God will give back the vineyards he took away, now received as gifts from him. And he will make “the Valley of Achor a door of hope”. Achor means “trouble”, and the ESV points to Joshua 7:26. There Achan was stoned for taking what God had devoted to destruction, just as Israel was entering the promised land (Joshua 7:25–26): a place of sin, shame and death at the very doorway of the land. God will turn it into the entrance to a new beginning, where she will answer him “as in the days of her youth”.

A door of hope. For the Christian, this is exactly what the cross is. The place of the worst trouble in history, where the Son of God bore the judgment for sin, has become the door of hope for all who come to him. “I am the door,” Jesus said; “If anyone enters by me, he will be saved” (John 10:9).

Uncertain wording. The verb translated “answer” can also mean “sing” (the King James Version reads “sing”), or more generally “respond”. The likely sense is her answering love, a bride responding to her husband’s wooing as she did when he first brought her out of Egypt.
verseByVerse.note: “Achor” means “trouble” (ESV note): the valley of judgment becomes a door of hope.

verseByVerse.quote: "And in that day, declares the LORD, you will call me 'My Husband,' and no longer will you call me 'My Baal.' For I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth, and they shall be remembered by name no more. And I will make for them a covenant on that day with the beasts of the field, the birds of the heavens, and the creeping things of the ground. And I will abolish the bow, the sword, and war from the land, and I will make you lie down in safety.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God wins his people back, they will call him “My Husband”, forget the Baals, and live in peace and safety under his covenant.

“My Husband,” not “My Baal.” Israel had so mixed the worship of the LORD with the worship of Baal that they had begun to speak of God himself as their Baal. The word baal was also an ordinary Hebrew word for “master” or “husband”, which made the confusion easy. In that day, God says, the confusion will end. She will call him “My Husband”, a name of love and belonging, and never again confuse him with the idols.

I will remove the names of the Baals. God himself does it. We cannot cleanse our own hearts of their idols; God must take them away, and he does it by his Spirit (Ezekiel 36:26–27). That is what the new covenant promises: “I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts” (Jeremiah 31:33).

A covenant on that day with the beasts of the field. In verse 12 the beasts were to devour her vineyards; now God makes a covenant with them for her sake. And he will abolish war (the ESV notes that the Hebrew says “break”, as with Israel’s bow in 1:5), and the restored bride will “lie down in safety”.

The peace of the new creation. This looks beyond anything Israel experienced in history, to the new creation, where “The wolf and the lamb shall graze together” (Isaiah 65:25) and “the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption” (Romans 8:21). The restoration of God’s people and of the world belong together, and both rest on Christ, through whom God was pleased “to reconcile to himself all things” (Colossians 1:20).
verseByVerse.note: “My Baal” also meant “my master”, a word now to be dropped.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy. I will betroth you to me in faithfulness. And you shall know the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will bind his people to himself in a marriage that can never fail, because he himself brings everything it needs, and they will truly know him.

I will betroth you to me. These are among the tenderest words in the prophets, and God says them three times. In ancient Israel betrothal was more than an engagement: it was a binding commitment, and the bridegroom paid a bride-price to the bride’s family. Many see here the bride-price God himself will pay: righteousness, justice, steadfast love, mercy and faithfulness. The bride brings nothing. The groom brings everything the marriage needs.

I will betroth you to me forever. The first marriage failed because the bride was unfaithful. This one cannot fail, because the Bridegroom himself guarantees it.

The Bridegroom and the price. The New Testament shows us both. “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her” (Ephesians 5:25–26): the bride-price was his own life. Paul told the Corinthians, “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). And the Bible ends with a wedding: “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his Bride has made herself ready” (Revelation 19:7).

And you shall know the LORD. That is the goal of the marriage. In the Bible, to know someone can mean the closest, most personal relationship. Israel had known about the LORD but had not truly known him. In the new covenant God promises, “they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34), and Jesus said, “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "And in that day I will answer, declares the LORD, I will answer the heavens, and they shall answer the earth, and the earth shall answer the grain, the wine, and the oil, and they shall answer Jezreel, and I will sow her for myself in the land. And I will have mercy on No Mercy, and I will say to Not My People, 'You are my people'; and he shall say, 'You are my God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In that day all creation will answer God with blessing, and every name of judgment will be reversed: God will say, “You are my people,” and they will say, “You are my God.”

I will answer the heavens. The whole creation joins in a chain of answers. God answers the heavens, the heavens send rain to the earth, the earth answers with grain, wine and oil, and the crops answer Jezreel, God’s people. The very things Israel once sought from Baal will flow freely from the true God, the one who really gives the rain.

I will sow her for myself in the land. The ESV notes at verse 22 that Jezreel means “God will sow”, and now God explains the name. The name that once meant scattering in judgment (1:4–5) now means planting in blessing.

I will have mercy on No Mercy. All three names of chapter 1 are reversed: Jezreel is sown, No Mercy receives mercy, and Not My People hears, “You are my people”. And the chapter ends with the simplest, most complete statement of what it means to belong to God. He says, “You are my people,” and they answer, “You are my God.”

Mercy for the Gentiles. Paul quotes this verse to show that God’s mercy reaches even the Gentiles: “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people,’ and her who was not beloved I will call ‘beloved’” (Romans 9:25). Peter echoes it too (1 Peter 2:10). If you belong to Christ, this is your story. You were not his people. You had not received mercy. Now you have, and the covenant that joins you to him will last for ever, because it rests on his faithfulness, not on yours.
verseByVerse.note: Heaven, earth and harvest answer one another, and God's people answer him.

2.title: I Will Betroth You to Me Forever
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 ended with the promise that those called “Not My People” would be called children of the living God. Chapter 2 opens by finishing that promise (v. 1), then steps back into the broken marriage, now spoken as God’s own case against his unfaithful wife, Israel.

The message. Israel has thanked Baal for the gifts the LORD gave her, so God will take the gifts back and block her road, not to be rid of her but to bring her home. Then, with a “therefore” no one expects, he promises to woo her again, betroth her to himself for ever and bring her to know him, supplying from his own side everything the marriage needs.

Why it was said. Israel’s farmers looked to Baal, the Canaanite god of storm and fertility, for rain and harvest, and kept the LORD’s feasts alongside Baal’s (see the introduction). The prosperity of Jeroboam II’s reign seemed to prove that the arrangement worked.

How the chapter makes its case. The end comes first: “You are my people” (v. 1). Then the charge: the children are to plead with their mother, who says her lovers feed and clothe her (vv. 2–5). So God hedges up her way until she longs for her first husband (vv. 6–7), and because she did not know who gave her the grain, the wine and the oil, he will take them back, end her feasts and show her lovers to be powerless (vv. 8–13). Then “therefore” turns from judgment to courtship: the wilderness, and the Valley of Achor made a door of hope (vv. 14–15); the Baals’ names removed and creation at peace (vv. 16–18); a betrothal for ever in righteousness, justice, steadfast love, mercy and faithfulness (vv. 19–20); and heaven and earth answering one another until every name of chapter 1 is reversed (vv. 21–23).

Where it leads. By covenant and by promise. The Bridegroom who pays the bride-price himself and makes a marriage that cannot fail is Christ, who “loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25); Paul betrothed the Corinthians “to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11:2). The valley of trouble made a door of hope is fulfilled at the cross, and Paul hears verse 23 as the gospel calling the Gentiles: “Those who were not my people I will call ‘my people’” (Romans 9:25).

For us. We still thank other lovers for what only God gives, and sometimes he loves us enough to let them fail. If your road is hedged with thorns, listen for his voice in the wilderness: he is not trying to be rid of you but to win you back.
2.theology:
Idolatry is spiritual adultery that credits false gods with the gifts of the true God and seeks the gifts rather than the Giver (vv. 5, 8, 12; Deut 8:17-18; Rom 1:21; Jas 1:17).

God in mercy frustrates the paths of his wandering people and takes away his gifts to bring them back to himself (vv. 6-7, 9; Ps 119:67; Heb 12:6; Luke 15:17).

Religious activity mixed with idolatry is worthless before God, and forgetting God is the root of unfaithfulness (vv. 11, 13).

God's grace pursues the unfaithful, turning the place of trouble into a door of hope, fulfilled at the cross (vv. 14-15; Jer 2:2; Josh 7:25-26).

God removes idols from his people's hearts and brings peace to the whole creation (vv. 16-18; Jer 31:33; Isa 65:25; Rom 8:21).

God betroths his people to himself forever, supplying the righteousness, love and faithfulness the covenant requires, fulfilled in Christ the Bridegroom who gave himself for his church (vv. 19-20; Eph 5:25-27; 2 Cor 11:2; Rev 19:7; Jer 31:34; John 17:3).

God's mercy reverses the names of judgment and makes those who were not his people his own (vv. 1, 23; Rom 9:25; 1 Pet 2:10).
2.examples: Children are asked to plead with their own mother, who thinks her lovers pay for her bread and melts God's silver and gold into an idol. A husband who wants his wife back blocks her road with thorns. Then a valley named Trouble becomes a door of hope, the Bridegroom pays the whole bride-price himself, and "You are my people" is answered at last by "You are my God."

keyVerse.quote: Therefore, behold, I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her.
keyVerse.note: This is the hinge of the chapter. After thirteen verses of charge and judgment, the same “therefore” that introduced punishment introduces courtship: the husband answers his wife’s betrayal by going after her. Everything that follows, the door of hope, the everlasting betrothal and the reversed names, flows from this love, which the New Testament shows us in Christ coming to seek and to save the lost.

2.reflection:
Israel said of the Baals, “I will go after my lovers, who give me my bread and my water” (v. 5), and “did not know that it was I who gave her the grain” (v. 8). What do people around us look to for security, comfort or approval? Where are you tempted to thank something other than God for his gifts?

God hedges up Israel’s way with thorns so that her lovers fail her (vv. 6–7). Have you known God block a road you were set on? How can we tell when frustration is God’s mercy, and what should we do when we see it?

Israel kept her feasts, new moons and Sabbaths while forgetting the LORD (vv. 11, 13). How is it possible to stay busy with religion and still forget God? What helps us remember him?

God promises to betroth his people “forever … in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy” (v. 19), bringing everything the marriage needs himself. How does Christ fulfil this? What difference does it make that your security rests on his faithfulness, not yours?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s love for his people is shown in a man who goes after his unfaithful wife, pays to get her back and binds himself to her. God commands Hosea, “Go again, love”, a woman who has betrayed him, as the LORD loves Israel though it turns to other gods (v. 1). So Hosea buys her for fifteen shekels of silver and a quantity of barley, a real price paid in full (v. 2). Then he tells her she must live as his alone for many days, with no other lovers, and promises to be hers in the same way (v. 3). Redemption is both rescue and belonging, and it is costly to the one who redeems.
verseByVerse.theology: God's love pays the price to redeem an unfaithful people and restores them to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, "Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells Hosea to love his unfaithful wife again, as a living picture of how he goes on loving Israel while it is still turning to other gods.

And the LORD said to me. This time Hosea tells the story himself, in one of the clearest pictures of the gospel in the prophets.

Go again, love a woman. The wife has left. Most readers take this woman to be Gomer, as “again” suggests, though some think it was another woman. And God tells Hosea, “Go again, love”. Not “Go, forgive her if she comes back”, nor “Go, bring her to justice”, but go and love.

Even as the LORD loves the children of Israel. How could any man do that? Only by looking to God, for Hosea’s love was to copy God’s love for his people. God does not love his people because they are faithful. He loves them though they turn away.

And love cakes of raisins. Raisin cakes were festive food (2 Samuel 6:19), here probably eaten at pagan feasts: Israel loved the pleasures of false religion more than God.

Love for sinners. This is the love the New Testament proclaims: “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8); “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us” (1 John 4:10).

Does this mean every betrayed husband or wife must take an unfaithful spouse back? No. Hosea’s marriage was a unique prophetic sign, commanded to him for a message to the nation. Jesus allows divorce where there has been adultery (Matthew 19:9), and this commentary holds, with the Westminster Confession, that adultery and desertion are grounds for it, and that persistent, serious abuse can amount to desertion. Every Christian must forgive from the heart, and many marriages have been restored, but reconciliation is a separate question, to be weighed with the elders, and no one should return to a home where they are in danger.

verseByVerse.quote: So I bought her for fifteen shekels of silver and a homer and a lethech of barley. And I said to her, "You must dwell as mine for many days. You shall not play the whore, or belong to another man; so will I also be to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hosea pays a real price to buy back his wife, then claims her as his alone and binds himself to her in return: a picture of the redemption God gives his people.

So I bought her. Hosea had to buy his own wife back. Perhaps she had fallen into debt or slavery; either way, someone had to pay.

Fifteen shekels of silver. The ESV notes put the barley, a homer and a lethech, at about nine bushels. The law set the value of a slave at “thirty shekels of silver” (Exodus 21:32), and some suggest that Hosea paid half in shekels and the rest in grain because he did not have enough money. If so, it cost him all he could scrape together. What is certain is that it was a real price, paid in full, for a wife who had betrayed him.

What redemption cost. To redeem is to buy back by paying a price, and this is what God did for us in Christ. We were ransomed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). Hosea paid silver and barley; Christ paid with his own life: “For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).

You must dwell as mine. Redemption is not only rescue but belonging, and her old life must end: “You shall not play the whore, or belong to another man”. Paul says the same to Christians: “You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). The order matters: first Christ buys us, then comes the command, and the Spirit who lives in us gives the power to keep it. Christ “gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession” (Titus 2:14).

So will I also be to you. Hosea binds himself to her as she is bound to him: grace does not only demand our faithfulness, it promises God’s. And there is a time of waiting, “many days”, a season of discipline in which the old ways are broken.

Love that pays, and love that claims. Our culture holds two ideas of love that do not fit together. One says real love accepts you as you are and asks nothing. The other, often in the same heart, says love must be earned: you are loved for your looks or usefulness and dropped when they fade. Hosea’s love overturns both. It is utterly unearned: he buys back a wife who has given him every reason to walk away. But it is not indifferent: “You must dwell as mine”. A love that did not care whether she went back to the men using her would be a kind of contempt. So with God’s love in Christ: it costs him everything and asks nothing in advance, which leaves no room for scorekeeping, and it claims the whole of us, which leaves no room for a God who shrugs. We are taken as we are, and loved far too much to be left there.

Uncertain wording. The lethech is named only here in the Old Testament and is usually taken as half a homer, but its size is not certain. And “so will I also be to you” is compressed, literally “and also I to you”: a promise of faithfulness, or perhaps that he too will wait, not living with her as husband during the “many days”, as Israel waits without its worship (v. 4). Either way, he binds himself to her.
verseByVerse.note: Fifteen shekels and a homer and a lethech of barley (ESV notes): perhaps together the price of a slave.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s discipline will be long, but its end is homecoming. As Gomer lives set apart, Israel will live “many days” without king or prince, without sacrifice or idolatrous pillar, without ephod or household gods: God will strip away both the true and the false supports it leaned on (v. 4). Afterwards the people will return and seek the LORD their God and David their king, the promised Son of David, and come trembling to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days (v. 5). The exile will not cancel God’s love; it will prepare his people to come home to him and to his King.
verseByVerse.theology: Discipline prepares God's people to return to him and to the promised King from David's line.

verseByVerse.quote: For the children of Israel shall dwell many days without king or prince, without sacrifice or pillar, without ephod or household gods.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel will go through a long season stripped of everything it leaned on, its rulers, its worship and its idols alike.

Without king or prince. As Gomer would live many days set apart, so Israel would live without the things it relied on: no government of its own, no sacrifice and no pagan pillar (a sacred standing stone), no ephod (a priestly garment used in seeking guidance) and no household gods. God would take away the true and the false supports together.

What exile did. Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom, and later Judah was carried to Babylon, losing its king and temple. But in that long wilderness hearts were being prepared to return.

Emptied hands. God sometimes takes away even good supports so that his people will lean on him alone. Israel lost its king and its altar; when it came home, it would find both in one person, the King who “offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins” (Hebrews 10:12).

Uncertain wording. The “household gods” (Hebrew teraphim) were images kept in homes and used in seeking oracles (Genesis 31:19; Judges 17:5), though exactly how is not known. Paired with them, the ephod is probably one used for divination (Judges 8:27), not only the high priest’s garment. Either way, every means of seeking guidance, lawful and unlawful, would be gone.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward the children of Israel shall return and seek the LORD their God, and David their king, and they shall come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the discipline, Israel will come home to the LORD and to the promised King from David’s line, trembling at what they deserved and amazed at his goodness.

Afterward the children of Israel shall return. Discipline is not the end. Repentance is returning and seeking, coming back to the husband they left.

And David their king. David was long dead, so this means the promised King from his family, the one the prophets looked for. Jeremiah spoke of “David their king, whom I will raise up for them” (Jeremiah 30:9), and Ezekiel of “one shepherd, my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23). This is the Messiah, Jesus Christ, the Son of David. To return to God is to come to his King.

They shall come in fear to the LORD and to his goodness. Fear and goodness belong together. Those who have been forgiven come trembling, knowing what they deserved, and amazed at the goodness they receive instead. “In the latter days” points to the time of fulfilment, the days that began with the coming of Christ.

Our story. Hosea’s marriage is our story. We were the unfaithful bride; God came after us, paid the price and bound himself to us for ever. The right response is to return to the LORD and his King, and come in reverent wonder to his goodness.

Where Christians differ: does this promise look to a future restoration of Israel? Dispensationalists (who see God’s purposes for Israel and for the church as separate tracks) read “the latter days” and “David their king” as a future national restoration of Israel under Christ’s reign in Jerusalem. This commentary’s view: the New Testament says the latter days began with Christ (Hebrews 1:2), and that the Son of David now reigns (Acts 2:30–36); on the most natural reading, Paul also looks for a great turning of Jewish people to him (Romans 11:26). So this commentary reads the promise as fulfilled in Christ’s present reign, while honouring the many faithful Christians who expect a future earthly kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: “David their king” is the Messiah from David’s line.

3.title: Go Again, Love
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapters 1 and 2 told of the broken marriage and God’s promise to win back his unfaithful people. Chapter 3, only five verses long and the first part told by Hosea himself, completes the story of the prophet’s marriage before the book turns to his sermons.

The message. God loves his people while they are still turning to other gods, and his love is not cheap: it pays to buy them back, claims them wholly, binds itself to them, and disciplines them through a long season until they come home. In the end they will return to the LORD and to the King he promised, trembling at what they deserved and amazed at his goodness.

Why it was said. Israel trusted its kings, its sacrifices and its household idols, all mixed together (see the introduction). Hosea’s hearers needed to know both that God would strip all of them away, and that the exile to come would not be the end of his love.

How the chapter makes its case. God commands Hosea to love his adulterous wife again, “even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods” (v. 1). Hosea buys her back with silver and barley, and tells her she must live as his alone for many days, as he will be to her (vv. 2–3). Then comes the meaning: Israel will live many days without king, sacrifice or idols (v. 4), and afterwards will return to the LORD and to “David their king”, coming “in fear to the LORD and to his goodness in the latter days” (v. 5).

Where it leads. By pattern and by promise. Hosea paying to redeem a wife who had betrayed him pictures Christ, who ransomed his people “not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ” (1 Peter 1:18–19). And “David their king” is the Son of David, Jesus, to whom God’s scattered people return; the latter days began when he came.

For us. God did not wait for us to become faithful before he loved us: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). But the love that bought us also claims us, and we are no longer our own. If you are in a season of “many days”, it is the waiting of a love that intends to bring you home.
3.theology:
God loves his people while they are unfaithful, and his love is the pattern for forgiving love (v. 1; Rom 5:8; 1 John 4:10).

Redemption is costly: the unfaithful are bought back at a price, fulfilled in the precious blood of Christ (v. 2; 1 Pet 1:18-19; Mark 10:45).

Those who are redeemed belong to their Redeemer, and he binds himself to them in faithfulness (v. 3; 1 Cor 6:19-20; Titus 2:14).

God uses seasons of loss and discipline to strip away false supports and prepare his people to return (v. 4).

True repentance returns to the LORD and to the promised Son of David, and comes with reverent fear to his goodness (v. 5; Jer 30:9; Ezek 34:23-24).
3.examples: A husband is told to love his wife while she is with another man, and he buys her back with fifteen pieces of silver and nine bushels of barley. "You must dwell as mine," he tells her, "so will I also be to you." A nation is left without king, temple or idols, until returning sinners come trembling to God's goodness.

keyVerse.quote: And the LORD said to me, “Go again, love a woman who is loved by another man and is an adulteress, even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods and love cakes of raisins.”
keyVerse.note: The whole book turns on this command. Hosea is not told to forgive his wife if she comes back, but to go after her and love her, and the reason is God’s own love for a people still turning away. It is the Old Testament’s clearest picture of a love that goes first, the love shown at the cross while we were still sinners.

3.reflection:
God tells Hosea to love his wife “even as the LORD loves the children of Israel, though they turn to other gods” (v. 1). What does it mean to you that God’s love does not wait for you to become faithful? Where do you find that hard to believe?

Hosea had to pay to buy his wife back (v. 2). How does this picture help you understand what Christ did for you (1 Peter 1:18–19; Mark 10:45)? Why does it matter that redemption costs something?

Having bought her, Hosea says, “You must dwell as mine” (v. 3). How does being bought with a price change the way we live (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)? Why is love that claims us not the opposite of grace but part of it?

Israel would live “many days” without king, sacrifice or idols before returning (vv. 4–5). Have you known a season when God took away things you leaned on? How can such seasons prepare us to come to him “in fear” and to his goodness?
