verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The LORD Brings a Case
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God takes his people to court, and the root of the charge is that they do not know him. The case opens formally: “the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land” (v. 1). Three things are missing, faithfulness, steadfast love and the knowledge of God, and the third is the root of the other two. In their place the commandments fall one by one, swearing, lying, murder, stealing and adultery, until bloodshed follows bloodshed (v. 2). And human sin wounds creation itself: the land mourns, and animals, birds and fish waste away (v. 3). What a people does before God is never merely private.
verseByVerse.theology: When a people loses the knowledge of God, every commandment falls, and even creation suffers.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear the word of the LORD, O children of Israel, for the LORD has a controversy with the inhabitants of the land. There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land; there is swearing, lying, murder, stealing, and committing adultery; they break all bounds, and bloodshed follows bloodshed. Therefore the land mourns, and all who dwell in it languish, and also the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens, and even the fish of the sea are taken away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God brings a legal case against Israel: because there is no knowledge of God in the land, faithfulness and love have vanished, the commandments are broken one by one, and creation itself suffers.

The LORD has a controversy. From chapter 4 the book gathers Hosea’s sermons, and the first opens like a courtroom. The LORD has a controversy, a legal case, “with the inhabitants of the land”. He is both the one who brings the charge and the judge.

No faithfulness or steadfast love. The charge begins with three things that are missing. No faithfulness: no one keeps their word. No steadfast love: no loyal, covenant love, toward God or toward one another. No knowledge of God: no real, personal acquaintance with the LORD and his ways. The third is the root of the other two. People who do not know God will not reflect his faithfulness and love.

Swearing, lying, murder, stealing. The list in verse 2 is almost a roll call of the Ten Commandments: “You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness” (Exodus 20:13–16). When a nation forgets God, it does not become neutral. It breaks the commandments one by one until “bloodshed follows bloodshed”. In Hosea’s day the northern kingdom saw one king after another murdered by the next.

Therefore the land mourns. Human sin wounds creation itself. Paul says that “the whole creation has been groaning together” (Romans 8:22) under the curse sin brought. What we do before God is never merely private.

Can we keep the fruit without the root? Hosea names the root first, no knowledge of God, and then the fruit that rots. Many today hope to keep the fruit while letting go of the root: honesty, faithfulness and the value of every life as plain decency, without the God who gave the commandments. Friedrich Nietzsche, no friend of Christianity, thought that hope naive. He mocked the English writers of his day who had given up the Christian God but clung all the harder to Christian morality, and warned that the one would not long outlive the other. Hosea would accept his diagnosis, though not his cure. A morality cut off from God can live for a generation or two on its inheritance, and then it runs out. But the prophet does not call Israel to try harder at being good. He calls Israel back to a Person, because only the knowledge of God, the God who comes near in Christ and writes his law on the heart (Hebrews 8:10–11), grows the faithfulness and steadfast love that no law can produce.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heaviest charge falls on the priests, whose task was to teach God’s law and who let the nation perish for lack of it. God’s quarrel is with the priest, and prophet and priest will stumble together (vv. 4–5). “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge”, not because it was unavailable but because it was rejected and forgotten, so God rejects the priests in turn (v. 6). As they grew, they sinned more, feeding on the offerings that the people’s sin produced (vv. 7–8). So it will be “like people, like priest”: both will eat and not be satisfied, because they have forsaken the LORD (vv. 9–10).
verseByVerse.theology: Leaders who fail to teach God's word lead God's people to ruin, and they will answer for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet let no one contend, and let none accuse, for with you is my contention, O priest. You shall stumble by day; the prophet also shall stumble with you by night; and I will destroy your mother. My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because you have rejected knowledge, I reject you from being a priest to me. And since you have forgotten the law of your God, I also will forget your children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s case falls hardest on the priests: they rejected the knowledge of God they were meant to teach, and the people are perishing for lack of it.

With you is my contention, O priest. God turns to those most responsible. The priests were supposed to teach Israel God’s law. Instead they had let the nation slide into ignorance.

The prophet also shall stumble with you. Priest and false prophet will fall together, by day and by night.

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge. One of the best-known verses in Hosea. Even here God says “my people”: he still calls them his, and he grieves over them. They were not destroyed because the knowledge was unavailable. It was rejected; the priests had God’s law and forgot it. The knowledge meant is not just information but knowing God himself, his character and his word, in a way that shapes how we live. Malachi describes what a priest should be: “the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and people should seek instruction from his mouth” (Malachi 2:7).

Ignorance is not harmless. This is a solemn word for every pastor, teacher and parent: those entrusted with God’s truth will give an account for how they handed it on (Hebrews 13:17). And it is a word for every church. God’s people are still destroyed for lack of knowledge, and he still gives them his word and his Spirit to teach them (John 14:26). In practice that means making room for his word: reading Scripture regularly, sitting under faithful preaching, asking questions of those who teach, and opening the Bible with our children, rather than leaving the knowledge of God to the professionals, as Israel left it to its priests.

Uncertain wording. Verse 4 is compressed and hard to translate. The ESV takes it as God silencing the people’s accusations of one another, because his quarrel is with the priest; its note gives another reading, “your people are like those who contend with the priest”. Either way, the priest is the one on trial. “I will destroy your mother” (v. 5) probably means the nation the priest belonged to, though some take it as his own family.

verseByVerse.quote: The more they increased, the more they sinned against me; I will change their glory into shame. They feed on the sin of my people; they are greedy for their iniquity. And it shall be like people, like priest; I will punish them for their ways and repay them for their deeds. They shall eat, but not be satisfied; they shall play the whore, but not multiply, because they have forsaken the LORD to cherish
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priests grew fat on the people’s sin instead of calling them from it, so priest and people will share the same judgment and the same emptiness.

The more they increased, the more they sinned against me. As the priesthood grew in number and wealth, it grew in sin. Success did not make them more faithful. It made them less, and God would change their glory into shame.

They feed on the sin of my people. A shocking charge. The ESV notes that “sin” can also be translated “sin offering”. Under the law, priests received a share of the sin offerings to eat (Leviticus 6:26). So the more the people sinned, the more sin offerings they brought, and the more the priests ate. The priests had every reason to want the people to keep sinning, and instead of calling them to repentance, they fed on their guilt.

Religion as a business. Religion can still be turned into a business that profits from people’s failures rather than healing them, and God hates it. The Priest God would give is the opposite of these priests. Jesus did not feed on his people’s sin offerings but became their sin offering (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 7:27), and under his new covenant “they shall all know me” (Hebrews 8:11).

Like people, like priest. The priests had sunk to the people’s level instead of lifting them up, and would share their judgment. Religious office gives no protection from God’s justice.

They shall eat, but not be satisfied. They turned to Baal for food and children, and would get neither. Sin always promises satisfaction and never delivers it, and the root cause is given plainly: “they have forsaken the LORD”. Jesus looked at crowds like this and saw them “harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin darkens the mind, spreads through families and finally leaves a people to their idols. Wine and whoredom take away understanding, until God’s people ask a piece of wood for guidance, led astray by a spirit of whoredom (vv. 11–12). They worship on hilltops under shady trees, and their daughters follow them into immorality, but God will not punish the women while the men go to cult prostitutes (vv. 13–14). Judah is warned not to copy Israel (v. 15). Israel is a stubborn heifer, joined to idols; God says, “leave him alone”, and a wind will sweep it away in shame (vv. 16–19).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin darkens the mind and hardens the will, until God gives people over to what they have chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: whoredom, wine, and new wine, which take away the understanding. My people inquire of a piece of wood, and their walking staff gives them oracles. For a spirit of whoredom has led them astray, and they have left their God to play the whore. They sacrifice on the tops of the mountains and burn offerings on the hills, under oak, poplar, and terebinth, because their shade is good. Therefore your daughters play the whore, and your brides commit adultery. I will not punish your daughters when they play the whore, nor your brides when they commit adultery; for the men themselves go aside with prostitutes and sacrifice with cult prostitutes, and a people without understanding shall come to ruin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin darkens the mind until God’s people ask a stick for guidance, and the men who lead their families into the shrines bear the greater guilt.

Which take away the understanding. Sexual sin and drunkenness cloud the mind until people cannot see what is obvious. Sin is not only wrong; it makes people foolish.

My people inquire of a piece of wood. God’s people, with the living God speaking through his prophets, were asking wood for guidance. The picture is almost comic, and deeply sad: that is what happens when the understanding is gone.

A spirit of whoredom has led them astray. Sin becomes a power, a spirit, that leads them astray. The sin they had chosen now ruled them: they were still guilty, but no longer free to stop. Only a stronger power can break that bondage, and Christ came to do it: “if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36).

Because their shade is good. Pagan worship took place on hilltops and under shady trees thought to be sacred, and the reason given is telling: their religion was chosen for comfort. It included sexual rites, which spread into the families. Fathers who worshipped this way saw their daughters and daughters-in-law follow them into immorality.

I will not punish your daughters. Verse 14 is remarkable for its time. God is not saying that the women’s sin does not matter. In that culture women were usually blamed and punished for sexual sin while men often went free, and God refuses that double standard. Why punish the young women when the men, their fathers and husbands, “go aside with prostitutes” in the name of religion? God holds the men responsible for the corruption they led. His justice does not favour the powerful.

Uncertain wording. The “piece of wood” and “walking staff” are probably a carved idol and a diviner’s rod, or sticks used for fortune-telling; exactly what practice is meant is not known. “Cult prostitutes” translates a word meaning “consecrated women”. Hosea plainly links the shrines with sexual sin, but scholars debate how widespread ritual sex was in Baal worship.

verseByVerse.quote: Though you play the whore, O Israel, let not Judah become guilty. Enter not into Gilgal, nor go up to Beth-aven, and swear not, "As the LORD lives." Like a stubborn heifer, Israel is stubborn; can the LORD now feed them like a lamb in a broad pasture? Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone. When their drink is gone, they give themselves to whoring; their rulers dearly love shame. A wind has wrapped them in its wings, and they shall be ashamed because of their sacrifices.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah is warned not to follow Israel, for stubborn Ephraim has bound itself to its idols, and God will leave it to them until the storm of judgment sweeps it away.

Enter not into Gilgal. Hosea warns the southern kingdom, Judah, not to follow Israel’s example. Gilgal had once been a sacred place where Israel camped after crossing the Jordan, but it had become a centre of corrupt worship. Beth-aven is most likely Hosea’s scornful name for Bethel, where Jeroboam son of Nebat had set up a golden calf (1 Kings 12:28–29; see 10:5). And do not swear, “As the LORD lives”: do not use God’s name to bless worship that dishonours him. Mixing the LORD’s name with idolatry was worse than silence.

Like a stubborn heifer. A stubborn young cow digs in its hooves and will not be led. How can God feed Israel like a lamb in a broad pasture when it refuses to move? He wanted to shepherd them into rest and plenty; their stubbornness shut them out.

Leave him alone. Ephraim, the leading tribe of the north, often stands for the whole nation. These are some of the most frightening words in the book. There comes a point when God stops warning and lets people have what they have chosen. Paul describes the same judgment: “God gave them up in the lusts of their hearts” (Romans 1:24). The worst thing God can do to a sinner is to leave him alone with his sin.

If you fear that God has left you alone. The fear itself is a sign that he has not: those he has given up do not grieve over it. Even of Ephraim, God would later cry, “How can I give you up, O Ephraim?” (11:8). Christ was forsaken on the cross so that no one who comes to him will ever be left alone (Hebrews 13:5).

Their rulers dearly love shame. Drinking leads to immorality, and the leaders (the ESV notes that the Hebrew calls them “shields”, the ones who should have protected the people) love shame. But a wind is coming, the whirlwind of judgment, which will sweep them away, and their sacrifices, the religion they trusted, will only bring them shame.

What is at stake. The root of Israel’s ruin was the loss of the knowledge of God, and the cure is not better ways of doing religion but knowing God himself, as he has made himself known in his word and, finally, in his Son.

Uncertain wording. Verses 16–19 are some of the hardest Hebrew in the book, and translations differ. The opening words of verse 18 are obscure. In verse 19 the same Hebrew word means both “wind” and “spirit”, so the wind that has “wrapped them in its wings” may be the storm of judgment carrying them into exile, or the “spirit of whoredom” of verse 12 that has swept them away. The overall sense is clear: Israel’s idolatry will end in shame.
verseByVerse.note: Beth-aven (“house of wickedness”) is probably a mocking name for Bethel (“house of God”).

4.title: No Knowledge of God in the Land
4.overview:
Where we are. The story of Hosea’s marriage is over, and the sermons begin. Chapter 4 opens the first round of them (chapters 4 to 7), and it opens like a courtroom: God brings his case against the land.

The message. Israel’s ruin has one root: it does not know God. Where the knowledge of God is lost, faithfulness and love disappear, the commandments fall one by one, and even the land suffers. The priests who should have taught that knowledge rejected it and profited from the people’s sin, so priest and people will fall together, and a nation that has chosen its idols will be left to them.

Why it was said. Israel was busy with sacrifices at hilltop shrines, mixed with Baal worship and its sexual rites, while its priesthood had grown numerous, prosperous and careless (see the introduction). Religion was flourishing, and the knowledge of God was gone.

How the chapter makes its case. First the charge: no faithfulness, no steadfast love, no knowledge of God, but every commandment broken, until the land mourns (vv. 1–3). Then the blame falls on the priests: they rejected knowledge, so God rejects them; they feed on the people’s sin, so it will be “like people, like priest” (vv. 4–10). Then the effects: wine and whoredom take away understanding, the people consult a piece of wood and worship under shady trees, and their daughters follow them, while God refuses to punish the women and spare the men (vv. 11–14). Judah is warned to stay away from Gilgal and Beth-aven; Israel is a stubborn heifer, joined to idols, and a wind will sweep it away (vv. 15–19).

Where it leads. By the need it exposes, and by covenant promise. Israel needed what no priest of Hosea’s day could give: the knowledge of God written on the heart. The new covenant promises it, “they shall all know me” (Jeremiah 31:34), and Christ keeps the promise. He is the priest who did not feed on his people’s sin but became their offering, and the one in whom God is truly known: “this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

For us. Ignorance of God is never harmless, for churches, families or individuals; God’s people are still destroyed for lack of knowledge. The cure is not more religious activity but knowing God himself, through his word, in his Son. Make room for that knowledge, and do not leave it to the professionals.
4.theology:
The lack of faithfulness, steadfast love and knowledge of God leads to the breaking of all God's commandments and to the suffering of creation (vv. 1-3; Exod 20:13-16; Rom 8:22).

God's people are destroyed for lack of knowledge, and those entrusted with teaching his word are especially accountable (vv. 4-6; Mal 2:7; Heb 13:17).

Religious leaders who profit from sin rather than calling people to repentance fall under God's judgment (vv. 7-9).

Sin never satisfies; it darkens the understanding and becomes an enslaving spirit (vv. 10-12).

God refuses a double standard and holds the powerful responsible for the corruption they lead (vv. 13-14).

Those who persist in idolatry may be given over by God to what they have chosen (v. 17; Rom 1:24).

The cure for a nation's ruin is the true knowledge of God, found in Jesus Christ (v. 6; John 17:3).
4.examples: God is both accuser and judge in a courtroom where a nation has broken the commandments one by one. Priests grow fat on the people's sin offerings, while the people ask a stick of wood for guidance and choose their worship because the shade is pleasant. Israel is a stubborn heifer that will not be led to green pasture, and the most frightening words are the shortest: "Leave him alone."

keyVerse.quote: My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge; because you have rejected knowledge, I reject you from being a priest to me.
keyVerse.note: This verse names the root of everything else in the chapter, and in much of the book. Israel was not short of religion but of the knowledge of God, and that knowledge was not unavailable but rejected, first by the priests who should have taught it. Even in judgment God still says “my people”, and the cure he promises is that they will know him, as they do in Christ.

4.reflection:
The charge begins with what is missing: “no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land” (v. 1). Why is the knowledge of God the root of the other two? What happens to a society, or a family, that tries to keep the fruit without the root?

“My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” (v. 6). What does it mean to know God, rather than only to know about him? What practical steps help you, your household and your church grow in that knowledge?

The priests fed on the people’s sin instead of calling them from it (v. 8). In what ways can religion become a business that profits from people rather than healing them? How is Jesus the opposite of these priests?

God refuses to punish the women while the men who led them go free (v. 14), and he says of stubborn Ephraim, “leave him alone” (v. 17). What do these verses teach about God’s justice and about the danger of persistent sin? What hope does 11:8 hold out?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — A Snare and a Net
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sin has trapped leaders and people alike, and religion without repentance cannot reach God. Priests, people and king are summoned to court, for those who should have guarded Israel have become a hunter’s snare and net, and God, who knows Ephraim through and through, will discipline them all (vv. 1–3). Worse, their sin now holds them: their deeds do not let them return, because a spirit of whoredom lives within them (v. 4). Pride testifies against them, and Judah stumbles too (v. 5). They will bring flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but he has withdrawn, and the festival they trust in will become the day of their ruin (vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.theology: Sin binds people so that they cannot return, and ritual without repentance cannot find God.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, O priests! Pay attention, O house of Israel! Give ear, O house of the king! For the judgment is for you; for you have been a snare at Mizpah and a net spread upon Tabor. And the revolters have gone deep into slaughter, but I will discipline all of them. I know Ephraim, and Israel is not hidden from me; for now, O Ephraim, you have played the whore; Israel is defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God summons priests, people and royal court to answer for trapping Israel in sin, and he reminds them that nothing they have done is hidden from him.

Hear this, O priests! Three groups are called to court: the priests, the house of Israel (the people) and the house of the king. Leaders, people and rulers are guilty together; those appointed to uphold justice now stand in the dock.

A snare at Mizpah and a net spread upon Tabor. The places that should have drawn people to God had become hunters’ traps that caught them in idolatry. Leaders who should protect God’s people can become the very ones who lead them into sin.

I will discipline all of them. “Discipline” is a father’s word: “as a man disciplines his son, the LORD your God disciplines you” (Deuteronomy 8:5). Even his judgment aims to correct.

I know Ephraim. Israel had lost the knowledge of God (4:1), but God had not lost his knowledge of Israel. That is a terror for those who hide their sin, and a comfort for those who long to be fully known and still loved. In Christ we meet that God: Jesus “knew what was in man” (John 2:25), and gave himself for us anyway.

Uncertain wording. Mizpah is probably the one in Gilead, east of the Jordan, with Mount Tabor to the west; what the snare there was is not said. Verse 2 is difficult Hebrew; some translations, by a small change, read a pit dug deep at Shittim, completing the picture of snare, net and pit.

verseByVerse.quote: Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God. For the spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the LORD. The pride of Israel testifies to his face; Israel and Ephraim shall stumble in his guilt; Judah also shall stumble with them. With their flocks and herds they shall go to seek the LORD, but they will not find him; he has withdrawn from them. They have dealt faithlessly with the LORD; for they have borne alien children. Now the new moon shall devour them with their fields.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s sin has become a power that holds it, so that even when the people come seeking God with sacrifices, they cannot find him.

Their deeds do not permit them to return. One of the most sobering verses in the book. Sin is not only something we do; it becomes something that holds us, for “the spirit of whoredom is within them”. Jesus said, “everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin” (John 8:34). No one should imagine they can live in sin for years and then turn back whenever they choose.

Can’t I stop whenever I want? Hosea says something our culture finds hard to believe: choices make choosers. In his Confessions Augustine describes his will as bound by a chain he had forged himself: a wrong desire, indulged, became a habit, and a habit, never resisted, became a necessity. That is the honest experience behind every addiction, and behind quieter habits too: the resentment that now rehearses itself, the screen we reach for without deciding to. Technique can help, but Augustine’s chain was broken when God turned his heart through a few words of Scripture in a garden in Milan, and the grace he had dreaded as the end of his freedom proved its beginning.

The pride of Israel testifies to his face. Israel’s pride stands up in court as a witness against it (the ESV notes that “to his face” may mean “in his presence”). Judah, warned in 4:15, will fall too.

But they will not find him. They bring flocks and herds to seek the LORD, but want his help without giving up their sin. “What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” (Isaiah 1:11). God cannot be bought with offerings; he is found by those who turn to him with the whole heart.

They have borne alien children. The parents’ unfaithfulness had produced children who did not belong to God, and the new moon, a festival they trusted, will bring judgment on their fields instead of blessing.

The Son who sets free. Jesus went straight on: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed” (John 8:36). Only his grace breaks the grip. And if you long to return, take heart: that longing is itself the sign that his grace is already at work in you (Philippians 2:13).

Uncertain wording. “Alien children” may be children born from the sexual rites of Baal worship, or a generation raised as strangers to God. Since the word for “new moon” can also mean “month”, verse 7 may mean that disaster will consume them within a month.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No earthly power can heal a wound that God has inflicted; he withdraws so that his people will seek him. Alarm horns sound along the border as Israel and Judah turn on each other, Judah’s princes grab land like boundary thieves, and Ephraim is crushed by its own settled choice (vv. 8–11). God has been the hidden moth and rot in both kingdoms. When they feel the sickness they send to Assyria, which cannot cure them, so God becomes a lion who tears and carries off (vv. 12–14). Then he returns to his place, waiting until they acknowledge their guilt and earnestly seek his face (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God's people must not seek healing from the powers of the world; God withdraws so that they will seek him.

verseByVerse.quote: Blow the horn in Gibeah, the trumpet in Ramah. Sound the alarm at Beth-aven; we follow you, O Benjamin! Ephraim shall become a desolation in the day of punishment; among the tribes of Israel I make known what is sure. The princes of Judah have become like those who move the landmark; upon them I will pour out my wrath like water. Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he was determined to go after filth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
War breaks out on the border between Israel and Judah, and God declares that both kingdoms, the one ruined by its idols and the other grabbing land in the chaos, will feel his judgment.

Blow the horn in Gibeah. Suddenly there is war. Alarm horns sound in Gibeah, Ramah and Beth-aven (Bethel, 4:15), border towns of Benjamin running north from Jerusalem, as if the alarm passed from town to town ahead of an army.

The historical background. Many think this describes the war of about 734 to 732 BC, when Israel joined Syria to attack Judah, and Judah’s King Ahaz called on Assyria for help (2 Kings 16:5–9; Isaiah 7:1–2). The two halves of God’s people were fighting each other, and both were about to be crushed by a foreign empire. Quarrelling believers still hand the advantage to the world.

Those who move the landmark. Moving a boundary stone stole a neighbour’s land, and God’s law forbade it (Deuteronomy 19:14). Judah’s leaders were doing it on a national scale, grabbing territory in the chaos of war.

Determined to go after filth. Ephraim’s suffering was the result of a settled choice.

Uncertain wording. “We follow you, O Benjamin” is obscure; the ESV notes it may be “after you”, perhaps a battle cry. In verse 11 “filth” translates a rare word that the ESV notes may mean “to follow human precepts”: man-made commands in place of God’s.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am like a moth to Ephraim, and like dry rot to the house of Judah. When Ephraim saw his sickness, and Judah his wound, then Ephraim went to Assyria, and sent to the great king. But he is not able to cure you or heal your wound. For I will be like a lion to Ephraim, and like a young lion to the house of Judah. I, even I, will tear and go away; I will carry off, and no one shall rescue.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself is the hidden decay eating away at both kingdoms and then the lion that tears them, and the Assyria they run to cannot heal a wound he has inflicted.

Like a moth to Ephraim. A moth eats through clothing unseen; dry rot eats wood from the inside. Nothing seems to happen, until one day the garment falls apart or the beam gives way. God’s judgment is not always sudden; sometimes it is a slow decay unnoticed until it is too late.

Ephraim went to Assyria. Both kingdoms noticed their sickness, but went to the superpower of the day instead of to God. King Menahem of Israel paid Assyria a fortune in silver (2 Kings 15:19–20), and King Ahaz of Judah begged, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me” (2 Kings 16:7). But “he is not able to cure you”; the same Assyria would destroy Israel.

Like a lion to Ephraim. Now the moth becomes a lion, the slow decay a sudden attack. And the lion is not Assyria but God: “I, even I, will tear”. Assyria would only be the instrument. Behind every judgment of history stands the Lord of history.

Who, then, can heal the wound? Only the God who struck it (6:1). And he did it in a way Hosea could hardly have imagined. Jesus came as the physician for the sick (Mark 2:17), and he healed his people by taking the wound himself: “by his wounds you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24, quoting Isaiah 53:5).

Our own Assyria. Every generation of believers is tempted to look for rescue in politics, money or human strength instead of in God. “In returning and rest you shall be saved,” God said through Isaiah, “But you were unwilling” (Isaiah 30:15).

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes that “the great king” may be a name, “King Jareb”. No Assyrian king of that name is known, so it is probably a title or a nickname (perhaps “King Quarrel”).

verseByVerse.quote: I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face, and in their distress earnestly seek me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God withdraws like a lion to its den, but his absence has a purpose: he waits until his people own their guilt and seek his face.

I will return again to my place. The lion goes back to its den and waits, but one word is full of hope: “until”. God waits not for better sacrifices or cleverer alliances, but for confession, and sometimes he lets his people run out of every other help so that they will finally look for him.

The prodigal’s return. That is exactly what the prodigal son did. “When he came to himself”, he said, “I will arise and go to my father”, and “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him” (Luke 15:17–20). The God who withdraws is watching the road. “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:8). And the Son was forsaken on the cross (Matthew 27:46) so that no one who seeks God through him will be turned away.

When God feels far away, is he punishing me? Not necessarily. Faithful believers have felt his absence without such a cause (Psalm 88), and to those in Christ he says, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). If sin has come between you, confess it. If the darkness does not lift, talk to your pastor or a biblical counsellor, and see a doctor too: a lasting low mood can have a physical side, and treating it is no failure of faith.

5.title: Until They Seek My Face
5.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 4 opened the sermons of Hosea with the LORD’s lawsuit against a land with “no knowledge of God” (4:1) and priests who fed on the people’s sin. Chapter 5 presses the same case against priests, people and king, and ends with God withdrawing like a lion to its den, just before the words “Come, let us return to the LORD” (6:1).

The message. Sin long loved becomes a grip that will not let go: Israel cannot simply decide to come back, cannot buy God’s favour with flocks and herds, and cannot find a cure for its wound in the superpower of the day. The God it has wounded is the only one who can heal it, and he withdraws, not to be rid of his people, but to wait until they own their guilt and seek his face.

Why it was said. These were the years of murdered kings and tribute paid to Assyria (see the introduction). Around 734 to 732 BC Israel and Judah were even at war with each other, while the shrines stayed busy.

How the chapter makes its case. The leaders who should have guarded Israel have trapped it, and God, who knows Ephraim through and through, will discipline them all (vv. 1–3). Their deeds now hold them, and they seek the LORD with their flocks and cannot find him (vv. 4–7). Alarm horns sound on the border as the two kingdoms turn on each other, and God’s wrath is coming on both (vv. 8–11). He has been the hidden moth and rot in their life; when they feel the wound they run to the great king, who cannot heal it, so the moth becomes a lion (vv. 12–14). Then the lion goes back to its place, “until” (v. 15).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and the character of God it reveals. Israel has a wound no king can heal, and Jesus came as the physician of the sick (Mark 2:17), healing his people by being wounded himself: “by his wounds you have been healed” (1 Peter 2:24). The God who withdrew from a people who would not seek him is the God who, at the cross, turned his face from his own Son, who cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that all who seek him in Christ will find him.

For us. We still run to our own Assyria when life hurts: money, influence, a new strategy, anything but humble return. If God seems far away, the way back is the one this chapter names: own your guilt, seek his face, and find that in Christ the Father has been watching the road.
5.theology:
Religious leaders, people and rulers are all accountable to God, and nothing is hidden from him (vv. 1-3).

Persistent sin enslaves, so that people cannot return to God without his grace (v. 4; John 8:34).

Religious ritual without repentance cannot find God (v. 6; Isa 1:11).

God's judgment may work slowly like decay or suddenly like a lion, and he stands behind the powers he uses (vv. 12, 14).

God's people must not seek from the world's powers the healing only God can give (v. 13; Isa 30:15).

God withdraws in order to bring his people to confess their guilt and seek his face, and he receives those who return (v. 15; Luke 15:17-20; Jas 4:8).
5.examples: Places of worship have become hunters' traps, and a people cannot return because their sins hold them; they bring their flocks and cannot find God. Judgment comes quietly, like a moth in the closet and rot in the beams, and a sick nation asks the superpower for a cure. Then the lion tears, goes back to its den, and waits for them to seek his face.

keyVerse.quote: I will return again to my place, until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face, and in their distress earnestly seek me.
keyVerse.note: The chapter has shown a people who cannot find God with their sacrifices and cannot find healing in Assyria. This verse shows why God has withdrawn and what he is waiting for: not better offerings, but confession and seeking his face. The little word “until” turns judgment into an invitation, and leads straight into the call to return in 6:1.

5.reflection:
Verse 4 says, “Their deeds do not permit them to return to their God.” How can a habit of sin come to hold a person? Where have you seen this, and what hope does the gospel give to someone who feels unable to turn back?

Israel went with flocks and herds to seek the LORD but did not find him (v. 6). Why can religious activity fail to reach God? What does it look like to seek him with the whole heart?

When Ephraim saw his sickness, he went to Assyria (v. 13). What are the “Assyrias” people run to when life hurts, and why can they not heal us? How has Christ dealt with the wound they cannot reach?

God withdraws “until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face” (v. 15). How can a season when God seems far away become a turning point? How should we help a friend who feels that God is absent?

When I restore the fortunes of my people,

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The words of return are right: the God who wounds is the God who heals, and he raises his people to live before him. The people urge one another to come back to the LORD, trusting that he has torn in order to heal (v. 1). They expect revival quickly, “after two days”, and a raising up “on the third day” (v. 2), and they resolve to press on to know the LORD, as certain of his coming as of sunrise and spring rain (v. 3). Every word is true. Whether the speakers mean them is the question the rest of the chapter answers, and the third day points beyond them to Christ.
verseByVerse.theology: The God who wounds in judgment heals those who return to him, and raises them up to live before him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people call one another back to the God who has wounded them in order to heal them; the words are right, but the chapter will ask whether they mean them.

Come, let us return to the LORD. God had withdrawn “until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face” (5:15). Now we hear words of return, and they are beautiful and exactly right: the lion of 5:14 is also the physician. “He has torn us, that he may heal us.” God’s wounds are meant not to destroy his people but to bring them back: the hand that strikes is the hand that binds up (Deuteronomy 32:39), as “the Lord disciplines the one he loves” (Hebrews 12:6).

Where Christians differ: who is speaking, and do they mean it? Many believe these are the people’s words, a quick, easy repentance that assumes God will simply fix everything, and that God’s sad reply in verse 4 shows it was not real. Others believe this is Hosea himself calling the people to genuine repentance, a pattern of what true return looks like. This commentary’s view: the first fits the passage better, because God’s reply treats this repentance as a morning cloud that goes early away (v. 4). Either way, the words are true; the question is whether they come from the heart. It is possible to say all the right things about returning to God and still not return.

verseByVerse.quote: After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up, that we may live before him. Let us know; let us press on to know the LORD; his going out is sure as the dawn; he will come to us as the showers, as the spring rains that water the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The people are confident that God will soon revive them and that he will come to them as surely as the dawn; their hope of a rising on the third day points beyond them to Christ.

After two days he will revive us. A way of saying “very soon”. The speakers are confident that God will revive the nation, raising it from its sickness as if from death, “that we may live before him”.

Let us press on to know the LORD. The missing knowledge of God (4:1, 6) is exactly what they now long for. They are sure God will come like sunrise and like the spring rains; the contrast with Baal, the supposed rain-giver, is deliberate.

On the third day. Many Christians have heard in this verse a pointer to something greater. Jesus said, “Thus it is written, that the Christ should suffer and on the third day rise from the dead” (Luke 24:46), and Paul says Christ “was raised on the third day in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4). Neither passage names Hosea, and we should not claim more than the text says, but the pattern is striking. Israel hoped to be raised up on the third day to live before God. That hope was fulfilled in the one true Israelite, Jesus, who was raised on the third day, and in whom all who belong to him are raised to new life. Our hope of revival is not in our own quick repentance but in his resurrection.

How do I press on to know the LORD? This is a good prayer to make our own, for knowing God is not a single moment but a lifelong pursuit. It is more than knowing about him, though it starts there; it is the knowledge of a friend, deepened by time together. Go where he has shown himself. Jesus said, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), so read the Gospels slowly, asking what each passage shows you of him. Answer him. Turn what you have read into prayer before you close the book, even a single sentence. Obey the next thing. You know a person better by walking with him than by reading his letters; the command you keep teaches you more of God than the one you only study. Keep going when it is dry. “Press on” means effort over time, and the morning-cloud love of verse 4 is the warning. Weeks when nothing seems to happen are part of the road. And remember who began it. Paul pressed on to know Christ “because Christ Jesus has made me his own” (Philippians 3:12).
verseByVerse.note: “On the third day”: many have heard in this an echo fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–11 — Your Love Is Like a Morning Cloud
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers that their love is as passing as morning mist; what he wants is steadfast love and the knowledge of himself, not ritual. He grieves over Ephraim and Judah, whose love vanishes like the dew, and so he has sent his prophets with words that cut (vv. 4–5). Then he states his desire: steadfast love rather than sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings, the verse Jesus quoted twice (v. 6). But Israel has broken covenant like Adam, Gilead runs with blood, and priests ambush travellers on the road to Shechem (vv. 7–9). God has seen the horror, and Judah too has a harvest appointed (vv. 10–11).
verseByVerse.theology: God is not satisfied with religious ritual; he desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? What shall I do with you, O Judah? Your love is like a morning cloud, like the dew that goes early away. Therefore I have hewn them by the prophets; I have slain them by the words of my mouth, and my judgment goes forth as the light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God grieves over a love that vanishes like morning mist, and so he has sent his prophets with words that cut.

What shall I do with you, O Ephraim? God answers like a heartbroken parent. He is not puzzled; he is grieved. Their love is like a morning mist that promises rain and is gone when the sun rises. The feeling in Israel’s repentance was real, but it was gone by mid-morning.

I have hewn them by the prophets. Because their love was so shallow, God sent them words that cut like an axe. His word is not only comfort; it wounds in order to heal. And his “judgment goes forth as the light”: clear, open and impossible to escape.

Morning-dew religion. Many of us know this kind of love for God. A moving sermon, a crisis, a season of revival, and we are full of devotion; a week later it has evaporated. God wants steadfast love, love that lasts through the heat of the day, and such love is not worked up by effort: it is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22), the answer of hearts into which God’s own love has been poured (Romans 5:5). “Godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation,” Paul says, “whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Corinthians 7:10). The difference is whether it changes the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What God wants above all religious ceremony is loyal love and a real knowledge of himself.

I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice. Perhaps the best-known verse in Hosea, and one of the most important in the Old Testament. God does not reject sacrifice altogether; he commanded it. “Not sacrifice” is a Hebrew way of saying “more than sacrifice”, as the second line shows: “rather than burnt offerings”. What he truly wants is steadfast love, loyal covenant love towards him and towards others, and the knowledge of God. Sacrifices without them are worthless to him. Samuel said it long before: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (1 Samuel 15:22). Micah, preaching in the same years, said it too: “what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8). David understood it: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

Jesus quoted this verse. Twice. When the Pharisees criticised him for eating with tax collectors and sinners, he said, “Go and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice.’ For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matthew 9:13). And when they condemned his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, he said, “if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless” (Matthew 12:7). (His wording follows the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, which reads “mercy”, as the ESV notes.)

How does Jesus use it? In Matthew 9 the Pharisees kept away from “sinners” to stay ceremonially clean, as if what mattered most to God were the rules of ritual purity. Jesus sends them back to their own Bible: God, through Hosea, puts loyal love and mercy above ritual. He is not inventing a new meaning. He is applying Hosea’s point to the very people who knew the verse best, and showing that in eating with sinners he was doing what God’s heart desires.

Why this matters. Religious people are always tempted to think God is pleased with correct ritual and attendance while their hearts stay cold. God says no. And Christ himself fulfilled this verse perfectly: he offered the one sacrifice that truly pleased God, out of steadfast love, and his perfect love is counted as theirs for all who trust him, though their own love has been like the dew.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus quoted this twice.

verseByVerse.quote: But like Adam they transgressed the covenant; there they dealt faithlessly with me. Gilead is a city of evildoers, tracked with blood. As robbers lie in wait for a man, so the priests band together; they murder on the way to Shechem; they commit villainy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has broken God’s covenant as Adam did, and its priests have turned even the road to a city of refuge into a place of murder.

Like Adam they transgressed the covenant. Whatever “Adam” means here (see Uncertain wording below), the charge is clear: they broke the covenant, and “there they dealt faithlessly with me”, the faithlessness of an unfaithful spouse.

Gilead is a city of evildoers. A town in Gilead, east of the Jordan, has blood on its streets. Hosea may be remembering how Pekah seized the throne with “fifty men of the people of Gilead” and murdered King Pekahiah (2 Kings 15:25).

So the priests band together. The priests behave like a gang of highway robbers, ambushing travellers on the road to Shechem. Shechem was one of the cities of refuge, where someone who had killed a person by accident could flee for protection (Joshua 20:7). The priests turned the road to safety into a place of murder. The shepherds had become wolves.

Another Adam. If, as this commentary judges likelier, Hosea means the first man, he reminds us of something the whole Bible teaches. Adam stood for all humanity, and in him we all sinned; Israel’s failure was the same failure repeated. That is why we need another Adam who would keep covenant perfectly, the one of whom Adam was “a type of the one who was to come” (Romans 5:14), Jesus Christ.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew can mean “like Adam” or “at Adam”, a town by the Jordan (Joshua 3:16), and “there” in the next line suggests a place. But no sin at the town of Adam is recorded, and the comparison with the first man who broke God’s command fits the charge. The likelier reading is “like Adam”, which supports the Reformed teaching that God dealt with Adam by covenant, though that doctrine rests on more than this verse (Romans 5:12–21).

verseByVerse.quote: In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing; Ephraim's whoredom is there; Israel is defiled. For you also, O Judah, a harvest is appointed. When I restore the fortunes of my people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has seen Israel’s unfaithfulness and is horrified, and Judah too faces a harvest of judgment, yet even here he speaks of restoring his people.

A horrible thing. God has seen it himself. The unfaithfulness of his people is not a small matter to him; it horrifies him.

A harvest is appointed. Judah too will reap what it has sown. The last line, “When I restore the fortunes of my people”, begins a sentence that continues into chapter 7. Even in a chapter of judgment, God speaks of restoring his people. He has not given up, but first he must deal with their sin.

Two truths we need. God truly heals those who return to him, and raises them up to live before him. But he is not fooled by morning-dew religion; he desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself. The only one who has ever offered God both perfectly is Jesus Christ, and it is in him, crucified and raised on the third day, that we can return and live.

Uncertain wording. A “harvest” in the prophets is usually a picture of judgment (Joel 3:13), and that fits the warning to Judah here; some read it as a harvest of blessing when God restores his people. The punctuation is uncertain too: the closing words may finish the sentence about Judah’s harvest, or, as the ESV takes them, begin a sentence that runs on into 7:1.

6.title: Steadfast Love and Not Sacrifice
6.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 5 ended with God withdrawing like a lion to its den, “until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face” (5:15). Chapter 6 opens with the very words he was waiting for, “Come, let us return to the LORD”, and then gives God’s answer. It is the heart of the first round of Hosea’s sermons (chapters 4 to 7).

The message. It is possible to say all the right words about returning to God and still not return. Israel’s love rises like a morning cloud and is gone by mid-morning, and its worship is full of sacrifice and empty of loyalty. What God wants is not more ritual but steadfast love and a real knowledge of himself, and he will not be satisfied with less.

Why it was said. Israel was a busy, religious nation in the last decades before its fall, quick to turn to God in a crisis and quick to forget him afterwards, while its priests and leaders shed blood (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. First the people speak: the God who tore will heal, he will raise us up on the third day, let us press on to know him (vv. 1–3). Then God answers with grief: what shall I do with you, when your love is like the dew (vv. 4–5)? He states what he truly desires: steadfast love, not sacrifice; knowledge of God, not burnt offerings (v. 6). And he shows how far they are from it: like Adam they have broken covenant, Gilead is tracked with blood, priests murder on the road to Shechem, and Judah’s harvest is coming too (vv. 7–11).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, by his own use of verse 6, and by the need the chapter exposes. Israel hoped to be raised “on the third day” to live before God; that hope came true in the one faithful Israelite, Jesus, raised on the third day “in accordance with the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:4). Jesus twice quoted verse 6 to explain why he ate with sinners (Matthew 9:13; 12:7). And a people who broke covenant “like Adam” needed another Adam who would keep it: Christ offered God the steadfast love Israel never gave, and his love is counted as ours.

For us. Our devotion can be as quick to rise and fade as Israel’s. The answer is not to work up stronger feelings but to come to Christ, whose love for us does not evaporate, and to press on to know the LORD, day after day, in his word, in prayer and in mercy to others.
6.theology:
The God who wounds in judgment heals those who return to him (v. 1).

God revives his people and raises them up to live before him, a hope fulfilled in Christ, raised on the third day (v. 2; Luke 24:46; 1 Cor 15:4).

Knowing God is a lifelong pursuit (v. 3).

Shallow, passing devotion does not satisfy God; true repentance changes the heart (v. 4; 2 Cor 7:10).

God desires steadfast love and the knowledge of himself more than religious ritual, as Jesus taught (v. 6; Matt 9:13; 12:7; 1 Sam 15:22; Mic 6:8; Ps 51:17).

Israel repeated Adam's covenant-breaking, and all humanity needs the last Adam, Jesus Christ (v. 7; Rom 5:14).
6.examples: A lion tears in order to heal, and a people promise themselves a rising on the third day. But their love vanishes like morning mist, like a worshipper with perfect attendance and a cold heart, and their priests ambush travellers on the road to a city of refuge. Centuries later Jesus eats with sinners and quotes Hosea to explain why.

keyVerse.quote: For I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice, the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.
keyVerse.note: Everything in the chapter turns on this verse. The people’s fine words and passing feelings (vv. 1–4) and their busy, bloody religion (vv. 7–10) are measured against what God actually wants: loyal love and a real knowledge of him. Jesus quoted it twice to explain why he welcomed sinners, and he alone has offered God the love it describes.

6.reflection:
The people’s words in verses 1–3 sound like genuine repentance, yet God answers that their love is “like a morning cloud” (v. 4). What is the difference between saying the right things and truly returning to God? How can we tell the difference in ourselves?

“Let us press on to know the LORD” (v. 3). What helps you know God, not just know about him? What makes it hard to keep going when it feels dry?

Jesus quoted verse 6 when he was criticised for eating with sinners (Matthew 9:13). Where might we put religious correctness above mercy today? What would it look like for your church to follow Jesus here?

Israel broke covenant “like Adam” (v. 7). How does Christ, raised “on the third day”, answer both our failure and our fading love? What difference does it make that his steadfast love is counted as ours?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Whenever God comes near to heal, he finds a nation burning with treachery, where kings fall one after another and no one calls on him. His desire to heal Israel exposes deceit, theft and banditry, and a people who forget that God remembers all their evil (vv. 1–2). The court delights in wickedness, and its passions are like a baker’s oven, smouldering through the night and blazing at dawn (vv. 3–4). At a royal feast the princes drink themselves sick while conspirators wait their moment (vv. 5–6). So the oven devours its rulers: “All their kings have fallen, and none of them calls upon me” (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Hearts inflamed by lust for power consume leaders and nations, while no one calls on God.

verseByVerse.quote: when I would heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim is revealed, and the evil deeds of Samaria, for they deal falsely; the thief breaks in, and the bandits raid outside. But they do not consider that I remember all their evil. Now their deeds surround them; they are before my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whenever God comes near to heal Israel, he uncovers more sin, and the people do not reckon with a God who remembers it all.

When I would heal Israel. The sentence begun in 6:11, “When I restore the fortunes of my people”, runs on: “when I would heal Israel, the iniquity of Ephraim is revealed”. Like a doctor who lifts the bandage to treat a wound and finds infection everywhere, God’s desire to heal exposes how sick Israel is. Inside the houses, thieves break in; outside, bandits raid. Society is coming apart.

They do not consider that I remember. Their great mistake was to think God forgets. Sin they have long forgotten is still “before my face”, and their deeds now surround them like witnesses in court. The only way for sin to be forgotten by God is for it to be forgiven, and that is what the new covenant in Christ’s blood promises: “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12).

verseByVerse.quote: By their evil they make the king glad, and the princes by their treachery. They are all adulterers; they are like a heated oven whose baker ceases to stir the fire, from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened. On the day of our king, the princes became sick with the heat of wine; he stretched out his hand with mockers. For with hearts like an oven they approach their intrigue; all night their anger smolders; in the morning it blazes like a flaming fire. All of them are hot as an oven, and they devour their rulers. All their kings have fallen, and none of them calls upon me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s court is like a baker’s oven, its passions and plots smouldering through the night and bursting into flame, so that one king after another is devoured and none of them prays.

By their evil they make the king glad. The rulers enjoy the wickedness around them and reward it. When leaders delight in evil, a nation is in deep trouble.

Like a heated oven. A baker lets his fire smoulder overnight while the dough rises with its leaven; in the morning it blazes. So the people’s passions, both sexual and political, smoulder quietly and then burst into flame.

On the day of our king. The scene seems to be a royal celebration. The king and his officials drink themselves sick, the king joins hands with mockers, and conspirators wait their moment: all night they plot, in the morning they strike.

All their kings have fallen. Exactly what happened in Hosea’s lifetime. Of the last six kings of Israel, four were murdered by the men who replaced them: Shallum killed Zechariah, Menahem killed Shallum, Pekah killed Pekahiah, and Hoshea killed Pekah (2 Kings 15:10, 14, 25, 30).

None of them calls upon me. The saddest line is the last. In all the turmoil, not one king or plotter turned to God. A nation in crisis burned through one leader after another and never once prayed. Against them stands the King who prayed all night (Luke 6:12) and whose throne no conspiracy could take.

Uncertain wording. The oven picture is some of the hardest Hebrew in the book, and the details (who the baker is, why he stops stirring) are uncertain, though the meaning of smouldering passion is clear. In verse 6 the Hebrew reads “their baker sleeps”; most translations, by a slight change, read “their anger smoulders”. “The day of our king” may be a coronation or a royal festival, and “he stretched out his hand with mockers” probably means he made common cause with scoffers.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel has compromised with the nations until it is half-baked, blind to its decline and turning everywhere except to God. Ephraim is a cake not turned, drained by foreigners and greying without noticing, yet for all this does not seek the LORD (vv. 8–10). It flutters like a silly dove between Egypt and Assyria, straight into God’s net, though he would redeem it (vv. 11–13). Its people wail on their beds and gash themselves for grain and wine instead of crying to God from the heart, and they use the strength he gave them against him (vv. 14–15). They turn, but not upward, like a bow that cannot shoot straight (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Compromise with the world leaves God's people half-baked, blind to their decline and turning everywhere except to God.

verseByVerse.quote: Ephraim mixes himself with the peoples; Ephraim is a cake not turned. Strangers devour his strength, and he knows it not; gray hairs are sprinkled upon him, and he knows it not. The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they do not return to the LORD their God, nor seek him, for all this.
verseByVerse.commentary:
By mixing with the nations Israel has become half-baked and is declining without noticing, yet for all its troubles it will not return to God.

Ephraim is a cake not turned. Israel “mixes himself with the peoples”, blending its faith and life with the nations’ gods, politics and ways. The result is a flat bread cooked on hot stones and never flipped: burned black on one side, raw on the other. Useless. When God’s people try to belong half to him and half to the world, they end up neither truly godly nor truly worldly; the world does not respect them, and their witness is spoiled.

He knows it not. Twice. Foreign powers were draining Israel’s wealth through tribute, and grey hairs, signs of age and decline, had appeared, and no one noticed. The nation thought it was still young and strong. Spiritual decline rarely announces itself; it creeps in until one day the strength is gone. Samson woke and meant to go out as before, “But he did not know that the LORD had left him” (Judges 16:20). Against that slow drift God gives his people one another: “exhort one another every day … that none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin” (Hebrews 3:13).

Yet they do not return. “For all this”: the disasters, the murdered kings, the tribute, the decline. Suffering alone does not bring people back to God; pride keeps them away. (The ESV notes that “to his face” may mean “in his presence”.)

verseByVerse.quote: Ephraim is like a dove, silly and without sense, calling to Egypt, going to Assyria. As they go, I will spread over them my net; I will bring them down like birds of the heavens; I will discipline them according to the report made to their congregation. Woe to them, for they have strayed from me! Destruction to them, for they have rebelled against me! I would redeem them, but they speak lies against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel flutters like a senseless dove between Egypt and Assyria, flying straight into God’s net, though he longs to redeem it.

Like a dove, silly and without sense. A dove flutters first one way, then the other, and so did Israel’s foreign policy. Its kings paid tribute to Assyria, and then the last king, Hoshea, secretly sent to So, king of Egypt, for help against Assyria (2 Kings 17:3–4). They looked for safety everywhere except in God, and neither power could save them.

I will spread over them my net. A bird that flies about carelessly ends up in the hunter’s net, and here God himself is the hunter. Their scheming led straight into his judgment, as they had been warned.

I would redeem them. Here is God’s heart in the middle of judgment. What stood in the way was not his unwillingness but their lies. Jesus wept over Jerusalem with the same sorrow: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). And he did what Hosea’s hearers refused: he paid the price of redemption himself.

Uncertain wording. “According to the report made to their congregation” is obscure. It may mean that God will discipline them just as the warnings read to Israel’s assembly had said (Deuteronomy 28), or as their own disasters were reported among them.
verseByVerse.note: Israel swung between Egypt and Assyria for help.

verseByVerse.quote: They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds; for grain and wine they gash themselves; they rebel against me. Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me. They return, but not upward; they are like a treacherous bow; their princes shall fall by the sword because of the insolence of their tongue. This shall be their derision in the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel cries out about its troubles but not to God, turning in every direction except upward.

They do not cry to me from the heart. They wailed on their beds about their troubles, and to get grain and wine they gashed themselves, as the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel “cut themselves after their custom with swords and lances” (1 Kings 18:28) while Elijah watched. Desperate enough to bleed for a harvest, not humble enough to turn to the God who gives it. There is a difference between being sorry for our troubles and being sorry for our sin.

Although I trained and strengthened their arms. God had given Israel its strength, trained it like a father teaching a son to fight, and they used that strength to plot against him: ingratitude twice over.

They return, but not upward. They turned, but to Egypt, to Assyria, to Baal, never up to God. They are like a treacherous bow, a warped bow whose arrows never hit the target, and the Egypt they trusted would one day laugh at them.

True repentance. It is not just turning away from trouble but turning upward, to God. And the good news of the gospel is that when we turn upward, we find that God has already come down to us in Christ.

Uncertain wording. Some manuscripts read “gash themselves”, which the ESV follows; most Hebrew manuscripts have a word differing by one similar-looking letter, usually taken to mean “they gather together” (perhaps for harvest rites). Either way they were seeking grain and wine, not God. For “not upward” the ESV notes that it may mean “not to the Most High”.

7.title: A Cake Not Turned
7.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 6 ended with God speaking of the day “when I restore the fortunes of my people”, and chapter 7 finishes the sentence: “when I would heal Israel”, he finds fresh sin. It closes the first round of Hosea’s sermons (chapters 4 to 7), which began with a land without the knowledge of God.

The message. Every time God comes near to heal, he uncovers more disease. Israel is burning up with lust and political intrigue, murdering its kings, mixing itself with the nations and fluttering between superpowers, and through all of it no one calls on God. He longs to redeem them, but they turn everywhere except upward.

Why it was said. In the thirty years after Jeroboam II died, four of Israel’s six kings were murdered by the men who replaced them, and its rulers swung between paying tribute to Assyria and begging help from Egypt (see the introduction). Hosea watched it happen.

How the chapter makes its case. God’s desire to heal exposes thieves and bandits and a people who think he forgets (vv. 1–2). Like an oven smouldering all night and blazing at dawn, the court’s passions and plots devour one king after another, and none of them calls on God (vv. 3–7). Ephraim is a half-baked cake, drained by foreigners and grey without knowing it, yet for all this does not return (vv. 8–10). He is a silly dove flying to Egypt and Assyria into God’s net, though God would redeem him (vv. 11–13). He wails on his bed and gashes himself for grain, and turns, but not upward (vv. 14–16).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need the chapter exposes and by the heart of God it reveals. A nation whose kings fall one after another, none of them praying, needs a King who calls upon God and cannot be overthrown. And the God who says, “I would redeem them”, is the God who wept in Jesus over Jerusalem’s refusal (Matthew 23:37) and then redeemed his people at the cross, where the sins he said he remembered were remembered no more (Hebrews 8:12).

For us. Spiritual decline rarely announces itself; it comes like grey hairs. We can be busy, anxious and full of plans and still never pray. The way back is not merely turning away from trouble but turning upward, to the God who has already come down to us in Christ.
7.theology:
God remembers all sin until it is forgiven, and his desire to heal exposes the depth of sin (vv. 1-2).

Lust for power and pleasure consumes leaders and nations, especially when no one calls on God (vv. 3-7).

Mixing with the world leaves God's people half-baked, and spiritual decline often goes unnoticed (vv. 8-9; Judg 16:20; Heb 3:13).

Trusting in worldly powers instead of God is senseless and ends in judgment (vv. 11-12; 2 Kgs 17:3-4).

God longs to redeem, but sinners refuse him (v. 13; Matt 23:37).

Crying out over troubles is not the same as crying to God from the heart; true repentance turns upward to God (vv. 14-16).
7.examples: A doctor lifts the bandage and finds infection everywhere, while the throne passes from one assassin to the next. Israel is a flatbread burned on one side and raw on the other, with grey hairs nobody notices, and a dove fluttering between two superpowers. Its people will bleed for a harvest but will not pray, and like a warped bow they never hit the target.

keyVerse.quote: The pride of Israel testifies to his face; yet they do not return to the LORD their God, nor seek him, for all this.
keyVerse.note: This verse gathers up the whole chapter. Murdered kings, foreign tribute and creeping decline have all failed to turn Israel back, because pride stands in the way. “For all this” is God’s verdict on a people who will turn anywhere but to him, and it sets up the chapter’s last picture: “They return, but not upward” (v. 16).

7.reflection:
“They do not consider that I remember all their evil” (v. 2). Why do people find it easy to assume God forgets? How does the promise “I will remember their sins no more” (Hebrews 8:12) change the way we deal with our sin?

Ephraim is “a cake not turned” and has grey hairs without knowing it (vv. 8–9). What are the signs of half-hearted faith or slow spiritual decline? How can Christian friends help each other notice them?

Israel’s kings fell one after another, “and none of them calls upon me” (v. 7). When life is in turmoil, why is prayer often the last thing we turn to? What would turning to God first look like this week?

“They return, but not upward” (v. 16). What is the difference between being sorry for our troubles and being sorry for our sin? How does God’s longing to redeem (v. 13), seen in Christ, invite us to turn upward?
