verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — They Made Kings, but Not Through Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel claims to know God while making its own kings and its own gods, and what it sows as wind it will reap as whirlwind. The trumpet sounds because an enemy hovers like an eagle over the LORD’s house, for Israel has broken his covenant and law, though it cries, “My God, we … know you” (vv. 1–3). It made kings without asking him and idols from the silver and gold he gave, and the calf of Samaria, made by a craftsman, will be smashed (vv. 4–6). Empty sowing brings a destroying harvest: the grain will fail, or strangers will eat it (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Religious words cannot cover a life that rejects God's rule, and those who sow emptiness will reap destruction.

verseByVerse.quote: Set the trumpet to your lips! One like a vulture is over the house of the LORD, because they have transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law. To me they cry, "My God, we—Israel—know you." Israel has spurned the good; the enemy shall pursue him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An enemy is circling over God’s people because they have broken his covenant, and their claim to know him is empty.

Set the trumpet to your lips! Blow the alarm! An enemy, Assyria, circles like a vulture over God’s people, ready to swoop. “The house of the LORD” here most likely means God’s land and people, his household. The reason is plain: “they have transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law.” The danger from outside was the result of sin inside, as Moses had warned of a nation “swooping down like the eagle” (Deuteronomy 28:49).

To me they cry. They say the right words: “My God, we (Israel) know you.” But chapter 4 has already said there was “no knowledge of God in the land” (4:1). Their confession was empty. “Israel has spurned the good”, God himself and his ways, so the enemy will pursue him.

Jesus’ warning. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father”; to many who claim great deeds in his name he will say, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:21–23). The question is not whether we claim to know God, but whether he knows us as his own, and the good shepherd says, “I know my own and my own know me” (John 10:14).

Uncertain wording. The bird is a nesher, a word used of both the eagle and the vulture; either way it is a bird of prey about to strike. Some take “the house of the LORD” as the temple, but in the northern kingdom it more likely means the land and people as God’s household (9:15).

verseByVerse.quote: They made kings, but not through me. They set up princes, but I knew it not. With their silver and gold they made idols for their own destruction. I have spurned your calf, O Samaria. My anger burns against them. How long will they be incapable of innocence? For it is from Israel; a craftsman made it; it is not God. The calf of Samaria shall be broken to pieces. For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. The standing grain has no heads; it shall yield no flour; if it were to yield, strangers would devour it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has made its own kings and its own gods without God, and what it sows as empty wind it will reap as a destroying whirlwind.

They made kings, but not through me. Two sins stand side by side. First, the northern kingdom’s kings came to power by murder and conspiracy (7:7), not by God’s choosing; “I knew it not” means not that God was unaware but that he had not approved. Second, they made idols from the silver and gold God had given them (2:8). Both took control away from God, in government and in worship.

I have spurned your calf, O Samaria. The golden calves that Jeroboam son of Nebat had set up at Bethel and Dan nearly two centuries earlier, telling the people, “Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (1 Kings 12:28). The people probably thought of it as a pedestal for the LORD; God calls it an idol. “How long will they be incapable of innocence?” he asks with sorrow: they had grown so used to sin that they could not imagine living without it.

A craftsman made it; it is not God. The simple truth about every idol: something people made cannot save the people who made it. Isaiah mocked the man who cooks his dinner over half a log, makes the other half into a god and “prays to it and says, ‘Deliver me, for you are my god!’” (Isaiah 44:17).

They sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. One of the most memorable sayings in the Bible. What they planted was empty, nothing but wind: idols, political schemes, false confidence. What they would harvest was a tornado of destruction. Sin always brings a far worse harvest than the little that was sown. “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

The standing grain has no heads. In Hebrew the line rhymes, like a proverb: stalks with no grain, and if any grain came, foreign armies would eat it.

The King God chose. Against all these self-made kings stands the King God himself appoints: “I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill” (Psalm 2:6). The New Testament hears that psalm fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 13:33), the King who came not by conspiracy but by God’s choosing. And Paul goes straight on from the harvest of the flesh to the other harvest: the one who sows to the Spirit reaps eternal life (Galatians 6:8). The God Israel spurned is still calling his people home (14:1).

Uncertain wording. “I have spurned” is literally “He has spurned”, as the ESV notes. The word translated “broken to pieces” occurs only here; the ESV notes it may mean “shall go up in flames”.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — Israel Has Forgotten His Maker
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Swallowed by the nations it imitated, Israel has forgotten its Maker and trusts in altars, palaces and walls. It has become a useless vessel among the nations, a stubborn wild donkey that has gone to Assyria and pays its lovers, and the tribute will crush its king and princes (vv. 8–10). Its many altars have become altars for sinning, God’s law seems foreign to it, and he will not accept its sacrifices, so they will go back to Egypt’s bondage (vv. 11–13). Israel has forgotten its Maker and built palaces, Judah has multiplied fortified cities, and fire will devour them both (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Those who forget their Maker and trust in their own security will lose everything they built.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel is swallowed up; already they are among the nations as a useless vessel. For they have gone up to Assyria, a wild donkey wandering alone; Ephraim has hired lovers. Though they hire allies among the nations, I will soon gather them up. And the king and princes shall soon writhe because of the tribute.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel tried to be like the nations and is being swallowed by them, paying lovers for a protection that will crush it.

A useless vessel. Israel wanted to be like the nations; now they were swallowing it, a cracked pot no one wants. God’s people were meant to be his treasured possession (Exodus 19:5). By imitating the world, they became worthless even in the world’s eyes. In Christ God makes a people his own possession again (1 Peter 2:9).

A wild donkey wandering alone. The Hebrew for wild donkey (pere) sounds like Ephraim. Even wild donkeys keep to their herd, but this one wanders alone, gone off to Assyria. And “Ephraim has hired lovers”: a prostitute is normally paid, but Israel was paying its lovers. That was the tribute Israel’s kings paid Assyria for protection (2 Kings 15:19–20; 17:3).

The king and princes shall soon writhe. The protection money would crush them. Alliances bought with money are chains, not safety.

Uncertain wording. Verse 10 is difficult Hebrew. The ESV’s “writhe because of the tribute” is one reading; another is that they will soon begin to dwindle under “the burden of the king of princes”, a title for the Assyrian emperor. Both describe the same crushing weight.

verseByVerse.quote: Because Ephraim has multiplied altars for sinning, they have become to him altars for sinning. Were I to write for him my laws by the ten thousands, they would be regarded as a strange thing. As for my sacrificial offerings, they sacrifice meat and eat it, but the LORD does not accept them. Now he will remember their iniquity and punish their sins; they shall return to Egypt. For Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces, and Judah has multiplied fortified cities; so I will send a fire upon his cities, and it shall devour her strongholds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s many altars and many buildings show that it has forgotten its Maker, and the fire of judgment will consume both.

Altars for sinning. Israel built many altars, supposedly to deal with sin, but because they served false worship, the altars themselves became places of more sin. Religion without truth does not remove sin; it multiplies it.

They would be regarded as a strange thing. Israel did not lack God’s law. He could write it ten thousand times, and they would still treat it as foreign, nothing to do with them. It is possible to have Bibles in every room and still treat God’s word as strange.

They sacrifice meat and eat it. Their sacrifices had become barbecues: they killed animals and enjoyed the feast, but God accepted none of it. And the punishment would be a terrible reversal: “they shall return to Egypt”. God had brought them out of slavery; now they would go back into bondage, as Moses had warned: “back in ships to Egypt, a journey that I promised that you should never make again” (Deuteronomy 28:68). Egypt here stands for the slavery and exile Assyria would soon bring.

Israel has forgotten his Maker. The root of it all. And forgetfulness of God looks like building palaces and fortified cities, trusting wealth and walls. Judah did it too, and God would send fire on both. Assyria destroyed Samaria’s palaces, and later Sennacherib “came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them” (2 Kings 18:13).

The Maker who came. The Maker Israel forgot came in person: “All things were made through him” (John 1:3), and “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11). He offered the sacrifice God accepted, and he gives what no wall can, “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).

How people still forget. Not usually by openly rejecting God, but by building their own security and forgetting they need him.

Uncertain wording. “My sacrificial offerings” translates a rare word of uncertain meaning, but the line plainly says that God refuses them.

8.title: They Sow the Wind
8.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 8 begins the second round of Hosea’s sermons (chapters 8 to 11), which traces Israel’s kings, calves and alliances to their end in exile. The first round ended with a people who turned everywhere “but not upward” (7:16); now the trumpet sounds, for the enemy is overhead.

The message. Israel says, “My God, we … know you”, but it has made its own kings without God and its own god out of his silver and gold, bought its own protection from Assyria and built its own palaces and walls. Everything it trusted was its own making, and so it will all be swept away: “they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind”. A people who forget their Maker lose everything they built without him.

Why it was said. In Hosea’s last years Israel’s kings came and went by murder, its shrines and calves flourished, and its rulers paid crushing tribute to Assyria while Judah strengthened its cities (see the introduction). Within a few years Samaria would fall.

How the chapter makes its case. The alarm: an eagle hovers over the LORD’s house because Israel has broken his covenant, whatever it claims (vv. 1–3). The charge: kings made without God and a calf made by a craftsman, wind sown and whirlwind reaped (vv. 4–7). The result: Israel swallowed by the nations it hired as lovers (vv. 8–10). The root: altars that multiply sin, a law treated as strange, sacrifices God will not accept, and a people who have forgotten their Maker and trusted in palaces and fortresses that fire will consume (vv. 11–14).

Where it leads. To Christ by covenant and by the need the chapter exposes. Israel made kings “not through me”; God has set his own King on Zion (Psalm 2:6), and the New Testament hears that fulfilled in Jesus (Acts 13:33). Israel offered sacrifices God would not accept; Christ offered the one sacrifice he did. And Israel forgot its Maker, as the world did when “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11), yet he came to bring the forgetful home.

For us. We still sow the wind: in self-made security, a faith that is mostly words, a Bible that sits unread like a strange book. The harvest of such sowing is always worse than the seed. But the God Israel forgot still calls his people home, and in Christ he gives a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
8.theology:
Claiming to know God is worthless without the life that shows it (vv. 2-3; Matt 7:21-23).

Governing without God and worshipping idols of human making are two forms of the same rebellion (vv. 4-6; 1 Kgs 12:28; Isa 44:17).

Those who sow emptiness reap destruction far greater than what they sowed (v. 7; Gal 6:7-8).

God's people who imitate the world become useless to it, and alliances bought with money become chains (vv. 8-10).

False worship multiplies sin, and having God's word is no benefit to those who treat it as strange (vv. 11-13).

Forgetting the Maker and trusting in human security brings judgment on everything built without him (vv. 13-14; Deut 28:68; 2 Kgs 18:13).
8.examples: A people say, "We know you," and do not. They crown kings by conspiracy without a prayer and call a craftsman's golden calf a god. They sow wind and harvest a whirlwind, and they pay their lovers. It is still possible to keep a Bible in every room and treat it as a strange book, and to build palaces and walls while forgetting the Maker.

keyVerse.quote: For they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind.
keyVerse.note: This proverb sums up the chapter. Self-made kings, a craftsman’s calf, bought alliances and fortified cities were all wind: empty things sown in place of trust in God. The harvest would be a whirlwind of destruction far greater than the seed, and only the grace that calls Israel home (14:1) can break the cycle.

8.reflection:
Israel cried, “My God, we … know you” (v. 2), yet God says they have broken his covenant. How can a person say the right words about God and still not know him? What did Jesus mean when he warned, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:23)?

“They sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (v. 7). Where have you seen small, empty choices grow into a harvest far bigger than the seed? How does the gospel offer hope to someone already reaping?

Israel made kings “but not through me” and idols with God’s own silver and gold (v. 4). In what areas of life are we tempted to make decisions without asking God, or to turn his gifts into idols?

“Israel has forgotten his Maker and built palaces” (v. 14). What does forgetting God look like for comfortable people today? What helps you remember him, and the kingdom in Christ that cannot be shaken?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Days of Punishment Have Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel’s feasts cannot survive Israel’s unfaithfulness, and mocking the messenger will not stop the judgment. Hosea interrupts a harvest celebration: the people have treated the grain as Baal’s payment, so the threshing floor will fail them and they will lose the LORD’s land (vv. 1–3). In exile there will be no drink offerings and no feasts; their bread will be like food from a house of mourning, eaten for hunger only (vv. 4–5). Those who flee to Egypt will be buried there, and nettles will grow over their silver (v. 6). The days of punishment have come, yet the people call the prophet a fool, though he is God’s watchman, for they have sunk as low as Gibeah (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: Festivals without faithfulness end in exile, and those who mock God's watchmen cannot escape his judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice not, O Israel! Exult not like the peoples; for you have played the whore, forsaking your God. You have loved a prostitute's wages on all threshing floors. Threshing floor and wine vat shall not feed them, and the new wine shall fail them. They shall not remain in the land of the LORD, but Ephraim shall return to Egypt, and they shall eat unclean food in Assyria. They shall not pour drink offerings of wine to the LORD, and their sacrifices shall not please him. It shall be like mourners' bread to them; all who eat of it shall be defiled; for their bread shall be for their hunger only; it shall not come to the house of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has thanked Baal for the harvest God gave, so God will take back the harvest, the land and the worship that went with them.

Rejoice not, O Israel! The setting may be a harvest festival, perhaps the autumn Feast of Booths, with the grain gathered on the threshing floors, the open spaces where it was separated from the chaff. Hosea interrupts the party. Israel was rejoicing “like the peoples”, thanking Baal for the harvest as wages for their devotion: “a prostitute’s wages”, as she called her lovers’ gifts (2:12).

The land of the LORD. The harvest they credited to Baal would fail (2:9). The land was God’s (Leviticus 25:23), given them to live in as his people; if they would not live as his people, they could not stay in it.

Ephraim shall return to Egypt. Exile would undo the exodus: the covenant curses had warned that God would send a faithless people back to Egypt, back to slavery (Deuteronomy 28:68). Some would flee there; others would be carried to Assyria, where they could not keep God’s food laws: “Thus shall the people of Israel eat their bread unclean, among the nations” (Ezekiel 4:13).

Like mourners’ bread. In exile there would be no offerings. Their food would be like bread from a house where someone had died, which made all who ate it unclean, unfit for worship (Numbers 19:14; compare Deuteronomy 26:14). Every meal would be “for their hunger only”, with nothing brought to God. Life without worship is just eating to stay alive.

Thank the Giver. We easily credit our harvest to the economy, hard work or luck. Every meal can be eaten for hunger only, or received with thanksgiving from God’s hand (1 Timothy 4:4–5).

verseByVerse.quote: What will you do on the day of the appointed festival, and on the day of the feast of the LORD? For behold, they are going away from destruction; but Egypt shall gather them; Memphis shall bury them. Nettles shall possess their precious things of silver; thorns shall be in their tents. The days of punishment have come; the days of recompense have come; Israel shall know it. The prophet is a fool; the man of the spirit is mad, because of your great iniquity and great hatred. The prophet is the watchman of Ephraim with my God; yet a fowler's snare is on all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God. They have deeply corrupted themselves as in the days of Gibeah: he will remember their iniquity; he will punish their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exile will end the feasts and bury those who flee, and a people who call God’s watchman a madman show how deep their sin has gone.

What will you do on the day of the appointed festival? They had corrupted the feasts; in exile they would lose them. Those who fled to Egypt would be buried at Memphis, a city famous for its burial grounds, while nettles and thorns took over the treasures and tents they left behind.

The prophet is a fool. The people called Hosea a fool and mad. Those who dislike the message often attack the messenger, as the governor Festus did: “Paul, you are out of your mind” (Acts 26:24). Their mockery showed their “great hatred”, aimed in the end at God.

The prophet is the watchman of Ephraim. Hosea was no madman but a watchman, set by God on the wall to warn of danger, as God later told Ezekiel: “I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 3:17). Yet the people set traps on his path, like a fowler snaring birds, and hated him even in the house of God.

As in the days of Gibeah. The phrase recalls one of the darkest stories in Israel’s history (Judges 19–21). At Gibeah a Levite’s concubine was abused and murdered, and the crime led to a civil war that almost wiped out the tribe of Benjamin. “Such a thing has never happened or been seen,” people said (Judges 19:30); Israel had sunk that low again.

The rejected watchman. Of Jesus, too, his hearers said, “He has a demon, and is insane; why listen to him?” (John 10:20), and he wept over the city that killed the prophets (Luke 13:34). Yet the Watchman they put to death rose again and called even those who crucified him to repent and be forgiven (Acts 2:36–38). When an unwelcome word comes to us, test it by Scripture (Acts 17:11), not by how it makes us feel.

Uncertain wording. In verse 7 the ESV takes “the man of the spirit is mad” as the people’s mockery of Hosea; others read it as Hosea’s verdict on the false prophets, made foolish by Israel’s sin. In the compressed Hebrew of verse 8 the ESV, with most modern translations, makes the true prophet Ephraim’s watchman; older translations such as the King James make the prophet himself the fowler’s snare, meaning false prophets who trap the people.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Like the Thing They Loved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: We become like what we love, and those who seek life from idols lose the very thing they sought. God remembers his first delight in Israel, like a traveller finding grapes in the wilderness, and their swift fall at Baal-peor, where they became as detestable as the idol they loved (v. 10). They looked to Baal for children; now their glory will fly away like a bird, and the worst woe of all is that God himself will depart (vv. 11–14). Every evil is gathered at Gilgal, and God will drive them from his house (v. 15). Ephraim, whose name sounds like “fruitful”, will bear no fruit, and because they would not listen they will wander among the nations (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology: We become like what we love; God's delight in his people turns to judgment when they give their love to idols.

verseByVerse.quote: Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel. Like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers. But they came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved. Ephraim's glory shall fly away like a bird— no birth, no pregnancy, no conception! Even if they bring up children, I will bereave them till none is left. Woe to them when I depart from them! Ephraim, as I have seen, was like a young palm planted in a meadow; but Ephraim must lead his children out to slaughter. Give them, O LORD— what will you give? Give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God delighted in Israel at the beginning, but they gave themselves to an idol and became like it; so the children they hoped Baal would give will be taken, and, worse, God himself will depart.

Like grapes in the wilderness. God remembers choosing Israel with the delight of a thirsty traveller finding grapes in the wilderness, or of the first ripe fig, the most prized of the year. His love began in his own delight, not in their worth (Deuteronomy 7:7–8).

But they came to Baal-peor. Before even entering the land, Israel joined the Moabites in worshipping Baal of Peor, with sexual immorality and idol feasts (Numbers 25:1–3). They “consecrated themselves to the thing of shame”, a scornful name the prophets used for Baal (compare Jeremiah 3:24).

Became detestable like the thing they loved. We become like what we worship. “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). Love money and we grow grasping; love approval and we grow hollow; love the true God and his Spirit transforms us into his likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18). Worship always shapes the worshipper.

Ephraim’s glory shall fly away like a bird. The judgment strikes at exactly what they had sought from Baal: fertility and children. And the worst woe is this: “Woe to them when I depart from them!” Losing children was terrible. Losing God was worse.

The woe Christ bore. On the cross the Son of God entered that woe for his people, crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46). Because he was forsaken, God can promise everyone joined to him by faith, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5).

What will you give? God had planted Israel in a good place, like a young palm; now its children would be led out to slaughter. Hosea begins a prayer, stops, and asks for the barren womb. He agrees with a judgment already announced (vv. 11–12), probably asking for the lesser grief: better no children than children born for slaughter. Jesus spoke similarly of Jerusalem’s coming destruction: “Blessed are the barren and the wombs that never bore” (Luke 23:29). Others hear the anguished cry of a prophet who has come to agree with God’s verdict. Either way, it is no pattern for personal curses; Christians bless and pray for their enemies (Matthew 5:44).

If you have lost a child. If you have suffered a miscarriage or lost a child, these verses are not a word about you. They describe a judgment announced on one nation for its long rebellion. Scripture never teaches that a child’s death is God’s punishment on the parents (John 9:3), and the Lord Jesus, who took little children in his arms and blessed them (Mark 10:16), is tender toward every grieving mother and father.

Uncertain wording. Verse 13 is hard to translate. The ESV notes that it may read “like Tyre”, comparing Ephraim to that rich and well-placed city, where its text has “like a young palm planted in a meadow”, and that “to slaughter” is literally “to him who slaughters”. Either way, a nation planted in privilege would see its children led to death.

verseByVerse.quote: Every evil of theirs is in Gilgal; there I began to hate them. Because of the wickedness of their deeds I will drive them out of my house. I will love them no more; all their princes are rebels. Ephraim is stricken; their root is dried up; they shall bear no fruit. Even though they give birth, I will put their beloved children to death. My God will reject them because they have not listened to him; they shall be wanderers among the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From the shrine at Gilgal to the palace Israel is in rebellion, so God will drive them from his house, and the “fruitful” nation will wither and wander among the nations. Yet wandering is not his last word.

Every evil of theirs is in Gilgal. Gilgal was a centre of corrupt worship (4:15; Amos 4:4). It may also be named because there they made Saul king (1 Samuel 11:15), the start of the monarchy that had led them astray: “all their princes are rebels”. “There I began to hate them.”

I will love them no more. Among the hardest words in the book, the language of a husband driving an unfaithful wife out of “my house”. God’s holy hatred of sin is real, and those who persist in rebellion face his rejection. Yet the book does not end here. In chapter 11 God will cry, “How can I give you up, O Ephraim?” (11:8), and in chapter 14 he will promise, “I will love them freely” (14:4). God’s wrath against sin is real, and his love is greater still, and they meet at the cross, where his judgment on sin and his love for sinners were both fully shown.

Their root is dried up. The palm tree of verse 13 withers. The name Ephraim, which Hosea uses for the whole nation, sounds like the Hebrew for “fruitful” (Genesis 41:52), and now Ephraim would “bear no fruit”.

My God will reject them. Hosea says “My God”: Israel had abandoned God; Hosea had not. The reason is that “they have not listened to him”, and the result is exile, “wanderers among the nations”, like Cain, who became “a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth” (Genesis 4:12). The northern tribes never returned as a kingdom, though some families kept their faith and their tribe, like Anna of the tribe of Asher (Luke 2:36).

Not the final word. The God who scatters in judgment sent his Son to gather wanderers from every nation into one flock (John 10:16; 11:52), and whoever has not listened may still turn back and find him merciful (14:1–2).

9.title: Grapes in the Wilderness
9.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 9 stands in the middle of the book’s second round of sermons (chapters 8 to 11), which trace Israel’s kings, calves and alliances to exile. Now Hosea arrives at a harvest festival and silences the party.

The message. Israel has taken God’s gifts and given the thanks to Baal, so God will take back the gifts, the land and, worst of all, himself. A people who loved an idol have become like it, and the fruitfulness they hoped Baal would give them will wither. “Woe to them when I depart from them!” (v. 12): the deepest judgment is not losing harvests or children, but losing God.

Why it was said. Israel’s harvests were celebrated at Baal’s shrines and its feasts went on as usual while Assyria gathered on the horizon (see the introduction). When Hosea warned them, they called him a madman.

How the chapter makes its case. First the feast is silenced (vv. 1–6): they will lose the LORD’s land, and in exile every meal will be like food from a house of mourning, with nothing offered to God. Then the messenger is mocked (vv. 7–9): the people call the prophet a fool, though God set him as their watchman, and they have sunk as low as Gibeah. Then God looks back (vv. 10–14): he found Israel like grapes in the wilderness, but at Baal-peor they became like the idol they loved, so the children they sought from Baal will be taken. Last comes the verdict (vv. 15–17): from Gilgal to the palace all are rebels, the root is dried up, and Ephraim, whose name sounds like “fruitful”, will bear no fruit, but wander among the nations.

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes, and by pattern. Israel’s worst woe was that God would depart. On the cross the Son of God entered that woe for his people, crying, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), so that God can say to all who are joined to him, “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5). The mocked watchman also points ahead to the greater prophet whose hearers said, “He has a demon, and is insane” (John 10:20). And those who would not listen were scattered among the nations; Christ died to gather the scattered children of God into one (John 11:52).

For us. We too can enjoy God’s gifts while giving our hearts elsewhere. Thank the Giver, listen to the watchmen he sends even when they are unwelcome, and prize his presence above every gift, for in Christ it is the one gift that will never be taken from those who trust him.
9.theology:
The land and the feasts belong to the LORD, and those who give his gifts to idols will lose both (vv. 1-6).

People who reject God's word often mock his messengers, but the prophet is a watchman whose warnings are true (vv. 7-8; Acts 26:24; Ezek 3:17).

God delighted in his people from the beginning, yet they turned quickly to idols and became like what they loved (v. 10; Num 25:1-3; Ps 115:8).

The worst judgment is God's departure from his people (v. 12).

God's holy rejection of persistent sin is real, yet his love proves greater, as the rest of Hosea shows and the cross reveals (vv. 15-17; 11:8; 14:4).
9.examples: The chapter moves through vivid pictures: a harvest party silenced, meals eaten for hunger only, a watchman mocked as a madman, and against them God's memory of finding Israel like grapes in the wilderness.

keyVerse.quote: Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel. Like the first fruit on the fig tree in its first season, I saw your fathers. But they came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved.
keyVerse.note: This verse holds the whole chapter’s grief: God’s first delight in his people, and their quick turn to an idol. Its last line explains why the judgment fits the sin: those who love an idol become like it, and lose the very life they hoped it would give. It also points the way back, for those who behold the Lord are changed into his likeness (2 Corinthians 3:18).

9.reflection:
Israel kept the harvest festival but thanked Baal for the harvest (vv. 1–2). Which good gifts in your life are you most tempted to credit to something other than God, and what would it look like to receive them with thanksgiving?

The people called God’s watchman a fool (vv. 7–8). Why do people attack the messenger when they dislike the message? How do you respond when Scripture, a preacher or a friend tells you what you do not want to hear?

They “became detestable like the thing they loved” (v. 10). Where have you seen people, or yourself, grow like what they worship? What hope does 2 Corinthians 3:18 give?

God calls his own departure the worst woe of all (v. 12). How did Jesus bear that woe on the cross, and what difference does the promise “I will never leave you nor forsake you” (Hebrews 13:5) make to you this week?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The More His Fruit Increased
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prosperity that feeds idolatry ends in the loss of every false security. Israel grew like a luxuriant vine, but the more fruit it bore, the more altars and sacred pillars it built, with a divided heart, so God will break them down (vv. 1–2). The day will come when the people admit they have no king because they did not fear the LORD, and that no king could have saved them; their treaties were empty oaths, and justice itself turned poisonous (vv. 3–4). The calf they trembled for will be carted off to Assyria as tribute, the king swept away like a twig, the shrines overgrown with thorns, and the people will beg the mountains to cover them (vv. 5–8).
verseByVerse.theology: Prosperity that feeds idolatry ends in the loss of every false security.

verseByVerse.quote: Israel is a luxuriant vine that yields its fruit. The more his fruit increased, the more altars he built; as his country improved, he improved his pillars. Their heart is false; now they must bear their guilt. The LORD will break down their altars and destroy their pillars.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The more God blessed Israel, the more it spent his gifts on idols, so God will tear down the altars it built with them.

Israel is a luxuriant vine. God had planted Israel as his vine (Psalm 80:8), and it grew rich. But each rise in wealth became a rise in idolatry: more altars, finer pillars (the sacred stones of Baal worship).

Their heart is false. Divided and deceitful: they wanted God’s blessings and Baal’s too, so God would destroy the altars built with his gifts. (The ESV notes that the second part of the verse literally says “He” will break down the altars.)

The true vine. Isaiah recorded God’s disappointment over his vineyard: “When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?” (Isaiah 5:4). Only one Vine has ever borne the fruit God desired: Jesus, who says, “I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit” (John 15:5). Israel’s fruit went to its altars; his brings glory to the Father (John 15:8).

Prosperity is a test. God gives good things so that we will love him more, but our hearts easily take the gifts and serve something else with them.

verseByVerse.quote: For now they will say: "We have no king, for we do not fear the LORD; and a king—what could he do for us?" They utter mere words; with empty oaths they make covenants; so judgment springs up like poisonous weeds in the furrows of the field.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the monarchy falls, Israel will see that no king could save a people who did not fear the LORD.

We have no king. Israel would soon have no king at all. Its last king, Hoshea, was imprisoned by Assyria (2 Kings 17:4), and the monarchy ended. Then they would see the connection, “We have no king, for we do not fear the LORD”, and ask bitterly what a king could have done for them. They had asked for a king to be like the nations (1 Samuel 8:5); now they saw that no king could save them.

With empty oaths they make covenants. They swore oaths and broke them, at home and in treaties abroad. (The ESV notes that “empty” may be “vain”, pointing to the command not to take God’s name in vain, Exodus 20:7.) So justice itself turned poisonous: courts and agreements meant to protect people spread harm, “like poisonous weeds in the furrows of the field”.

The King who saves. Hosea has already answered their bitter question: one day they will seek “David their king” (3:5). Christ is that King, who keeps every oath and gives his own life to save his people.

verseByVerse.quote: The inhabitants of Samaria tremble for the calf of Beth-aven. Its people mourn for it, and so do its idolatrous priests— those who rejoiced over it and over its glory— for it has departed from them. The thing itself shall be carried to Assyria as tribute to the great king. Ephraim shall be put to shame, and Israel shall be ashamed of his idol. Samaria's king shall perish like a twig on the face of the waters. The high places of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed. Thorn and thistle shall grow up on their altars, and they shall say to the mountains, "Cover us," and to the hills, "Fall on us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The idol Israel trusted cannot even protect itself; when it is carried off and the shrines fall, the people will beg the mountains to hide them from God.

The inhabitants of Samaria tremble for the calf. Something almost comic: the people tremble for their god. The golden calf at Bethel (called Beth-aven, “house of wickedness”, as in 4:15) is about to be carried off, and its worshippers and priests mourn. What kind of god has to be protected by its worshippers? Its “glory”, they lament, “has departed”, the very words spoken when the ark was captured long before: “The glory has departed from Israel!” (1 Samuel 4:21).

Carried to Assyria as tribute. The calf would end up on a cart as a present for the Assyrian king: the object they worshipped would become loot. Every idol finally shames those who trust it, and the king would be swept away as helplessly as a twig in a flood.

The high places of Aven. The hilltop shrines would be destroyed, and “thorn and thistle”, the curse of Eden (Genesis 3:18), would grow over their altars. The people would beg the mountains to fall on them and hide them.

Fall on us. Jesus used these words on the way to the cross, warning the women of Jerusalem of the judgment coming on their city: “Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us’” (Luke 23:30). At the final judgment, Revelation says, people will call on the mountains to hide them “from the wrath of the Lamb” (Revelation 6:16). There is no hiding place from God except in Jesus, the Lamb who took that wrath for us.

Uncertain wording. The ESV notes several uncertain words. “Calf” may be “calves”. “Departed” may mean “gone into exile”, so that the god goes into exile with its people. “The great king” may be a name, “King Jareb” (as in 5:13), and Israel’s “idol” may be its “counsel”, its own scheming.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: It is still the time to seek the LORD, but those who trust their own strength will reap war. Israel’s sin is as old as Gibeah, and God will gather the nations to discipline it (vv. 9–10). Ephraim, a heifer used to the easy work of threshing, will be put to the yoke, with Judah beside it (v. 11). In the middle of the judgment comes the invitation: sow righteousness, reap steadfast love, break up the fallow ground, so that the LORD may come and rain righteousness on you (v. 12). But Israel has ploughed iniquity and trusted its warriors, so its fortresses will fall as Beth-arbel fell, and at dawn its king will be cut off (vv. 13–15).
verseByVerse.theology: It is time to seek the LORD, breaking up hard hearts so that he may rain righteousness on us.

verseByVerse.quote: From the days of Gibeah, you have sinned, O Israel; there they have continued. Shall not the war against the unjust overtake them in Gibeah? When I please, I will discipline them, and nations shall be gathered against them when they are bound up for their double iniquity. Ephraim was a trained calf that loved to thresh, and I spared her fair neck; but I will put Ephraim to the yoke; Judah must plow; Jacob must harrow for himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s sin is as old as Gibeah, so God will discipline it, and the pampered heifer will be yoked to the plough.

From the days of Gibeah. Hosea again recalls the days of Gibeah (9:9), when the crime there led to war. Israel’s sin had gone on for centuries, and as war came to Gibeah then, it would come again. (“The unjust” is literally “the children of injustice”, as the ESV notes.)

When I please, I will discipline them. God will choose the time, and the nations will be his instruments.

Ephraim was a trained calf. A young cow used for threshing had an easy job: it walked round over the grain and was allowed to eat as it worked, for God’s law said, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4). Israel had enjoyed that easy life. Now it, and Judah with it, would be yoked to plough hard ground.

Uncertain wording. Hosea does not explain “their double iniquity”. It may mean Israel’s two great sins, idolatry and rebellion against the king God appointed, or simply sin piled on sin.

verseByVerse.quote: Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in judgment God invites Israel to break up the hard ground of the heart and seek him now, and he will come and rain righteousness on them.

Sow for yourselves righteousness. One of Hosea’s most beautiful invitations. The God who planted this vine (v. 1) still calls it home. “Sow for yourselves righteousness”: justice, honesty and obedience. “Reap steadfast love”: the harvest will be God’s covenant love.

Break up your fallow ground. Fallow ground is a field left unploughed so long that the soil has crusted hard; nothing grows until the plough breaks it open. Jeremiah used the same words: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” (Jeremiah 4:3). Israel’s heart had become that field, and needed breaking up by repentance.

It is the time to seek the LORD. Now, not tomorrow. And the promise is wonderful: Israel had begged Baal for rain; the LORD promises to come himself and rain righteousness on the very people who wronged him. We do the ploughing and sowing, but only God sends the rain, and even the will to repent is his gift (Acts 11:18).

Christ sowed it for us. None of us has sown righteousness as we should; Christ sowed it perfectly, and his righteousness is counted as ours (2 Corinthians 5:21). His Spirit breaks up the hard ground and makes new life grow (Galatians 5:22). “Whoever sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6), and “Those who sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy!” (Psalm 126:5).

How do I break up the fallow ground? Hard ground is ground left alone: a part of life you have stopped letting God touch. Find the crusted field. Where do you no longer expect to change? A temper, an old resentment, the way you spend money, prayer that has become a formality. Let the plough in. Bring it deliberately under God’s word this week, and let it cut. Sow one seed. Do one concrete right thing there: the apology, the gift, the honest figure, ten minutes of real prayer. Do it now. “It is the time,” Hosea says, and Isaiah agrees: “Seek the LORD while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6). Then leave the harvest to God: you cannot make it rain, but he has promised to come, and in Christ he already has. “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (James 4:8).

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew verb behind “rain” is spelled like the verb “teach”, so some ancient translators read “teach you righteousness”. The farming picture favours “rain”; either way, the righteousness comes from God, not from the soil.

verseByVerse.quote: You have plowed iniquity; you have reaped injustice; you have eaten the fruit of lies. Because you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your warriors, therefore the tumult of war shall arise among your people, and all your fortresses shall be destroyed, as Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel on the day of battle; mothers were dashed in pieces with their children. Thus it shall be done to you, O Bethel, because of your great evil. At dawn the king of Israel shall be utterly cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel has ploughed iniquity and trusted its army, so war will flatten its fortresses and cut off its king.

You have plowed iniquity. Israel had done the opposite of verse 12: they ploughed iniquity, harvested injustice, and were now eating “the fruit of lies”. The root of it all: “you have trusted in your own way and in the multitude of your warriors”. Self-reliance and military strength were their gods.

As Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel. Their warriors would not save the fortresses. Hosea recalls a massacre his hearers knew, when mothers and children were killed together: so it would be in Israel. Hosea is not approving such cruelty but describing what ancient war did. Elsewhere God condemns the nations for these very atrocities (Amos 1:13).

Thus it shall be done to you, O Bethel. Bethel was where Jacob met God and said, “This is none other than the house of God” (Genesis 28:17). It had become the home of the golden calf, and would bring destruction on the nation. “At dawn”, as suddenly as the sun rises, “the king of Israel shall be utterly cut off”. This was probably fulfilled when Assyria captured Hoshea.

Two harvests. The chapter holds out two harvests: righteousness and steadfast love rained down on those who seek God, or war and destruction for those who trust their own way. The field is still before every reader: “it is the time to seek the LORD.”

Uncertain wording. We no longer know which event “Shalman destroyed Beth-arbel” refers to. Some think Shalman was the Assyrian king Shalmaneser, others a Moabite king called Salamanu, known from Assyrian records; Beth-arbel may be Arbela, east of the Jordan. The horror itself was plain to Hosea’s hearers.

10.title: Break Up Your Fallow Ground
10.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 10 continues the book’s second round of sermons (chapters 8 to 11). Hosea now takes the three things Israel trusted instead of God, its altars, its kings and its warriors, and shows each one failing.

The message. Every blessing God gave Israel became fuel for idolatry, and every false security it built will be swept away: the calf carted off as tribute, the king carried off like a twig on the water, the fortresses destroyed. Yet in the middle of the judgment God still pleads: “it is the time to seek the LORD, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you” (v. 12). Life does not come from ploughing harder in our own strength, but from hearts broken open to him.

Why it was said. Under Jeroboam II Israel had grown rich, and its wealth went into altars and sacred pillars; then, as king after king fell and Assyria pressed in, its leaders made and broke treaties and trusted in their armies (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. The richer the vine grew, the more altars it built, so God will break them down (vv. 1–2). No king can save a nation that does not fear the LORD (vv. 3–4). The calf they trembled for will be taken to Assyria, the king swept away, the shrines overgrown, and the people will beg the mountains to cover them (vv. 5–8). Israel has sinned since Gibeah, and the pampered heifer will be yoked to hard labour (vv. 9–11). Then comes the call to break up the fallow ground and seek the LORD (v. 12); but they have ploughed iniquity and trusted their warriors, so war will come (vv. 13–15).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and by promise. Israel was God’s vine that bore fruit for itself; Jesus is “the true vine” (John 15:1), who bore the fruit God looked for. The cry to the mountains, “Fall on us”, Jesus took on his own lips on the way to the cross (Luke 23:30), and Revelation hears it again from those who flee “the wrath of the Lamb” (Revelation 6:16): the only shelter from that wrath is the Lamb who bore it. And the promised rain of righteousness falls in him, whose righteousness is counted to all who seek God through him (2 Corinthians 5:21).

For us. Prosperity tests the heart: what do we build with what God gives? Ask which part of your life has become hard ground, left unturned for years, and let God’s word break it open now. It is still the time to seek the LORD, and in Christ he still comes to those who do.
10.theology:
Prosperity not received with gratitude becomes fuel for idolatry, and idols that must be guarded by their worshippers end by shaming them; only Christ, the true vine, bears the fruit God desires (vv. 1-6; Isa 5:4; John 15:5).

No mountain can hide anyone from God's judgment; the only shelter is the one who bore it (v. 8; Luke 23:30; Rev 6:16).

Now is the time to seek the LORD: hard hearts must be broken up in repentance so that God may rain righteousness upon them (v. 12; Jer 4:3; 2 Cor 9:6; Ps 126:5).

Those who plough iniquity and trust in their own strength reap destruction (vv. 13-15; Gal 6:7-8).
10.examples:
Hosea's pictures stay in the mind: worshippers trembling for the safety of their god as it is loaded on a cart for Assyria, and people begging the mountains to fall on them.

Over against them stands a hard, crusted field waiting for the plough, and the promise of righteousness falling like rain on broken ground.

keyVerse.quote: Sow for yourselves righteousness; reap steadfast love; break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD, that he may come and rain righteousness upon you.
keyVerse.note: In a chapter of collapsing altars, kings and fortresses, this verse is the open door. It calls hard hearts to be broken up in repentance and promises that God himself will come and pour down righteousness like rain. In Christ that promise is kept: his righteousness is given to all who seek God through him.

10.reflection:
“The more his fruit increased, the more altars he built” (v. 1). How can God’s good gifts, such as money, success or comfort, draw our hearts away from him? What helps you hold them with thanks rather than worship?

The people trembled for their calf (v. 5), a god that had to be protected by its worshippers. What do people today feel they must protect and worry about, while also looking to it for security?

Verse 12 calls us to break up the fallow ground. Is there an area of your life you have stopped letting God touch? What would one concrete step of seeking the LORD there look like this week?

Jesus quoted verse 8 on the way to the cross (Luke 23:30). Why is Christ the only shelter from God’s judgment, and how should that shape the way we speak about judgment to others?

11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.<sup>2</sup>The more they were called, the more they went away; they kept sacrificing to the Baals and burning offerings to idols.<sup>3</sup>Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms, but they did not know that I healed them.<sup>4</sup>I led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love, and I became to them as one who eases the yoke on their jaws, and I bent down to them and fed them.<sup>5</sup>They shall not return to the land of Egypt, but Assyria shall be their king, because they have refused to return to me.<sup>6</sup>The sword shall rage against their cities, consume the bars of their gates, and devour them because of their own counsels.<sup>7</sup>My people are bent on turning away from me, and though they call out to the Most High, he shall not raise them up at all.<sup>8</sup>How can I give you up, O Ephraim?
