verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — When Israel Was a Child
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s love for Israel is a father’s love, given first and met with ingratitude. He loved Israel when it was a slave nation and called his son out of Egypt (v. 1), but the more he called, the more they ran to the Baals (v. 2). He remembers what a parent does: teaching Ephraim to walk, lifting him up, healing him, leading him with cords of kindness, easing his yoke and bending down to feed him, though Israel never noticed (vv. 3–4). Because they refused to return to him, they will have Assyria for their king, the sword will rage through their cities, and calling to God with their lips alone will not raise them up (vv. 5–7).
verseByVerse.theology: God's love for his people is the love of a father who carried, taught and fed a child who turned away.

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called my son.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God loved Israel as a father loves a child, before it had done anything, and called his son out of Egypt; Matthew sees the pattern completed in Jesus, the true Son.

A father remembers. Chapter 11 is one of the tenderest passages in the Old Testament. Until now Hosea has mostly pictured God as a husband betrayed by his wife; here God speaks as a father remembering his child.

When Israel was a child, I loved him. God’s love came first, before Israel had done anything, while it was still a weak slave nation in Egypt. Moses told Pharaoh, “Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22), and God brought his son out.

Out of Egypt I called my son. Matthew quotes this verse in a surprising place. When Joseph took the baby Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod and later brought him back, Matthew writes, “This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, ‘Out of Egypt I called my son’” (Matthew 2:15).

Is Matthew misreading Hosea? Some readers object that Hosea was looking back to the exodus, not forward to Jesus. That is true, and Matthew knew it. He is not saying Hosea predicted a trip to Egypt, but that Jesus is the true Son of God, who lived out Israel’s story faithfully. Israel, God’s son, came out of Egypt, turned away (v. 2) and failed when tested in the wilderness. Jesus, God’s Son, came out of Egypt, was tested in the wilderness and did not fail. Where Israel broke his Father’s heart, Jesus always did what pleased his Father. He obeyed in the place of the sons and daughters who turn away, and God counts his obedience as theirs (Romans 5:19). This way of reading is called typology: seeing a pattern in God’s dealings with Israel that God himself completes in Christ. And Hosea himself looks beyond the first exodus to a new one, in which God’s children come home (vv. 10–11).

How Jewish readers take it. Jewish readers take the verse as it stands in Hosea: God’s son is the people of Israel, called out of Egypt at the exodus, and they do not read it as a prediction of the Messiah. On that plain sense there is no quarrel, and both readings treasure the same truth, that Israel is God’s beloved firstborn (Exodus 4:22). This commentary goes on to see Jesus as the faithful Son who sums up Israel’s story in himself, which is why Matthew can say his return from Egypt fulfilled the prophet’s words.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew sees this fulfilled when Jesus, the true Son, came back from Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: The more they were called, the more they went away; they kept sacrificing to the Baals and burning offerings to idols. Yet it was I who taught Ephraim to walk; I took them up by their arms, but they did not know that I healed them. I led them with cords of kindness, with the bands of love, and I became to them as one who eases the yoke on their jaws, and I bent down to them and fed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s love was patient and practical: he called, taught, carried, healed and fed his child, and the child kept running to idols without noticing who had cared for him.

The more they were called, the more they went away. Here is the tragedy. God kept calling through Moses, the judges and the prophets, and every call was answered by running further toward the Baals, like a child who runs faster the more a parent calls him home.

It was I who taught Ephraim to walk. God remembers the little things a parent does. Picture a father holding a toddler’s hands, catching him when he stumbles, taking him “up by their arms”. Moses had said the same: in the wilderness “the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son” (Deuteronomy 1:31).

They did not know that I healed them. The heartbreaking line. Like children who take their parents’ care for granted, Israel never realised it, and we rarely know how often God has picked us up and kept us.

With cords of kindness. God did not drive his people like cattle. He led them “with cords of kindness, with the bands of love”. (The ESV notes that “kindness” may be “humaneness”, literally cords of a “man”: the ties by which one person draws another, not ropes for animals.) He was like a farmer who lifts the yoke off an ox’s neck so it can eat, and he “bent down to them and fed them”. The God of heaven stooped to feed his children.

I bent down to them. That picture reaches its fullest meaning in the incarnation. In Christ, God did not only bend down: he came all the way down, took our human nature and gave himself to be our food, the bread of life (John 6:35).

Uncertain wording. In verse 4 the Hebrew letters for “yoke” can also be read as “infant”, so some translations have “like one who lifts a little child to the cheek”. Either picture, the farmer easing the yoke or the father lifting his baby, shows the same stooping tenderness.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not return to the land of Egypt, but Assyria shall be their king, because they have refused to return to me. The sword shall rage against their cities, consume the bars of their gates, and devour them because of their own counsels. My people are bent on turning away from me, and though they call out to the Most High, he shall not raise them up at all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Israel refused to return to God, it will be carried off to serve Assyria, and calling on God with the lips while the heart is set on leaving him will not save it.

Assyria shall be their king. Their real master would be Assyria, “because they have refused to return to me”. There is a play on the word “return”: they would not return to God, so they would be carried into captivity. Their own “counsels”, trusted instead of God, would bring the sword.

My people are bent on turning away from me. Even now God calls them his. But they are bent on turning away, determined and set in their course, and calling on God with their lips while their hearts were set on leaving him would not save them.

Uncertain wording. Verse 5 can seem to contradict earlier warnings that Israel would “return to Egypt” (8:13; 9:3). The ESV notes that it may be read “surely” they shall return to Egypt; or the point may be that this time Egypt will not be their master, Assyria will. Either way, the main point is clear. The Hebrew of verse 7 is also very obscure, and translations differ; the ESV takes it to mean that their cries to God are empty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–12 — My Heart Recoils Within Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God’s holy compassion will not let his people go. In the most moving words of the book, God asks four times how he can give Ephraim up and make him like Admah and Zeboiim, cities wiped out with Sodom (v. 8). His heart recoils, and he will not come to destroy, because he is God and not a man, the Holy One in their midst (v. 9). Instead the LORD will roar like a lion, and his scattered children will come trembling home, like birds from Egypt and doves from Assyria (vv. 10–11). The section ends by returning to the present: Ephraim still surrounds God with lies (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: God's holy compassion will not let his people go, and his mercy triumphs over the judgment they deserve.

verseByVerse.quote: How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender. I will not execute my burning anger; I will not again destroy Ephraim; for I am God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst, and I will not come in wrath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s heart recoils from destroying his people as he destroyed the cities of the plain; because he is the Holy One and not a man, his compassion will not let them go.

How can I give you up, O Ephraim? Now we hear something astonishing: God arguing aloud with himself. Through ten chapters Hosea has brought charge after charge and sentence after sentence; the guilt is beyond dispute and the sentence is written. Yet the Judge of all the earth cries out that he cannot bring himself to carry it out. Four times he asks how, and every question is a cry of wounded love.

How can I make you like Admah? Admah and Zeboiim were cities destroyed together with Sodom and Gomorrah, “which the LORD overthrew in his anger and wrath” (Deuteronomy 29:23), wiped out, never to rise again. Israel deserved the same, but God’s heart “recoils”: it turns over within him at the sentence he himself has spoken.

My compassion grows warm and tender. This is not weakness in God but the deep, passionate love of a Father who will not let his child go. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him” (Psalm 103:13). Jesus showed the same heart when he wept over Jerusalem: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings” (Luke 13:34).

Why will God not destroy them completely? “For I am God and not a man.” A human being betrayed like this would give up and say, “Enough.” God’s love is not like ours; it does not run out. And he calls himself “the Holy One in your midst”. We might expect his holiness to be the reason he destroys them; instead it is the reason he does not. God’s holiness is not only his purity. It is everything that sets him apart from us, and that includes a mercy far greater than ours.

How does this fit with the rest of the book, which warns that Israel will fall? The northern kingdom did fall to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17). Judgment came. But God did not make them like Admah, wiped out without a future. He preserved a people and promised to bring them home.

A deeper answer. God’s anger against sin is real, and it must go somewhere. In the end God did not simply decide to overlook Israel’s sin, or ours. He poured out his burning anger on his own Son, the true Israel who came out of Egypt. “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). “How can I give you up?” God asked of Israel. At the cross he gave up his Son, so that he would never have to give up his people.

Isn’t God just ourselves, written large? The nineteenth-century philosopher Ludwig Feuerbach argued that God is human nature projected onto the sky: we take our own best qualities, magnify them and worship the result. As a description of idols it is often right, since idols always look like their makers. But Hosea’s God says the one thing a projection could not say: “I am God and not a man.” A god who was our sense of justice magnified would carry out the sentence, as most of us, betrayed this often, would. A god who was our wish for comfort magnified would have shrugged long ago. What no human imagination produced is a holiness that burns against sin and, for that very reason, will not let the sinner go: a Judge whose integrity shows itself in finding a way to be both just and merciful (Romans 3:26). We could not even have hoped for it, until the Holy One came into our midst as a man and bore the anger himself.

Does God have changing emotions? Scripture speaks of God in human terms so that we may know his heart: his compassion is real. But “I am God and not a man” (v. 9) is the point: he is not driven by passions as we are, and he does not change his purpose (Numbers 23:19). The “turning” of his heart shows his unchanging love triumphing over the judgment Israel deserved.

Uncertain wording. The last words of verse 9 may also be read “I will not come into the city”, as the ESV notes. Its main text, “I will not come in wrath”, fits the verse’s promise of mercy; either way, God will not come to destroy.
verseByVerse.note: Admah and Zeboiim are first named beside Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis 10:19 and 14:2.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall go after the LORD; he will roar like a lion; when he roars, his children shall come trembling from the west; they shall come trembling like birds from Egypt, and like doves from the land of Assyria, and I will return them to their homes, declares the LORD. Ephraim has surrounded me with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit, but Judah still walks with God and is faithful to the Holy One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lion who once tore his people will roar to call them home, and his scattered children will come back trembling; but for now Ephraim still surrounds God with lies.

He will roar like a lion. The lion appears again, but this time the roar is not a threat; it is a call home. In 5:14 God was a lion who tore his people; here his roar gathers his children. They will “go after the LORD”, following him instead of running away, and come trembling, with reverent awe, from the far places where they were scattered.

Like doves from the land of Assyria. In 7:11 Ephraim was “like a dove, silly and without sense”, flying to Egypt and Assyria for help. Now the same doves fly home from Egypt and Assyria, returning to God. Isaiah foresaw the same homecoming: “the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt” (Isaiah 11:11). God’s final purpose is not scattering but gathering, and in Christ he is gathering his children from every nation.

Ephraim has surrounded me with lies. After the promise, the prophet returns to present reality. Ephraim still surrounds God with lies, but for the moment “Judah still walks with God”. The contrast is both a rebuke to Israel and a warning to Judah to remain faithful. (The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 12.)

The heart behind the book. Chapter 11 shows the heart behind the whole book. All the warnings, all the judgments, all the pleading come from a Father’s love.

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of the last line of verse 12 is uncertain. The ESV reads it as praise of Judah’s faithfulness; some translations read it as a charge that Judah too is wayward toward God.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea 11:12 is 12:1 in Hebrew (ESV note).

11.title: How Can I Give You Up?
11.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 11 closes the book’s second round of sermons (chapters 8 to 11). After three chapters heading for exile, Hosea suddenly lets us hear God’s heart, and the picture changes from the betrayed husband of chapters 1 to 3 to a father remembering his child.

The message. God’s love for his people came first, and it is stronger than their ingratitude. He called his son out of Egypt, taught him to walk, carried and fed him, and the son ran to the Baals; so judgment must come, and Assyria will rule. But God will not give his people up. Because he is “God and not a man, the Holy One in your midst” (v. 9), his compassion overrules the destruction they deserve, and one day his roar will bring his children trembling home.

Why it was said. Israel had been warned of exile chapter after chapter, and the warnings were about to come true (see the introduction). A people facing the end needed to know whether God had finished with them, and the chapter answers: judgment, yes; abandonment, never.

How the chapter makes its case. First the memory of love (vv. 1–4): God called his son out of Egypt, taught him to walk and bent down to feed him, while the more he called, the more they ran to idols. Then the judgment (vv. 5–7): Assyria will be their king. Then the turn (vv. 8–9): God cries, “How can I give you up?”, his heart recoils from making them like Admah and Zeboiim, and he will not come to destroy. Then the promise (vv. 10–11): the LORD roars like a lion, and his children come home like doves. A last line (v. 12) brings us back to the present: Ephraim still surrounds God with lies.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, and by the character of God revealed in him. Matthew saw that Jesus, brought back from Egypt as a child, is the true Son, who lived out Israel’s story without turning away (Matthew 2:15). And the question “How can I give you up?” is finally answered at the cross. God “did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), so that he could be just and still never give up his people.

For us. If you have run from God, this chapter tells you the Father has not stopped calling, and that his holiness, far from shutting you out, is the reason his mercy holds. And if you are trying to love someone who keeps running away, here is the love to lean on and to copy, and the hope that God brings his children home.
11.theology:
God loved his people first, and his love is undeserved and fatherly (vv. 1, 3-4; Exod 4:22-23; Deut 1:31; Ps 103:13).

Jesus is the true Son of God who relived Israel's story and remained faithful where Israel failed (v. 1; Matt 2:15).

God's people rarely realise how much he has carried, healed and fed them, and those who refuse to return to him are carried where they do not want to go (vv. 3-7).

God's holy compassion will not let his people go. He did not give them up, because he gave up his own Son for them (vv. 8-9; Luke 13:34; Rom 8:32).

God's final purpose is to gather his scattered children home (vv. 10-11; Isa 11:11).
11.examples:
The chapter is full of a parent's pictures: a father holding a toddler's hands as he learns to walk, cords of kindness instead of ropes for cattle, and the God of heaven bending down to feed his children.

It ends with a lion's roar that no longer terrifies but calls the children home, and with doves flying back from Egypt and Assyria.

keyVerse.quote: How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender.
keyVerse.note: This is the heart of the chapter and perhaps of the whole book. After all the charges, the Judge cries out that he cannot give his people up, because he is God and not a man. The question is finally answered at the cross, where God gave up his own Son so that he would never have to give up his people.

11.reflection:
God remembers teaching Ephraim to walk, lifting him up and bending down to feed him, and says, “they did not know that I healed them” (vv. 3–4). Where can you look back and see God’s care that you did not notice at the time?

Matthew says Jesus’ return from Egypt fulfilled verse 1 (Matthew 2:15). How does seeing Jesus as the faithful Son, who succeeded where Israel failed, encourage you when you fail?

God says his holiness is the reason he will not destroy Ephraim (v. 9). How does that change the way you think about God’s holiness? How does Romans 8:32 show holiness and mercy meeting at the cross?

Is there someone you love who keeps running away? What does this chapter teach about how God loves the wayward, and how might it shape your patience and your prayers for them?

12.text: <sup>1</sup>Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long; they multiply falsehood and violence; they make a covenant with Assyria, and oil is carried to Egypt.<sup>2</sup>The LORD has an indictment against Judah and will punish Jacob according to his ways; he will repay him according to his deeds.<sup>3</sup>In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God.<sup>4</sup>He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. He met God at Bethel, and there God spoke with us—<sup>5</sup>the LORD, the God of hosts, the LORD is his memorial name:<sup>6</sup>"So you, by the help of your God, return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God."<sup>7</sup>A merchant, in whose hands are false balances, he loves to oppress.<sup>8</sup>Ephraim has said, "Ah, but I am rich; I have found wealth for myself; in all my labors they cannot find in me iniquity or sin."<sup>9</sup>I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast.<sup>10</sup>I spoke to the prophets; it was I who multiplied visions, and through the prophets gave parables.<sup>11</sup>If there is iniquity in Gilead, they shall surely come to nothing: in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; their altars also are like stone heaps on the furrows of the field.<sup>12</sup>Jacob fled to the land of Aram; there Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he guarded sheep.<sup>13</sup>By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt, and by a prophet he was guarded.<sup>14</sup>Ephraim has given bitter provocation; so his Lord will leave his bloodguilt on him and will repay him for his disgraceful deeds.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The God who met and changed Jacob still calls his children back. Ephraim feeds on the wind, piling up lies and violence and courting Assyria and Egypt at once, and the LORD brings a charge against Jacob’s children (vv. 1–2). Hosea holds up their ancestor as a mirror: Jacob grabbed his brother’s heel in the womb, but as a man he wrestled with God, wept and sought his favour, and met him at Bethel, where God spoke to the whole nation (vv. 3–5). So they too, by the help of the same God, are to return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for him (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who met and changed Jacob still calls his descendants to return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait for him.

verseByVerse.quote: Ephraim feeds on the wind and pursues the east wind all day long; they multiply falsehood and violence; they make a covenant with Assyria, and oil is carried to Egypt. The LORD has an indictment against Judah and will punish Jacob according to his ways; he will repay him according to his deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s clever foreign policy is as empty as a meal of wind, and the LORD brings a charge against the whole people of Jacob.

Ephraim feeds on the wind. Imagine filling your stomach with air, and not just any wind but “the east wind”, the scorching desert wind that withered crops. Israel’s policies were exactly that: empty and destructive. They made “a covenant with Assyria” while sending oil, a valuable gift, to Egypt, trying to keep both superpowers happy. It was the same double-dealing that finally ruined King Hoshea (2 Kings 17:4).

Will punish Jacob according to his ways. Jacob here means the whole people, Judah included, and Hosea is about to tell Jacob’s own story as a mirror for them.

verseByVerse.quote: In the womb he took his brother by the heel, and in his manhood he strove with God. He strove with the angel and prevailed; he wept and sought his favor. He met God at Bethel, and there God spoke with us— the LORD, the God of hosts, the LORD is his memorial name: "So you, by the help of your God, return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel’s ancestor Jacob was a grasper whom God met, broke and blessed as he wept and clung to him; his children, by the help of the same God, are to return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait for him.

In the womb he took his brother by the heel. Hosea goes back to the beginning: Jacob, the father of the nation, was a grasper from birth: he came out holding Esau’s heel (Genesis 25:26), and his name sounds like the Hebrew for “heel”. Esau later said, “Is he not rightly named Jacob? For he has cheated me these two times” (Genesis 27:36). His descendants were grasping by deceit just like him.

In his manhood he strove with God. On the night before he met Esau, alone by the river Jabbok, Jacob wrestled all night with a mysterious man and would not let go: “I will not let you go unless you bless me.” And God gave him a new name: “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel, for you have striven with God and with men, and have prevailed” (Genesis 32:26, 28).

He strove with the angel and prevailed. Jacob prevailed by weeping, clinging to God and begging for his blessing. His strength was broken, and in his weakness he received grace.

Who was this wrestler? Genesis calls him a man, Hosea calls him “the angel”, and Jacob said he had seen God face to face (Genesis 32:30). Many Christians, from the early church onward, have seen here the Son of God appearing before he became man, the one who would one day take our flesh and be wounded so that grasping sinners might be blessed. Scripture does not say so outright, so it is best held humbly.

He met God at Bethel. Bethel was where Jacob first saw the stairway to heaven and said, “This is none other than the house of God” (Genesis 28:17), and where God later confirmed his name Israel (Genesis 35:9–10). (The ESV notes that “He met God” is literally “He met him”.) Then Hosea says something remarkable: “there God spoke with us”. What God said to Jacob, he said to all Jacob’s children. Jesus later told Nathanael that he himself is the meeting place between heaven and earth that Jacob glimpsed at Bethel: “you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of Man” (John 1:51).

He wept and sought his favor. Israel had become Jacob the grasper again, but the God who changed Jacob could change them, the same way: weeping, clinging to God and seeking his favour. God does not bless the strong who grasp; he blesses the broken who cling to him.

The LORD is his memorial name. This is the God they deal with: “the LORD, the God of hosts”, commander of heaven’s armies, whose name is the one he gave Moses at the burning bush: “This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations” (Exodus 3:15). The God of Jacob is the same God still.

By the help of your God. Verse 6 gives the life of faith in one sentence, and it is lived “by the help of your God”: they cannot do it in their own strength, any more than Jacob could. For the Christian that help is the Holy Spirit living within, who produces love and faithfulness (Galatians 5:22). By that help they are to return to God, to “hold fast to love and justice”, the loyal love and fair dealing missing in the land (4:1), and to “wait continually for your God” instead of scheming or running to Assyria or Egypt. Waiting is one of the hardest disciplines of faith; Jacob spent his early life grabbing by trickery what God had already promised him. We still hold fast imperfectly, but Christ held fast to love and justice perfectly in our place, and when we fail, the way back is the one Jacob found: to seek God’s favour again (v. 4).

What this looks like. Waiting for God is not doing nothing; it is refusing to grab. Name your Assyria. Notice the shortcut you reach for when anxious: the lie that would close the deal, the pressure that would force a decision, the relationship that would ease the loneliness. Hold fast to love and justice meanwhile. Keep doing the honest, kind thing while the answer is delayed. Tell him you are waiting. “But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me” (Micah 7:7). Put it into words each morning. Remember what he has already given. We have even more reason to wait than Jacob: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32). God is not withholding good from you; he is timing it.

Uncertain wording. Genesis does not say that Jacob wept at the Jabbok, and verse 4 does not name who wept. Most take it, as the ESV does, as Jacob pleading with the angel; some think Hosea is recalling Jacob’s meeting with Esau the next morning, when the brothers wept and Jacob sought his brother’s favour (Genesis 33:4, 8). Either way, the grasper had become a suppliant.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–14 — I Am the LORD Your God from the Land of Egypt
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Prosperity built on dishonesty blinds people to their sin, but God has spoken, and his word will not be ignored. Ephraim is a merchant with false scales who boasts that no one can find sin in him (vv. 7–8). God answers that he is the LORD who brought them out of Egypt, and that he will send them back to tents (v. 9). He has spoken through prophets, visions and parables, yet Gilead is full of iniquity and Gilgal of empty altars (vv. 10–11). Jacob was once a fugitive shepherd, and Israel was rescued and guarded by a prophet (vv. 12–13); Ephraim, having bitterly provoked its Lord, will carry its own guilt (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: Self-satisfied prosperity blinds people to their sin, but God's word through his prophets calls them back.

verseByVerse.quote: A merchant, in whose hands are false balances, he loves to oppress. Ephraim has said, "Ah, but I am rich; I have found wealth for myself; in all my labors they cannot find in me iniquity or sin." I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; I will again make you dwell in tents, as in the days of the appointed feast.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim has become a cheating merchant who thinks his wealth proves his innocence, but the God who brought him out of Egypt will strip him back to tents.

A merchant, in whose hands are false balances. Israel was not holding fast to justice. It was like a crooked merchant with rigged scales, cheating customers and loving it. The Hebrew word for “merchant” is “Canaan”: the people called to be unlike the Canaanites had become one. “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). Jacob the cheater lived on in his children.

Ah, but I am rich. Ephraim takes the credit for his wealth, and adds: “they cannot find in me iniquity or sin”. In other words, “My business is legal; no one can prove I did anything wrong.” Few things blind people to their sin like prosperity. The risen Christ said the same to the church in Laodicea: “For you say, ‘I am rich, I have prospered, and I need nothing,’ not realizing that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked” (Revelation 3:17).

Isn’t being a decent person enough? Ephraim’s defence is the one most of us would make: I have broken no law, and nobody can prove anything against me. Ask people today whether they will be all right with God, and the commonest answer is much the same: I am a good person; I have never really hurt anyone. The trouble is the measure. Ephraim measured himself by what could be proved in court, and false balances are perfectly safe if no inspector checks them. Jesus moved the measure from the scales to the heart, where contempt counts as murder and lust as adultery (Matthew 5:21–28), and by that measure no one is decent enough. There is a deeper problem too. Even when “I am a good person” is true, it becomes the thing I rest on instead of God, a moral bank balance, and it makes me hard on those whose balance looks lower than mine. Respectable people need the gospel as much as rebels do. The good news is not that God marks on a curve, but that Christ, the only truly good man, gives his righteousness to everyone who stops pleading their own.

I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt. God answers the boast by reminding them who he is. Everything they had came from the God who rescued them from slavery, and he would take them back to where they started: “dwell in tents”. Every year at the Feast of Booths, Israel lived in simple shelters for a week to remember that God had brought them through the wilderness (Leviticus 23:42–43). Now the whole nation would lose its houses and live that way again. It was a judgment, but also a chance to start over, as in the wilderness of 2:14.

verseByVerse.quote: I spoke to the prophets; it was I who multiplied visions, and through the prophets gave parables. If there is iniquity in Gilead, they shall surely come to nothing: in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls; their altars also are like stone heaps on the furrows of the field. Jacob fled to the land of Aram; there Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he guarded sheep. By a prophet the LORD brought Israel up from Egypt, and by a prophet he was guarded. Ephraim has given bitter provocation; so his Lord will leave his bloodguilt on him and will repay him for his disgraceful deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God warned Israel through prophet after prophet and saved it by a prophet, so a people who reject his word must carry their own guilt.

I spoke to the prophets. God had spoken through prophet after prophet, with visions and parables, and Hosea’s own marriage was a living parable. Israel could never say it had not been warned.

If there is iniquity in Gilead. Gilead, east of the Jordan, was full of iniquity (6:8); Gilgal, west of the Jordan, was full of false sacrifices (4:15; 9:15). Their altars would become piles of stones, like the heaps a farmer clears from his field. Both names sound like the Hebrew for “heap”, and Gilead was where Jacob had once raised a heap of stones as a witness (Genesis 31:46–48).

Jacob fled to the land of Aram. After cheating Esau, Jacob had to run for his life to Aram, where he worked as a shepherd for years to win Rachel: “So Jacob served seven years for Rachel” (Genesis 29:20). The proud ancestor of the nation began as a fugitive and a hired hand; everything Israel became was by God’s grace.

By a prophet he was guarded. The contrast is deliberate: Jacob “guarded sheep” for a wife (v. 12), but God guarded Israel by a prophet, Moses, who led them out of Egypt and through the wilderness. God saved his people not through their cleverness but through his word, spoken by his prophet.

The Prophet like Moses. Moses had promised that God would raise up “a prophet like me from among you” (Deuteronomy 18:15), and Peter declared that this prophet is Jesus (Acts 3:22). God’s people are still brought out of slavery and guarded on the way home by a Prophet: the Lord Jesus Christ, who is himself God’s final word (Hebrews 1:1–2).

Ephraim has given bitter provocation. Ephraim had ignored the prophets and provoked God bitterly, so their bloodguilt, the guilt of the blood they had shed, would remain on them. Those who refuse the Prophet God sends must carry their own guilt. Those who receive him find their guilt carried away.

Uncertain wording. Verse 11 is obscure. The ESV takes its opening as a condition, “If there is iniquity in Gilead”; it can also be read as a plain statement, that Gilead is iniquity and will come to nothing. Either way, the shrines on both sides of the Jordan would become ruins.
verseByVerse.note: A pun: Gilgal’s altars will become “heaps” (gallim) of stones.

12.title: Return and Wait for Your God
12.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 12 belongs to the book’s third and final round of sermons (11:12 to 14:9), which opens with Ephraim surrounding God with lies. Having heard the Father’s heart in chapter 11, Israel is now made to look in a mirror: the story of its own ancestor, Jacob.

The message. Israel has become Jacob the grasper again: scheming with Assyria and Egypt, cheating with false scales, and proud that no one can prove anything against it. But Jacob’s story also shows the way back. God met the grasper, broke him and blessed him as he wept and clung; so Jacob’s children, by the help of their God, are to “return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God” (v. 6). The God who brought them out of Egypt and guarded them by a prophet is the same God still.

Why it was said. Israel’s kings were playing Assyria against Egypt to survive, and its merchants were growing rich by dishonest dealing (see the introduction). They felt secure and respectable, and could not see their sin.

How the chapter makes its case. First the charge (vv. 1–2): Ephraim feeds on the wind, courting Assyria and Egypt. Then the mirror (vv. 3–6): Jacob grabbed his brother’s heel, yet wrestled with God, wept, sought his favour and met him at Bethel, and his children are called to return the same way. Then the self-portrait (vv. 7–9): a merchant with false balances who boasts that no one can find sin in him, and whom God will send back to tents. Last, the record (vv. 10–14): God spoke by the prophets and saved Israel by a prophet, but Ephraim has provoked him bitterly and will bear its own guilt.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, by promise and by the need it exposes. Jesus told Nathanael that he himself is the meeting place of heaven and earth that Jacob glimpsed at Bethel (John 1:51). The prophet by whom God brought Israel out of Egypt was Moses, and Moses promised a greater prophet like himself (Deuteronomy 18:15), whom Peter names as Jesus (Acts 3:22), who still leads his people home. And Ephraim’s boast, “they cannot find in me iniquity or sin” (v. 8), exposes the need only Christ meets: the one man in whom no sin could be found gives his righteousness to all who stop pleading their own.

For us. Jacob’s children are not saved by being cleverer, richer or more respectable than others, but by the God who meets graspers and makes them new. Stop scheming and justifying yourself. Return to God, hold fast to love and justice, and wait for him, by his help, for he has already given his Son.
12.theology:
Seeking security through worldly alliances is feeding on the wind (v. 1).

God changed Jacob the grasper through wrestling and weeping, and by his help Jacob's children may still return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait for him (vv. 3-6; Gen 32:24-28).

Dishonest gain and self-satisfied wealth blind people to their sin (vv. 7-8; Prov 11:1; Rev 3:17).

God speaks to his people through his prophets, and he saves and guards them by his word, fulfilled in Jesus the Prophet like Moses (vv. 10, 13; Deut 18:15; Acts 3:22).

Those who refuse God's word bear their own guilt, but those who receive his Prophet find it carried away (v. 14).
12.examples:
Hosea paints a nation trying to fill its stomach with the desert wind, and a merchant who says, "No one can prove I did anything wrong."

Behind them he sets Jacob: a baby grabbing his twin's heel, a man who won a wrestling match by weeping, and a shepherd guarding sheep, while God guarded a whole nation by a prophet.

keyVerse.quote: So you, by the help of your God, return, hold fast to love and justice, and wait continually for your God.
keyVerse.note: Set between Jacob’s story and Ephraim’s boast, this verse is the call the whole chapter makes. It sums up the life of faith: returning to God, holding fast to loyal love and fair dealing, and waiting for him instead of grabbing. And it is all “by the help of your God”, the help Jacob found when he wept and clung, and that Christ’s people find in his Spirit.

12.reflection:
Hosea holds up Jacob as a mirror for Israel (vv. 3–4). Where do you see the grasper in yourself, reaching by scheming or pressure for what God has promised to give?

Jacob prevailed by weeping and clinging, not by strength (v. 4). What does it look like in practice to cling to God and seek his favour when you are struggling?

Ephraim said, “they cannot find in me iniquity or sin” (v. 8). Why are prosperity and respectability so blinding? How does the gospel answer the belief that being a decent person is enough?

Verse 6 calls God’s people to return, to hold fast to love and justice, and to wait continually for God. Which of these is hardest for you right now, and how does “the help of your God” make it possible?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Besides Me There Is No Savior
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim’s idols cannot save it, and the God it forgot is the only Saviour it ever had. The tribe that once made others tremble died when it turned to Baal, and instead of repenting it made more idols and kissed metal calves, so it will vanish like mist, dew, chaff and smoke (vv. 1–3). Against all that vanishes stands the LORD, their God since Egypt, who cared for them in the desert; but when they had eaten their fill they grew proud and forgot him (vv. 4–6). So the God who shepherded them will meet them like a lion, a leopard and a bear robbed of her cubs, because they have turned against their only helper (vv. 7–9).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no saviour but the LORD, and those who forget him in their fullness meet him as judge.

verseByVerse.quote: When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling; he was exalted in Israel, but he incurred guilt through Baal and died. And now they sin more and more, and make for themselves metal images, idols skillfully made of their silver, all of them the work of craftsmen. It is said of them, "Those who offer human sacrifice kiss calves!" Therefore they shall be like the morning mist or like the dew that goes early away, like the chaff that swirls from the threshing floor or like smoke from a window.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ephraim, once the proudest tribe in Israel, died when it turned to Baal, and a people who live for things that vanish will vanish with them.

When Ephraim spoke, there was trembling. Ephraim, the tribe of Jeroboam, the north’s first king (1 Kings 11:26), led the north, and when it spoke, others trembled. But when it turned to Baal it “died”: it prospered for years, yet before God it was already dead. Sin kills before it buries.

They sin more and more. Instead of repenting, they made more idols of their own silver, still only “the work of craftsmen” (8:6). Kissing an idol was an act of worship (1 Kings 19:18), and the ESV’s reading of the saying fits what Kings records of the north, whose people “burned their sons and their daughters as offerings” (2 Kings 17:17). The contrast is grotesque: love for a statue, cruelty to children.

Like the morning mist. Four pictures of things that vanish: mist and dew when the sun rises, chaff blown from the threshing floor, smoke drifting out of a window. In 6:4 Israel’s love was “like the dew that goes early away”; now Israel itself will be. Those who live for what does not last will not last either.

Kiss the Son. The homage Israel gave a metal calf belongs to God’s anointed King: “Kiss the Son” (Psalm 2:12), who demands no children in sacrifice but gave himself for us.

Uncertain wording. In verse 1 “trembling” translates a rare word: others trembled when Ephraim spoke (ESV), or Ephraim once spoke humbly, with trembling, and was exalted. In verse 2 the Hebrew is literally “sacrificers of man”: “those who offer human sacrifice” (ESV, likely, given 2 Kings 17:17) or simply “men who sacrifice”. Either way, people kiss metal calves.

verseByVerse.quote: But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; you know no God but me, and besides me there is no savior. It was I who knew you in the wilderness, in the land of drought; but when they had grazed, they became full, they were filled, and their heart was lifted up; therefore they forgot me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD alone saved Israel and cared for it in the desert, but when it was full it grew proud and forgot him.

But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt. Against all the vanishing things stands the God who brought them out of Egypt. No other god had any right to them, and “besides me there is no savior”: not Baal, not Assyria, not money or armies. (Compare Isaiah 43:11.)

It was I who knew you in the wilderness. God knew them, cared for them personally, in “the land of drought”, where they had nothing and he gave them manna, water and protection.

Therefore they forgot me. Here is the pattern of spiritual decline. In need, they depended on God; when they “had grazed” (literally “according to their pasture”, the ESV notes, like cattle growing fat), they were full, “their heart was lifted up”, and “therefore they forgot me”. Moses had warned of exactly this: “lest, when you have eaten and are full ... then your heart be lifted up, and you forget the LORD your God” (Deuteronomy 8:12, 14). Hard times are dangerous. Good times may be more dangerous still.

The only Saviour has come. The New Testament applies this exclusive claim to Jesus: “there is salvation in no one else” (Acts 4:12). And he walked the opposite road to Israel’s. Israel was fed in the wilderness and forgot God; Jesus, hungry in the wilderness, answered the tempter from Moses’ same warning: “Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4; Deuteronomy 8:3). And though he was rich, he became poor for our sake, that we might become rich (2 Corinthians 8:9).

Unbelief by drift. We often picture people leaving God after a crisis of faith. Hosea describes the commoner road: nobody in verse 6 decides that God is not real; they are simply full. As societies grow richer and safer, belief tends to thin, not because affluence has disproved anything but because comfort makes God feel unnecessary. When the hospital, the pension and the supermarket answer most of our prayers before we pray them, God slides to the edge of life, kept for weddings and funerals, and the drift never announces itself. The answer is not to wish for hardship but to see what fullness hides: the comfortable person is still dust, still guilty and still sought by a God who knows him by name.

Thanks at a full table. Moses also gave the remedy: “you shall eat and be full, and you shall bless the LORD your God for the good land he has given you” (Deuteronomy 8:10). Deliberately thanking God for each full table and each good season keeps fullness from turning into forgetfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: So I am to them like a lion; like a leopard I will lurk beside the way. I will fall upon them like a bear robbed of her cubs; I will tear open their breast, and there I will devour them like a lion, as a wild beast would rip them open. He destroys you, O Israel, for you are against me, against your helper.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God who shepherded Israel will now come against it like a wild beast, because it has turned against the only one who could help it.

Like a bear robbed of her cubs. The God who fed them like a shepherd now comes against them like the beasts that attack a flock: a lion, a leopard lying in wait, and most terrifying of all, “a bear robbed of her cubs” (compare Proverbs 17:12). Those who grew fat in his pasture (v. 6) are now the prey. God’s love is not soft towards sin.

Against your helper. The tragic irony: Israel is destroyed because it turned “against your helper”. The one who could help them was the one they opposed. Yet when Hosea first used the lion, God added, “until they acknowledge their guilt and seek my face” (5:15). Even the lion’s attack aims at their return.

The Lion and the Lamb. In Christ the Lion of the tribe of Judah is also the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 5:5–6), and the blow his scattered flock deserved fell on the Shepherd himself (Zechariah 13:7; Matthew 26:31).

Uncertain wording. Verse 9 is compressed Hebrew. The ESV reads “He destroys you”, noting “I will destroy you”; others read “your ruin is your own doing”. Every reading lands in one place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — I Shall Ransom Them from the Power of Sheol
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No king can save Israel from death, but God can, and one day will. The kings Israel demanded are gone, given in anger and taken away in wrath (vv. 10–11). Ephraim’s sins are stored up for judgment, and in the hour of crisis he is like a child who will not be born (vv. 12–13). Then comes the chapter’s great surprise: God speaks of ransoming his people from Sheol and taunts Death to bring out its plagues and its sting (v. 14), words Paul sings over Christ’s resurrection. Yet for Samaria judgment must come first: the east wind of the LORD will dry up its springs and strip its treasures, and the city will fall to the sword (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology: Only God can deliver from death, and in Christ he has taken away death's sting.

verseByVerse.quote: Where now is your king, to save you in all your cities? Where are all your rulers— those of whom you said, "Give me a king and princes"? I gave you a king in my anger, and I took him away in my wrath. The iniquity of Ephraim is bound up; his sin is kept in store. The pangs of childbirth come for him, but he is an unwise son, for at the right time he does not present himself at the opening of the womb.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kings Israel demanded cannot save it, its sins are stored up for judgment, and at the very hour it could be born into new life it refuses to come.

Where now is your king? Israel’s last king, Hoshea, was seized by Assyria before Samaria fell (2 Kings 17:4): where was he when they needed saving? The demand “Give me a king and princes” recalls the day Israel asked Samuel for a king, and God told him, “they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them” (1 Samuel 8:7).

I gave you a king in my anger. This may refer to Saul, given when Israel rejected God’s rule and later removed, or to the whole line of northern kings, who came and went in God’s judgment. Either way, God gave them what they insisted on, and it did not save them. Sometimes the worst thing God can do is give people what they demand.

His sin is kept in store. Ephraim’s sins are not forgotten. They are wrapped up and stored away, like documents kept for a trial. Every unforgiven sin is kept for the day of reckoning.

The pangs of childbirth come for him. The labour pains have begun, but the baby will not come out, and both mother and child are in mortal danger. Israel was at the moment when it should have come out into new life by repenting, and it refused to move. Every crisis God sends is a summons to turn to him while there is time (2 Corinthians 6:2).

The King who saves. No king Israel demanded could save it, so God gave his own, “David their king” (3:5), not in anger but in love, a King who laid down his life instead of taking theirs. And for all who trust him, the sins kept in store were laid on him (Isaiah 53:6).

verseByVerse.quote: I shall ransom them from the power of Sheol; I shall redeem them from Death. O Death, where are your plagues? O Sheol, where is your sting? Compassion is hidden from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will ransom his people from death itself and taunt it in its defeat, a promise Paul sings over Christ’s resurrection. It is famous and much debated (see the boxes at the end of this note).

The power of Sheol. Sheol is the Old Testament word for the grave, the realm of the dead. To “ransom” and “redeem” is to pay a price to set someone free.

O Death, where are your plagues? God taunts Death and Sheol like defeated enemies. On this reading, “Compassion is hidden from my eyes” means that God will not pity death, or will not change his mind about this promise.

O Sheol, where is your sting? The apostle Paul shows what this verse means for Christians. In his great chapter on the resurrection he quotes it as a shout of victory: “‘O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?’ The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). Paul writes “victory” where Hosea has “plagues”, because he quotes freely, joining Hosea to Isaiah 25:8, which he has just cited: “Death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54). Whatever judgment Israel faced in Hosea’s day, God’s final answer is resurrection.

How the two readings come together. Death does have a sting, and its sting is sin. Israel deserved death, and so do we. But God himself paid the ransom. Christ, the true Israel, went down into death bearing the sting of sin, “that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death” (Hebrews 2:14). For those who belong to him, death is still an enemy, “the last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26), and we still weep at its coming, but not “as others do who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). We can stand at a grave, with tears, and ask, “O Death, where are your plagues?”

Isn’t death just part of life? So we have learned to say: death is natural, and the mature thing is to accept it. But hardly anyone believes it at a graveside. We do not grieve over autumn leaves; we grieve over something that should not have happened, and our tears are more honest than our philosophy. Hosea and Paul take the side of the tears. Death has plagues and a sting; it is an intruder, the wages of sin. That sounds bleaker than the modern view, but it is the only view with hope in it. If death is natural, there is nothing to be rescued from. If death is an enemy, it can be defeated, and the gospel says it has been, by the one who walked into it on our behalf and walked out again on the third day. A Christian at a funeral does not say that death is fine. He says that death is finished.

Where Christians differ. The ESV notes that the first two lines may be translated as questions: “Shall I ransom them from the power of Sheol? Shall I redeem them from Death?” Read that way, the verse is a threat: God will not rescue Israel, he calls on Death and Sheol to bring on their plagues and sting, and he will not relent. Many think this fits the judgment all around it (vv. 13, 15–16). Others, with the ESV text, read a promise: God interrupts the judgment to announce that he will conquer death itself.

This commentary’s view. This commentary takes the reading as a promise to be the more likely, though careful interpreters differ: God often breaks into Hosea’s warnings with mercy (11:8–9; 14:4), and Paul hears this verse exactly so.

Uncertain wording. The little word translated “where” (as in v. 10) is unusual. The King James Version took it as “I will be”: “O death, I will be thy plagues”, God himself death’s destroyer. The ancient Greek translation, which Paul follows, read “where”, as do most modern versions. “Sting” usually means destruction or pestilence (Psalm 91:6), and “compassion” translates a word found nowhere else in the Old Testament, perhaps pity or a change of mind.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes this in his great resurrection chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Though he may flourish among his brothers, the east wind, the wind of the LORD, shall come, rising from the wilderness, and his fountain shall dry up; his spring shall be parched; it shall strip his treasury of every precious thing. Samaria shall bear her guilt, because she has rebelled against her God; they shall fall by the sword; their little ones shall be dashed in pieces, and their pregnant women ripped open.
verseByVerse.commentary:
However fruitful Ephraim seems, the LORD’s east wind is coming to dry up its life and strip its wealth, and Samaria will fall in the full horror of war.

The east wind, the wind of the LORD. “Flourish” plays on Ephraim’s name, which Joseph gave him because “God has made me fruitful” (Genesis 41:52). But the scorching desert wind would come, and it is “the wind of the LORD”: Assyria, coming from the east, was his instrument. Every spring would dry up, and every treasure would be carried away.

Samaria shall bear her guilt. (The ESV notes that in the Hebrew Bible this verse is numbered 14:1.) The chapter ends with the horrors of ancient warfare. Invading armies really did such things (2 Kings 8:12), as had Israel’s own king Menahem (2 Kings 15:16). Samaria would “bear her guilt” “because she has rebelled against her God”.

Does God approve of such cruelty? No. He names what the invader will do, but he later judged Assyria for its savagery (Isaiah 10:5–12; Nahum 3:1–7), and the Judge of all the earth will do right by every little one (Genesis 18:25). It is painful, and we should not soften it. Rebellion against God has terrible consequences, which often fall on the innocent too.

Not the last word. The book does not end here. The next words are among the most hopeful in Hosea: “Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God” (14:1). The God who named the full horror of judgment still invites his people home. Jesus wept over a city that would suffer the same (Luke 19:41–44), then went to the cross to ransom his people from death.
verseByVerse.note: Hosea 13:16 is 14:1 in Hebrew (ESV note).

13.title: O Death, Where Are Your Plagues?
13.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 13 is the last sermon in the book’s third round (11:12 to 14:9), and its darkest. After Jacob held up as a mirror in chapter 12, Hosea traces Ephraim’s story from greatness to the grave, before the final call to return (14).

The message. Israel is already dead, and only the LORD can raise the dead. Ephraim turned from the only Saviour it ever had to Baal, to metal calves and to kings, and none of them can save it; when it was full it forgot him, so the God who fed it will meet it like a wild beast. Yet in the middle of the death sentence God speaks of ransoming his people from Sheol itself: death will not have the last word.

Why it was said. These are Samaria’s last years: kings murdered, tribute paid and withheld, Assyria closing in, the last king seized before the city fell in 722 BC (see the introduction). The people still sacrificed and could not believe it would end.

How the chapter makes its case. Ephraim, once feared, died through Baal, and its sin has only grown, so it will vanish like mist, dew, chaff and smoke (vv. 1–3). Against the vanishing things stands the LORD, their only Saviour since Egypt, who knew them in the desert; but when they were full they forgot him (vv. 4–6). So the Shepherd becomes lion, leopard and bear (vv. 7–9). The kings they demanded cannot save them (vv. 10–11); their sin is stored up, and in the hour of labour they are a child who will not be born (vv. 12–13). Then God speaks of ransom from death and taunts Death itself (v. 14), before the east wind dries up Ephraim’s spring and Samaria falls by the sword (vv. 15–16).

Where it leads. To Christ by the need it exposes and by promise. No king could save Israel: “besides me there is no savior” (v. 4), and that only Saviour came in Jesus (Acts 4:12). Verse 14 is the promise, and Paul sings it over the empty tomb (1 Corinthians 15:55–57), because Christ went down into death bearing the sin that is its sting and came out holding “the keys of Death and Hades” (Revelation 1:18). Israel was the child who would not be born; Christ is “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18).

For us. Comfort makes it easy to forget the God who gave it. Ask what you trust to save you, and turn to the only Saviour while there is time. And at every graveside, those who belong to Christ may grieve with hope, for death has been ransomed and robbed of its sting.
13.theology:
Turning to idols brings spiritual death even while outward life goes on, and those who live for what vanishes will vanish with it (vv. 1-3).

There is no saviour but the LORD, who has come in Jesus Christ (v. 4; Isa 43:11; Acts 4:12). Fullness can make his people forget him, and then the Shepherd meets them as judge (vv. 5-9; Deut 8:12-14).

God may give people the kings they demand, and those kings cannot save (vv. 10-11; 1 Sam 8:7).

Death's sting is sin, but God has ransomed his people from death through the death and resurrection of Christ (v. 14; 1 Cor 15:55-57; Heb 2:14-15; 2 Tim 1:10).
13.examples:
The images are stark: a tribe dead long before it was buried, people who kiss a metal calf and sacrifice their children, and a baby who will not be born when the time comes.

The last picture is of a Christian at a graveside, grieving yet able to ask, "O Death, where is your sting?"

keyVerse.quote: But I am the LORD your God from the land of Egypt; you know no God but me, and besides me there is no savior.
keyVerse.note: Everything else in this chapter vanishes or fails: Baal, the calves, the kings, Ephraim’s own strength. This verse names the one Saviour left standing, the God who brought Israel out of Egypt, and verse 14 shows how far his saving reaches, even into death. The New Testament says that Saviour has come in Jesus, and there is salvation in no one else (Acts 4:12).

13.reflection:
Verse 6 traces Israel’s forgetting of God not to doubt but to being full. Where have comfort or success made God feel less necessary to you, and what habits help you remember him when life is going well?

Israel looked to Baal, metal calves and kings, and none of them could save (vv. 1–2, 10–11). What do people around you look to for rescue, and what do you reach for first when trouble comes?

God describes himself as the one who knew Israel in the wilderness and as a lion and a bear (vv. 5–8). Why do we need to know both sides of God, and how does the cross hold them together?

Paul turns verse 14 into a song of victory (1 Corinthians 15:55–57). How should Christ’s resurrection shape the way we grieve, face our own death and speak at a funeral?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Repentance is coming home to God with honest words, renouncing every false saviour and trusting his mercy. Hosea calls Israel back one last time to the LORD who is still its God, naming the cause of its fall plainly: its own iniquity (v. 1). God even supplies the prayer: ask him to take away all iniquity and accept what is good, and offer him what the lips have vowed (v. 2). True repentance names its idols, so the prayer renounces the three false saviours Hosea has exposed throughout the book, foreign alliances, military power and handmade gods, and rests on the God in whom the orphan finds mercy (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: True repentance brings honest words of confession, renounces every false saviour and trusts God's mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: Return, O Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled because of your iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even after all its unfaithfulness Israel may still come home, for the LORD is still its God, and its fall is its own doing.

Return, O Israel. Israel had refused to return (5:4; 7:10; 11:5); now the call comes once more. The word runs through the chapter: Israel is to return (vv. 1–2), God’s anger has turned (v. 4), and the people shall return to his shade (v. 7); even “apostasy” (v. 4) comes from the same root, a turning away.

For you have stumbled because of your iniquity. He is still “the LORD your God”: the relationship is not beyond repair. And the problem is named honestly: they fell not by bad luck or enemies but by their own sin. Returning always begins with owning that.

A person, not a programme. We often hear repentance as a self-improvement plan: feel bad enough, tidy up, and perhaps God will have you back. But you return to a person, and we hang back because we want to arrive already clean. God puts the order the other way round: “return to me, for I have redeemed you” (Isaiah 44:22). The price comes first, and in Christ it has been paid in full; so Peter can write, “you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (1 Peter 2:25). When you have drifted, do not wait until you feel worthy: take words (v. 2) and name the thing to him plainly, today. See Repentance.

verseByVerse.quote: Take with you words and return to the LORD; say to him, "Take away all iniquity; accept what is good, and we will pay with bulls the vows of our lips. Assyria shall not save us; we will not ride on horses; and we will say no more, 'Our God,' to the work of our hands. In you the orphan finds mercy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his people the very words of repentance: a prayer that asks him to take all sin away, renounces every false saviour and casts itself on his mercy.

Take with you words. Israel had brought God plenty of animals; now he asks for honest words, and supplies them. That is grace: he not only invites us back, he teaches us how to pray.

Take away all iniquity. Not some of it, all of it, and only God can do that. “Accept what is good”: receive us graciously. Then they promise to pay “the vows of our lips” (see the box below).

Assyria shall not save us. True repentance names and renounces its idols, here the three false saviours Hosea has exposed throughout the book: political alliances (“Assyria shall not save us”), military power (“we will not ride on horses”) and handmade gods (“we will say no more, ‘Our God,’ to the work of our hands”). Ours may be savings, reputation or competence.

In you the orphan finds mercy. An orphan has no one to protect or provide, and Israel comes to God just so, helpless and with nothing to offer. “Mercy” takes us back to the little girl named No Mercy (1:6). Those who were No Mercy find mercy in God.

The Father who runs. Jesus told of a son who rehearsed his confession on the road home, but “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20). That is the God of this chapter, and so every sinner comes: with words, empty hands and no other saviour.

Uncertain wording. “We will pay with bulls the vows of our lips” is compressed Hebrew, literally something like “we will pay bulls, our lips”. The ESV notes that the ancient Greek and Syriac translations read “pay the fruit of our lips”; on that reading the offering is now praise. Hebrews uses the same idea: “a sacrifice of praise to God, that is, the fruit of lips that acknowledge his name” (Hebrews 13:15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — I Will Be Like the Dew to Israel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers repentance with free, healing love, and all his people’s life and fruit come from him. He promises to heal their turning away and to love them freely, for his anger has turned from them (v. 4). Then he pictures the result: he will be like the dew to Israel, and the nation will blossom like the lily, take root like the cedars of Lebanon, grow beautiful as the olive and dwell in his shade, enjoying the grain and wine it once sought from Baal (vv. 5–7). God has nothing to do with idols; he answers and cares for Ephraim, an evergreen from whom all its fruit comes (v. 8). The book closes by calling the wise to walk in the LORD’s right ways (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers repentance with free, healing love, and all his people's fruitfulness comes from him.

verseByVerse.quote: I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers repentance by curing the heart that wanders and loving his people freely, because his anger has turned away.

I will heal their apostasy. God’s answer is overwhelming. Their apostasy, their constant turning away, is a sickness he will heal: he does not only forgive past wandering, he cures the heart that wanders. Assyria could not heal them (5:13); the God they wounded will.

I will love them freely. It may be the book’s best summary. God’s love is free: not earned, deserved or paid for, but given out of his own heart. In 9:15 God had said, “I will love them no more”. Now he says, “I will love them freely”. Nothing in Israel had changed to make them lovable; the change came from God. “He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy” (Titus 3:5).

My anger has turned from them. God’s anger was real, but it has turned away. How can a holy God turn his anger from sinners? The New Testament answers: it fell on Christ, who bore it in our place (Romans 3:25). The anger that should have fallen on the unfaithful bride fell on the faithful Bridegroom, and nothing is left for her but love.

What it does not mean. Free love is not cheap love. God heals apostasy; he does not bless it, and the love that would not let Israel go also disciplined it through exile (Hebrews 12:6).

verseByVerse.quote: I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon; his shoots shall spread out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon. They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God himself will be his restored people’s life, like dew in a dry land, and they will flourish in beauty, strength and fruit.

I will be like the dew to Israel. In 6:4 Israel’s love was “like the dew that goes early away”, and in 13:3 Israel itself would vanish like dew. Now God says, “I will be like the dew to Israel”. Through the rainless summer, heavy dew kept plants alive. Israel’s love was passing dew; God’s is faithful dew.

He shall blossom like the lily. Israel will be like the quick-blooming lily, the deep-rooted cedars of Lebanon and the long-lived olive, with the fragrance of Lebanon’s forests. The land cursed with drought and thorns (2:12; 9:6; 10:8) is now a garden.

They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow. In 4:13 the people worshipped idols under oaks “because their shade is good”. Now they find real shade in God: “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). (The ESV notes that “my shadow” is literally “his shadow”.) The grain and wine they once credited to Baal (2:8), God now gives freely.

Fulfilled in Christ. Peter hears Hosea’s promise of mercy kept as the gospel gathers a people: “once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy” (1 Peter 2:10). Rooted in Christ, they flourish now, and the garden is completed in the new creation (Revelation 22:1–2).

Where Christians differ. Some, especially dispensationalists, expect these promises to be fulfilled in a future restoration of the nation of Israel in its land; others see them fulfilled in Christ and his church.

This commentary’s view. The New Testament reads such promises as fulfilled in Christ and the one people of God, Jew and Gentile together (Romans 9:25–26), now in part and fully in the new creation; Romans 11 most naturally also looks for a future turning of many Jewish people to Christ within that one people.

verseByVerse.quote: O Ephraim, what have I to do with idols? It is I who answer and look after you. I am like an evergreen cypress; from me comes your fruit. Whoever is wise, let him understand these things; whoever is discerning, let him know them; for the ways of the LORD are right, and the upright walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, not the idols, answers his people and makes them fruitful, and the wise will walk in his right ways.

O Ephraim, what have I to do with idols? Nothing. God will not share his people with idols. “It is I who answer and look after you.” (The ESV notes that “you” is literally “him”.) Baal never answered. God does (2:21).

I am like an evergreen cypress. Nowhere else in the Old Testament does God compare himself to a tree. The Baal cult used sacred trees; God says, in effect, “I am the true evergreen, always alive, never withering.”

From me comes your fruit. Jesus said the same about himself: “As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me” (John 15:4). Christian fruitfulness is never our own achievement; it comes from union with Christ, as his Spirit bears his fruit in us (Galatians 5:22).

Whoever is wise, let him understand. The book ends with a call to each reader, in the voice of the wisdom books (compare Psalm 107:43), speaking past Hosea’s first hearers to all who would read him later, Judah first. The same ways of the LORD lead to two results: the upright walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them, as Israel had stumbled (v. 1). It is the choice of Psalm 1 (Psalm 1:6). Peter says the same of Christ: precious to believers, but to those who do not believe, “A stone of stumbling, and a rock of offense” (1 Peter 2:8).

The gospel’s invitation. So Hosea ends with the gospel’s own invitation. God has loved an unfaithful people with a love that will not let them go, paid the price to buy them back, and promised to heal them and love them freely. The question left for the wise reader is simple: will you return to the LORD your God?

Uncertain wording. The Hebrew of verse 8 does not mark who speaks its first line. The ESV, with most modern versions, gives it to God; the King James Version supplied “Ephraim shall say”, and some read the verse as a dialogue. Either way, the idols are renounced and God is the source of all fruit.

14.title: I Will Love Them Freely
14.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 14 closes the book. After its darkest chapter, ending in Samaria’s fall (13:16), Hosea’s third round of sermons ends as each round has, with hope, and this time with God’s last word to his people.

The message. God calls his unfaithful people home and even gives them the words to say. When they come, owning their sin and renouncing every false saviour, he answers with healing and free love: “I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely” (v. 4). He will be to them like dew in a dry land, and all their fruit will come from him.

Why it was said. Israel had spent its history running to Assyria, horses and idols, and exile was at the door (see the introduction). This chapter told those going into it, and Judah after them, that the way home was still open, and how to come.

How the chapter makes its case. First the call: return, for your own iniquity has tripped you (v. 1); take words, ask God to take away all iniquity, renounce Assyria, horses and idols, and come as an orphan who finds mercy (vv. 2–3). Then God’s answer: he will heal, love freely and turn his anger away (v. 4), and be like the dew, so that Israel blossoms like the lily, takes root like Lebanon and lives in his shade (vv. 5–7). Last, God himself, the evergreen, is the source of their fruit (v. 8), and the book closes with a word to the wise: the LORD’s ways are right, and everything depends on how we walk in them (v. 9).

Where it leads. To Christ by God’s character revealed in him, and by promise. The God who gives the wanderer words to say is the Father in Jesus’ parable, who runs to meet his son before the speech is finished (Luke 15:20–22). The free love of verse 4 turns God’s anger away by bearing it in his Son, “the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 4:10). The evergreen from whom all fruit comes is the vine of John 15, and the promise of mercy to No Mercy is kept as the gospel gathers Jews and Gentiles into one people (Romans 9:25–26; 1 Peter 2:10).

For us. You do not have to clean yourself up before you come home; God gives you the words. Name your false saviours, ask him to take away all your iniquity, and come with empty hands. He loves freely, and everything fruitful in your life will grow from him.
14.theology:
God calls sinners to return and even gives them the words. True repentance owns its iniquity, asks God to take it all away, renounces every false saviour and offers the praise of its lips, and helpless sinners find mercy (vv. 1-3; 1:6; Heb 13:15).

God heals the wandering heart and loves his people freely, turning his anger away, as he does in Christ (v. 4; Titus 3:4-5).

God's faithful love makes his people flourish, and their fruit comes from union with him (vv. 5-8; Ps 91:1; John 15:4).

The ways of the LORD are right; the wise walk in them, but transgressors stumble (v. 9; Ps 1:6; 1 Pet 2:7-8).
14.examples:
A people bring words instead of more sacrifices, give up their three false saviours of alliances, armies and idols, and come like orphans who find mercy.

God answers as dew that does not go away, turning a dry land into a garden of lilies, cedars and olives, and offers himself as an evergreen tree.

keyVerse.quote: I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.
keyVerse.note: This is God’s answer to the whole book and its best summary. The people who kept turning away will be healed of their turning, and loved not because they have earned it but freely, out of God’s own heart. In Christ we see how his anger could turn away: it fell on the Son, so that nothing is left for his people but love.

14.reflection:
God tells Israel to “take with you words” and even supplies them (v. 2). Why is it hard to name our sin plainly to God, and how does it help to know that he gives us the words?

Israel renounced Assyria, horses and handmade gods (v. 3). What are the false saviours of our own day, and which one are you most tempted to lean on?

“I will love them freely” (v. 4). How does free, undeserved love differ from the love we often expect from God? How does the cross show that it is not cheap love?

God says, “from me comes your fruit” (v. 8), and Jesus says, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). What would it look like this week to abide in Christ rather than try to produce fruit on your own?
